#5551. CommonSpirit Health logs $544M operating loss to begin its FY2027

CommonSpirit Health logs $544M operating loss to begin its FY2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

CommonSpirit Health kicked off its 2027 fiscal year with a $544 million operating loss as decreasing acuity, dampening payer mix and other expenses outpaced the large nonprofit’s strong volumes and improving operating efficiency, according to financial results for the quarter ended Sept. 30.

That operating loss excludes $65 million non-routine special charges incurred by the health system—most notably severance costs and other fees tied to its strategic, multi-billion-dollar decision to end a long-term revenue cycle contract with Tenet Healthcare—during the quarter, and reflect a -5.3% operating margin. The system had reported a $396 million operating loss and -4% margin during the same period a year prior.

Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) was $77 million in the quarter, also a dip from the prior year’s $129 million.

“Our first-quarter performance reflects steady operational progress, even amid persistent cost and reimbursement headwinds, as patients continue to choose CommonSpirit for quality care,” Chief Financial Officer Michael P. Browning said in a release.

CommonSpirit, already one of the country’s largest health systems, said it grew its quarterly operating revenue 5.3% year over year to $10.3 billion. The uptick included a 2.8% year-over-year increase in adjusted admissions as well as $165 million in net income from the California provider fee program, as opposed to no such benefit recorded the year prior. At the same time, the organization said its revenues were affected by “revenue yield challenges” and increases in self-pay, Medicare and Medicaid among its payer mix—both issues cited in recent financial reports from other major health systems.

Meanwhile, CommonSpirit’s operating expenses (before special charges) rose 6.6% year over year to nearly $10.9 billion. Much of the increase was tied to higher volumes as well as salary inflation, the latter of which came even as the organization improved its labor productivity (hospital full-time equivalents per adjusted admission decreased by 1.4%) and cut down its contract labor spend.

CommonSpirit’s results also included $115 million of net nonoperating income, substantially less than the year before due to “market fluctuations” affecting its investment returns. That left a bottom-line net loss of $496 million for the quarter and, as of Sept. 30, 160 days of cash on hand.

Management, in the filing and an accompanying press release, noted that the quarter’s numbers land as the system continues to execute on a sweeping operating performance improvement plan. That effort includes work to boost volumes through a focus on its care network, revenue realization efforts surrounding denials and managed care negotiations, standardizing department staffing models to trim labor costs and potential service line rationalization “for those markets where performance is currently below requirements.”

“We are making deliberate, near-term investments to unify our electronic health record, enterprise resource planning and revenue cycle platforms, while advancing responsible AI adoption to strengthen our system for the long term,” Browning said. “Keeping patients at the center of everything we do requires disciplined expense management and fair, timely reimbursement for the care we deliver.”

“Financial sustainability is what makes our mission possible,” added President and CEO Wright Lassiter III in the release. “Through disciplined operations, we are supporting our team members, strengthening our ministry and protecting access to compassionate, high-quality care across the communities we serve.”

CommonSpirit Health comprises about 2,600 care sites, including 132 hospitals, and more than 160,000 employees across 24 states. In the most recent fiscal year ended June 30, it reported $42.4 billion in total operating revenue and a $430 million operating loss (-1% operating margin) before special charges, an improvement from the prior fiscal year.

#5550. A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes

Researchers have identified a protein that may play an important role in Type 2 diabetes by interfering with the body's ability to respond to insulin. The discovery could provide a promising new target for treatments designed to improve blood sugar control.

The protein, known as Miro1, was found at higher levels in the skeletal muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes. In preclinical experiments, scientists discovered that removing Miro1 restored the muscles' response to insulin. They also found that exercise lowered Miro1 levels in people with the disease, offering new insight into how physical activity improves insulin sensitivity.

The findings were published in Nature Communications and could help researchers better understand the biological processes behind insulin resistance, a central feature of Type 2 diabetes.

How a Hidden Muscle Protein Affects Insulin Resistance

Miro1 (Mitochondrial Rho GTPase1) is located on the outer membrane of mitochondria, the tiny structures inside cells responsible for producing energy. Researchers believe that excessive amounts of this protein may interfere with how muscles respond to insulin, making it more difficult for the body to regulate blood sugar effectively.

To investigate this connection, the research team studied Miro1 in laboratory cells, preclinical models, and people living with Type 2 diabetes. By examining the protein across these different settings, they were able to explore its effects on muscle function and determine whether the findings could be relevant to human disease.

The results showed that Miro1 buildup impaired the muscles' response to insulin. When researchers removed the protein in preclinical models, insulin responsiveness returned, providing evidence that Miro1 contributes directly to this process.

Exercise Reduces a Protein Linked to Type 2 Diabetes

The researchers also investigated whether exercise could influence Miro1 levels in people with diabetes. In a randomized controlled trial involving participants with obesity and Type 2 diabetes, they compared the effects of aerobic exercise with those of standard medical care.

People assigned to the exercise group experienced a decline in Miro1 levels in their muscles. These changes occurred alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity and the muscles' capacity to produce energy.

The findings suggest that reducing Miro1 may be one of the ways exercise helps the body respond more effectively to insulin. They also raise the possibility that treatments designed to target the protein could eventually provide additional benefits alongside physical activity.

"Insulin resistance in muscle is at the heart of Type 2 diabetes, and its molecular causes have remained frustratingly unclear. This study, the product of years of work, identifies Miro1 as a key part of the answer. By tracing Miro1 from cells to preclinical models to patients, we show that Miro1 accumulation impairs the muscle's response to insulin, that removing it causally restores that response in our models, and that exercise reverses its buildup in people. For the field, this is a new therapeutic target. For patients, it deepens our understanding of why exercise is so effective and opens a path toward treatments that could one day complement it," said Dr. John P. Kirwan, the study's senior author.

A Promising New Direction for Diabetes Treatment

Kirwan recently became executive director of the OU Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center at the University of Oklahoma. He carried out the research while working at LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and has since brought his internationally recognized translational research program to the University of Oklahoma.

He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the university and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.

The study's first author, Elizabeth Heintz, is a doctoral candidate who worked in the Integrated Physiology and Molecular Medicine Laboratory at Pennington Biomedical. Christopher Axelrod, the study's co-corresponding author, has also moved to the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center, joining Kirwan in continuing this line of research.

Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical, emphasized the importance of connecting laboratory discoveries with research involving patients and broader populations.

"This research exemplifies the breadth of scientific discovery at Pennington Biomedical, where research spans all levels, from basic science that reveals the biological mechanisms underlying disease to clinical studies and population-based research that informs public health," said Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical. "Dr. Kirwan and his team's findings on Miro1 demonstrate the value of this integrated approach, connecting fundamental discoveries about muscle function with insights into insulin resistance and the benefits of exercise in people with Type 2 diabetes. This work is advancing our understanding of diabetes and helping lay the foundation for future approaches to prevention and treatment."

Could Targeting Miro1 Lead to New Diabetes Therapies?

Although the results are encouraging, scientists still need to establish whether directly targeting Miro1 can produce safe and effective treatments for people with Type 2 diabetes. The restoration of insulin responsiveness was demonstrated in preclinical models, while the human trial showed that exercise reduced Miro1 levels alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity.

Kirwan plans to continue investigating these findings at the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center. His research will combine laboratory experiments with studies involving people to uncover more of the biological mechanisms responsible for diabetes and explore new strategies for preventing and treating the condition.

"Type 2 diabetes is an affliction in Oklahoma and nationally," he said. "Ultimately, we are looking for cures, and we hope these recent findings could be part of the solution."

The study received funding from the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the National Institute on Aging, the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration announced Friday that it is giving states an additional six months to begin enforcing Medicaid work requirements.

States have been racing to prepare their Medicaid systems by Jan. 1 to include the work requirements passed last year in the One Big Beautiful Bill. The legislation required states that expanded Medicaid after Democrats passed the Affordable Care Act to ensure all working-age recipients without dependent children are employed, in school, or volunteering at least 80 hours each month, unless they are disabled, caring for young children, or “medically frail.”

A federal judge recently rejected the federal government’s medical frailty definition and ruled that states did not have adequate time or resources to overhaul their eligibility systems.

In Greenville, SC, the market has experienced a downturn in starter home availability in recent years.

#5547. Trump administration delays enforcement of Medicaid work requirements for six months

Trump administration delays enforcement of Medicaid work requirements for six months" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration is giving states an optional six-month grace period for enforcing new Medicaid work requirements, which were due to go into effect January 1.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) announced Friday an optional "hold harmless" period through June 30, 2027, to give states a transition period to further modernize systems, improve processes and streamline the applicant and beneficiary experience.

During the "hold harmless" period, states will still assess whether Medicaid applicants and beneficiaries meet the work requirements or qualify for an exclusion, but otherwise eligible people will not lose or be denied coverage solely because they fail to meet the requirement, CMS said.

CMS says the transition is intended to give states time to improve eligibility systems, automate verification, train workers and improve the beneficiary experience.

"States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries—at scale and for the long term," Dan Brillman, Deputy Administrator and Director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services, said in a statement. "If the state can use data to show that someone is working or qualifies for an exclusion, that person should not have to track down paperwork to prove it. And when someone needs support, they should know exactly what to do, when to do it, and where to go. That’s how we build a Medicaid program that works better for people, connects them to work, education, and training opportunities, and supports paths to prosperity."

During the six-month enforcement pause, CMS encourages states to use existing data to automatically verify qualifying activities and exemptions before requesting additional information from beneficiaries.

States are also encouraged to simplify notices and make the process easy to navigate so beneficiaries understand what the state has already verified, what information is still needed and how to respond or get help. States should also test eligibility systems end-to-end, particularly how the systems handle missing, outdated or conflicting information, to resolve operational issues and minimize inappropriate coverage disruptions.

CMS also called on states to coordinate with community partners to connect applicants and beneficiaries who need assistance with opportunities for employment, education, job training and volunteering.

The work requirements were established as part of last summer's massive H.R. 1 legislation, or the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Under the mandate, certain Medicaid applicants and beneficiaries ages 19 to 64 must meet a statutory work requirement, unless excluded. There are exemptions in place for the medically frail, disabled and others who are unable to meet the mandates.

CMS’ June 2026 interim final rule outlines qualifying activities, including 80 hours per month of work, community service or participation in a work program; enrollment in an educational program at least half-time; a combination of qualifying activities totaling at least 80 hours per month; or meeting the specified monthly income threshold.

State Medicaid administrators, health insurers, physicians and hospitals have pushed back on the Medicaid work requirements, citing concerns about financial and operational challenges, a spike in uncompensated care and the rule's strict "medical frailty" exemptions.

Industry groups argue the requirements impose onerous documentation burdens. The Alliance of Community Health Plans said that the final rule adds documentation requirements and tightens criteria for exemptions to the requirements, which will make it harder for individuals who need coverage to secure exemptions they may qualify for.

The organization also noted that most individuals enrolled in Medicaid are already working or in school.

Jennifer Tolbert, deputy director of the program on Medicaid and the uninsured at KFF, said in a quick take post back in June that "the rule adopts a restrictive definition of medical frailty that differs from states’ early expectations."

"Given the complexity of the provisions in the rule, states will likely face significant challenges in operationalizing the requirements in the next six months," Tolbert wrote. "With the short implementation timeline, states were already making implementation decisions that may not align with the rule."

Studies estimate that between 5 million and 10 million people could lose Medicaid coverage in 2028 following the rollout of new work requirements.

The Trump administration's tight definitions of medical frailty and documentation burdens have triggered multiple lawsuits from states, medical organizations and advocacy groups. A coalition of 26 states sued the Trump administration over its rollout of Medicaid work requirements. arguing that key provisions could cause eligible people to lose coverage and disrupt states’ implementation efforts. The states argue CMS’ new definition of who qualifies as “medically frail” is too restrictive and could make it harder for people with serious health conditions to receive exemptions.

In October, a Massachusetts judge sided with the states and rejected the Trump administration's definition of "medical frailty" for critical exemptions.

A group of physician groups, individual Medicaid enrollees and the city of Columbus also sued the federal government to challenge the work requirements.

State Medicaid agencies have warned that the accelerated IT and administrative build required by January 1, 2027, is putting severe pressure on local welfare offices and safety-net hospital operating margins, as Senior Writer Anastassia Gliadkovskaya reported.

#5546. Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

Protein is everywhere these days. From breakfast cereals and coffee to bottled water, manufacturers are adding extra protein to an expanding range of everyday products. But while consumers are being encouraged to eat more of it, a major scientific review suggests that cutting back on protein could offer surprising benefits for health and longevity.

After examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan. The potential benefits appear to involve several processes that influence how the body uses energy, responds to nutrients, protects cells from damage, and maintains healthy cellular function.

The findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets. Could many people be consuming far more protein than their bodies actually need?

"It's absolutely crystal clear that there are benefits of protein to muscle growth and exercise response of active individuals," says Dudley Lamming, the paper's corresponding author, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "But because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences."

Why Eating Less Protein Could Promote Longevity

Scientists have long understood that reducing calorie intake can extend lifespan in numerous organisms. Research has also linked calorie restriction to a lower risk of diseases associated with aging, including cancer. However, consistently eating fewer calories is challenging, making it difficult for many people to maintain such a diet over time.

An alternative approach has attracted increasing scientific interest: reducing protein without necessarily eating less food.

Experiments involving flies and rodents have demonstrated that limiting protein intake can increase lifespan even when total calorie consumption remains unchanged. This suggests that the benefits of dietary restriction may depend not only on how much food is consumed, but also on which nutrients make up that food.

Human research has produced encouraging findings as well. Several recent clinical trials have shown that people who reduce their protein intake can lose weight, decrease body fat, and improve fasting blood sugar levels, even when they consume more calories overall. Fasting blood sugar measures glucose in the bloodstream after a period without eating and is an important indicator of metabolic health.

These findings do not establish that protein restriction extends human lifespan, but they suggest that changing protein intake can influence processes associated with aging and disease.

The Debate Over How Much Protein We Really Need

The picture becomes more complicated when exercise and muscle health enter the equation.

Other studies have demonstrated that higher protein intake can support weight loss and help older adults preserve muscle mass, particularly when combined with physical activity. Maintaining muscle becomes increasingly important with age because muscle loss can contribute to weakness, reduced mobility, and a greater risk of falls.

Research highlighting these benefits helped motivate US authorities to revise dietary recommendations this year, encouraging daily protein consumption of 1.2-1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight (0.5-0.7 grams per pound). That represents nearly twice the previous recommended amount.

With protein consumption reaching new highs in the United States and older adults increasingly being advised to eat more, Lamming and a colleague examined decades of research to better understand the relationship between protein intake and aging.

Their analysis brought together findings from more than 350 papers, identifying several biological mechanisms that repeatedly appeared across studies. Together, these mechanisms suggest that lowering protein consumption may improve metabolic function, alter the way cells detect nutrients, limit cellular damage, and help preserve the processes that keep cells functioning properly.

A Hormone That May Help Explain Slower Aging

One particularly intriguing finding involves fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a hormone that becomes more abundant when dietary protein is limited.

FGF21 helps the body adjust to changes in nutrient availability and influences how energy is used. Higher levels of this hormone can increase energy expenditure, support healthier blood sugar regulation, and reduce inflammation.

These effects are especially interesting because metabolism and chronic inflammation are closely connected to aging. Over time, disruptions in these processes can contribute to conditions such as obesity, diabetes, and other age-related diseases.

Studies in mice have shown that animals with elevated FGF21 levels live longer than mice with normal levels. The lifespan benefit was particularly strong in males, suggesting that biological sex may influence how the body responds to this hormone.

Researchers have also established that eating less protein increases FGF21 levels in humans. Whether this hormonal response produces the same longevity benefits seen in mice remains an important unanswered question.

How Certain Amino Acids Could Influence Aging

The amount of protein someone eats may not be the only factor that matters. The types of amino acids that make up that protein could also play an important role.

Amino acids are the building blocks the body uses to produce proteins, which are essential for maintaining muscles, repairing tissues, and carrying out countless cellular functions. Beyond these basic roles, certain amino acids also act as signals that influence metabolism and cellular growth.

The review identifies three amino acids that appear especially important: methionine, isoleucine, and valine.

Research suggests that excessive intake of these amino acids can stimulate biological pathways that encourage growth. Although growth-related processes are essential for normal development and tissue repair, excessive or prolonged activation of certain pathways may contribute to obesity, inflammation, and other conditions associated with aging.

Limiting specific amino acids could therefore produce some of the benefits observed in protein-restricted diets. This possibility has attracted attention because it suggests that the relationship between protein and longevity may be more complicated than simply eating more or less of a single nutrient.

"These studies show that the amount of protein sedentary people are eating today may have negative health consequences, at least at the population level," Lamming says.

Why Exercise Could Change the Effects of Protein

The researchers emphasize that protein requirements are not the same for everyone.

Pregnant women, for example, need additional protein to support fetal development, while some older adults require higher amounts to help maintain muscle and physical function. People who exercise regularly may also benefit from greater protein consumption because their muscles use those nutrients to recover, repair tissue, and adapt to training.

For many adults who spend most of their day sitting, however, adding protein to everyday foods may offer little additional benefit.

Lamming points out that athletes frequently consume large amounts of protein without developing the metabolic diseases sometimes associated with protein-rich diets. One possible explanation is that physical activity changes how the body handles those nutrients.

Regular exercise stimulates muscle growth and repair, potentially allowing the body to put additional protein to productive use while reducing some of the harmful metabolic effects associated with high protein intake.

This distinction may help explain why studies sometimes reach seemingly contradictory conclusions about protein. A diet that benefits someone who exercises intensely may not be ideal for someone with a largely sedentary lifestyle.

Rather than recommending the same amount of protein for everyone, the researchers argue that dietary advice should better reflect individual circumstances, especially physical activity levels and age.

"Recent recommendations have encouraged people to eat more protein, but they've also encouraged people to exercise more," Lamming says. "We probably need to personalize protein recommendations based not just on age, but also on how physically active people are."

The findings challenge the assumption that adding more protein automatically leads to better health. Although protein remains essential, the growing body of longevity research suggests that for some people, consuming less may offer benefits that have been overlooked in the rush toward protein-rich foods.

The work was supported by the National Institute on Aging, the Wisconsin Partnership Program, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

#5545. STAT+: FDA rejects lung cancer treatment ivonescimab from Summit Therapeutics

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Adam Feuerstein is a senior writer and biotech columnist, reporting on the crossroads of drug development, business, Wall Street, and biotechnology. He is also a co-host of the weekly biotech podcast The Readout Loud and author of the newsletter Adam’s Biotech Scorecard. You can reach Adam on Signal at stataf.54.

The Food and Drug Administration rejected a treatment for a type of lung cancer developed by the U.S.-based biotech Summit Therapeutics and the Chinese drugmaker Akeso, Summit said on Sunday.

In a letter sent to the companies, FDA regulators said the drug, called ivonescimab, could not be approved because it didn’t help patients live longer. While the drug was found to slow lung cancer worsening in patients, the absence of a survival benefit “does not support the positive benefit-risk profile in support of approval,” FDA reviewers concluded.

The FDA’s rejection of ivonescimab is a regulatory setback for Summit, which oversees development of the drug outside of China, although one that was not entirely unforeseen.

#5544. HLTH26: Apple launches 200K-person study to examine how consumers use health AI

HLTH26: Apple launches 200K-person study to examine how consumers use health AI" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—Consumers are rapidly adopting consumer health AI. Roughly 1 in 3 U.S. adults have turned to an AI chatbot for health information, according to a KFF survey, and the use of health AI is even more prevalent among younger adults.

But questions remain about whether consumers understand and trust AI-generated health advice, and whether it influences how they manage their health or seek care.

Tech giant Apple launched the Apple Health AI Usage Study today with plans to recruit 200,000 participants in the U.S. to gain a better understanding of how people interact with conversational health AI tools.

The study is open to individuals 21 or older who live in the U.S., and participants must have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro or later) running iOS 26 or later. Apple will run the virtual research study on a dedicated Apple Health AI Study App, separate from the Apple Health and Research apps. Participants may remain in the study for up to 12 months, Apple said.

The tech company is collaborating with OpenEvidence on the research initiative, as the startup provides the underlying clinical AI technology for Apple’s Health AI Usage Study. OpenEvidence is a widely used AI-powered clinical decision support tool and medical search engine for clinicians. The company's platform pulls directly from licensed, peer-reviewed literature and clinical guidelines through formal partnerships with The New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), JAMA, Nature, Cochrane, and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN).

Through Apple’s study app, participants can ask everyday health questions and receive answers in approachable language, with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources, Apple said. Users can ask about symptoms, general health questions, recovery from procedures, fitness and other health concerns. They can rate the AI's answers and indicate what was useful or lacking, Apple said.

Study participants can also choose to share HealthKit data types—such as resting heart rate, activity and sleep—to get more personalized responses to health questions. If study participants have imported clinical records into the Health app and separately agree to share them with the Health AI Usage study, the app can incorporate that information, primarily lab results, Apple representatives said.

"At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life. Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey," Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement.

Apple described the research initiative as a formal study overseen by an independent review board.

Participants will complete a mandatory onboarding process that includes informed consent, and they'll be asked to share demographic information such as age, race and education so researchers can examine how these variables affect participant preferences and communication needs, Apple said.

The company said study participants will receive baseline and monthly surveys, allowing researchers to examine how people use the information they receive and what happens afterward.

The Health AI Usage study app also includes tools to help people prepare for healthcare appointments, along with surveys after visits to gauge whether the use of health AI chatbots makes patients feel better prepared or empowered and improves their interactions with providers, Apple said.

Apple said it has implemented security measures to protect the study data it maintains, as well as the confidentiality of participants’ information. User queries on the Health AI Usage Study app are first processed on the iPhone to remove identifying information. The queries then flow to a secure study environment managed by a third-party study support contractor where they are de-linked from individual participant IDs and screened again before being sent to OpenEvidence where answers are generated using supporting reference materials, Apple said.

The study app also features safety guardrails that are intended to detect certain concerning questions and suggest that a participant follow up with a provider or other resources if needed.

Consumers are increasingly using general AI chatbots powered by LLMs to get answers to health questions. But research indicates a wide gap exists between an AI's technical accuracy and a patient's ability to safely use that information.

"Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds. When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly. Connecting these tools, and rigorously studying what works, is how we’ll get there," Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, said in a statement.

The Health AI Usage study builds on Apple's growing research initiatives. In 2019, the company launched its Research app and three medical studies to test how well its Apple Watch can track a person's mobility and cardiovascular health, changes in hearing and women's health and fertility. Last year, it began the Apple Health Study to use its devices, including iPhones, Apple Watch and AirPods along with third-party devices, for a longitudinal, virtual study to monitor changes in participants’ health, spanning a wide range of health and disease areas.

#5543. Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%

A specially engineered chewing gum could offer an unexpected new weapon against viruses and bacteria linked to head and neck cancer. In laboratory tests using samples from cancer patients, researchers found that extracts from the gum reduced levels of human papillomavirus, or HPV, by as much as 93%. An enhanced version also nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species while leaving beneficial bacteria unharmed.

The findings, reported in Scientific Reports, suggest that this experimental approach could eventually help prevent certain infections and support existing cancer treatments. Researchers believe the plant-based technology could also provide a more affordable option for patients.

The research was led by Henry Daniell of the University of Pennsylvania's School of Dental Medicine. His team has been exploring ways to use specially engineered plants to produce proteins with potential medical benefits.

Why Scientists Are Targeting Cancer-Linked Microbes

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a common form of cancer that develops in the tissues lining the mouth and throat. It begins in squamous cells, the thin, flat cells that cover many surfaces throughout the body. These cancers can be particularly difficult to treat once they have spread, and patients diagnosed at advanced stages often face poor outcomes.

According to Daniell, recently approved cancer medications have generally failed to produce major improvements in patients' quality of life or their chances of surviving five years after diagnosis. This highlights the continuing need for more effective treatments and new strategies that could help prevent the disease or reduce complications.

One promising area of research involves the microorganisms living in the mouth. Although many oral microbes are harmless or beneficial, certain viruses and bacteria have been associated with the development or progression of head and neck cancers.

The researchers focused on three of these microbes. The first was HPV, a common virus that can cause certain cancers when infections persist. The other two were Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn), bacterial species associated with oral disease and poorer outcomes in some cancer patients.

"The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection," says Daniell. "And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies."

Oropharyngeal cancer affects the middle portion of the throat, including areas such as the tonsils and base of the tongue. Metastatic cancer refers to cancer that has spread beyond its original location, while adjuvant treatments are additional therapies given to improve the effectiveness of primary treatment.

A Chewing Gum Made From Beans Delivers Surprising Results

The new study builds on the team's earlier development of a chewing gum made from lablab beans (bean gum). This gum contains FRIL, a naturally occurring protein with antiviral properties.

To investigate its potential benefits, the scientists tested extracts from the gum against microbes found in oral samples collected from patients with head and neck cancer.

The results were striking. The bean gum extracts lowered HPV levels by 93% in saliva samples and by 80% in oral rinse samples. These findings suggest that proteins delivered through a chewing gum could potentially help reduce the presence of a virus associated with certain head and neck cancers.

The team then took the technology a step further by engineering the gum to contain protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Some antimicrobial peptides can attack and destroy harmful microorganisms, making them promising candidates for new infection treatments.

With this additional ingredient, the researchers found that a single dose of the engineered gum extract reduced the two targeted bacterial species, Pg and Fn, to almost undetectable levels.

Harmful Bacteria Nearly Disappear While Good Bacteria Survive

One of the most encouraging findings was the gum's ability to target harmful bacteria without disrupting the beneficial microorganisms that naturally inhabit the mouth.

The oral microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microscopic organisms living inside the mouth, plays an important role in maintaining oral health. Many of these microbes coexist harmlessly with the body and help maintain a balanced environment.

Some cancer treatments can disturb that balance. Radiation therapy, for example, can reduce populations of beneficial oral bacteria while encouraging the growth of potentially harmful yeast, including Candida albicans.

In contrast, the experimental gum extract sharply reduced the targeted bacteria without affecting the beneficial bacterial populations examined by the researchers. This selectivity could be especially valuable for patients whose oral health has already been affected by cancer or its treatment.

Importantly, the results came from laboratory testing of patient samples rather than clinical trials in which people chewed the gum. Further research will be needed to determine whether the same effects occur in the human mouth and whether reducing these microbes can meaningfully improve cancer outcomes.

Could Chewing Gum Become Part of Cancer Prevention and Treatment?

The researchers believe their findings justify moving the technology toward human clinical trials, particularly because head and neck cancers remain a serious global health challenge.

"Lip and oral cavity cancer was the seventh leading cancer type in cancer incidence and mortality rate worldwide in adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022," says Daniell. "Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission."

Prophylaxis refers to measures taken to prevent disease or infection before it occurs. In this case, the researchers envision a future in which specially designed chewing gum might help limit exposure to harmful microbes or reduce their levels in people already receiving cancer treatment.

Such an approach could offer a relatively simple and potentially inexpensive way to deliver protective proteins directly into the mouth, where the targeted microorganisms are found.

For now, the technology remains experimental, and there is no evidence yet that chewing the gum prevents or treats cancer in humans. Nevertheless, the ability to substantially reduce HPV and nearly eliminate two cancer-associated bacterial species in laboratory tests offers a promising starting point for further investigation.

If future clinical trials confirm its safety and effectiveness, a familiar everyday product could become an unexpected addition to the medical toolkit against dangerous oral infections and cancers.

Henry Daniell is the W.D. Miller Professor in the Department of Basic & Translational Sciences at the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania.

Other authors are Geetanjali Wakade, Rahul Singh, and Smruti Nair of Penn Dental Medicine; Andrés M. Bur and Sufi M. Thomas of the University of Kansas Medical Center; Eri S. Srivatsan and Marilene B. Wang of the University of California at Los Angeles; and Saroj K. Basak of the Veterans Administration Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System.

This work was supported by NIH (grant 5-R01-HL 107904-13 awarded to Henry Daniell), the Academic Senate Grant of David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA (the Surgical Education Research program), and National Cancer Institute Cancer Center (Support Grant P30 CA168524).

#5539. Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study

A common class of drugs used to treat osteoporosis may have an unexpected benefit: lowering the risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. In a study involving more than 120,000 older adults, researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed) found that patients taking certain medications to strengthen their bones were significantly less likely to develop dementia.

The medications, known as nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (NBPs), are widely prescribed to prevent bone loss and fractures. The findings suggest that these established treatments could potentially serve a second purpose by helping protect the aging brain. The research, conducted by scientists in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed's LKS Faculty of Medicine, was published in Alzheimer's & Dementia.

More than 55 million people worldwide currently live with dementia, and that number is projected to climb to 139 million by 2050. The World Health Organization has identified dementia as a major global health priority. Although the first medications designed to slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) have recently gained approval, their high costs, limited suitability for some patients, and questions about their effectiveness remain important challenges.

These obstacles have increased interest in finding affordable ways to prevent or delay dementia before symptoms develop. One promising approach is to identify existing medications that might offer benefits beyond the conditions they were originally designed to treat.

The Surprising Connection Between Bone Health and Dementia

Osteoporosis and dementia often affect the same older adults. Osteoporosis causes bones to become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures, while dementia progressively affects memory, thinking, and the ability to carry out everyday activities. The two conditions also share several risk factors, including older age, being female, and low levels of physical activity.

Previous research by the same HKUMed team established that osteoporosis and fractures are independent risk factors for dementia. The researchers also found that people already living with dementia face an increased likelihood of falling and breaking bones.

This relationship raises an intriguing possibility: medications that treat osteoporosis might also help reduce dementia risk.

Among the most commonly prescribed osteoporosis treatments are alendronate and zoledronate, both of which belong to the NBP drug class. These medications work by slowing the breakdown of bone tissue, helping maintain bone strength and reduce the likelihood of fractures.

Scientists have also begun uncovering evidence that some of the biological processes influenced by these drugs may be involved in the development of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. This overlap has prompted researchers to investigate whether NBPs might provide benefits for the brain as well as the skeleton.

Study of 120,000 Patients Finds Up to 24% Lower Dementia Risk

To explore this possibility, the HKUMed researchers examined electronic medical records from across Hong Kong, analyzing data from more than 120,000 patients aged 60 and older. All participants had osteoporosis or fragility fractures, which are breaks that can occur after relatively minor injuries because the bones have become weakened.

The records covered the period from 2005 through 2020, allowing the team to investigate how different osteoporosis treatments were associated with dementia risk over time.

The results revealed a notable difference. Patients taking NBPs had a 16% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease and related dementias compared with patients who received no osteoporosis medication.

The association was even stronger when NBP users were compared with patients taking other types of osteoporosis drugs. In that comparison, dementia risk was 24% lower among those receiving NBPs.

Women and patients who had experienced hip fractures appeared to show particularly strong associations between NBP treatment and reduced dementia risk.

The researchers also estimated that treating 48 patients with NBPs over five years could potentially prevent one case of dementia. If future research confirms that the medications directly reduce dementia risk, the implications could be substantial, particularly for older adults who already need treatment for osteoporosis.

Because the findings come from an observational study, they do not establish that the drugs themselves prevent dementia. However, they provide evidence supporting further investigation into whether these medications could help delay or prevent cognitive decline.

Could Existing Osteoporosis Drugs Help Prevent Alzheimer's?

Professor Cheung Ching-lung, Associate Professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed, believes the findings highlight the possibility that a familiar osteoporosis treatment could deliver two important health benefits.

"Our study provides evidence that NBPs may offer dual benefits in strengthening bones and reducing fracture risk, as well as potentially preventing ADRD. Their potential neuroprotective role provides an empirical basis and supports future research on the actual effectiveness of this medication in preventing or delaying cognitive decline associated with ADRD."

The potential advantage of this approach is that NBPs are already widely available and have an established history of use in treating osteoporosis. Rather than developing an entirely new medication from scratch, researchers could investigate whether these existing treatments offer additional protection for people at elevated risk of dementia.

The findings are particularly relevant as populations around the world grow older and the number of people affected by dementia continues to rise.

"These findings are significant as they demonstrate a potential approach for reducing dementia risk in a vulnerable population using safe and widely available NBPs. In our rapidly aging society, these findings suggest that while waiting for the novel therapies, existing medications can also provide additional protection for high-risk populations," said Professor Cheung.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether NBPs can directly prevent or delay Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Nevertheless, the results suggest that medications already prescribed to protect aging bones may also have an important role to play in protecting brain health.

The research was led by Professor Cheung Ching-lung of the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed. Dr Sing Chor-wing, from the same department, served as the study's first author.

Additional researchers included Professor Chan Koon-ho, Dr Patrick Chiu Ka-chun, and Professor Kathryn Tan Choon-beng, all from the Department of Medicine in the School of Clinical Medicine at HKUMed.

#5538. Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising new approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China. Scientists found that pantethine can calm immune cells involved in autoimmune inflammation, preventing psoriasis from developing in mice and improving symptoms in a small human clinical trial.

The findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system. By interfering with this process, pantethine may help reduce the excessive immune activity responsible for psoriasis and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis

At the center of the discovery are dendritic cells, specialized immune cells that help organize the body's defenses. These cells act as coordinators, identifying potential threats and directing other immune cells to respond.

Dendritic cells perform this role by capturing foreign substances called antigens and presenting them to T cells, which are immune cells that recognize specific threats. They also release chemical signals that recruit additional immune cells and trigger inflammation.

Although these activities are essential for fighting infections, problems can arise when dendritic cells become excessively active. Instead of helping protect the body, they can contribute to persistent inflammation and autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis.

"Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored."

Zhang led the research alongside Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li, and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Link Between Cholesterol and Psoriasis

The researchers identified unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from people with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. These enzymes help regulate the processing of certain substances involved in cellular metabolism.

When the scientists reduced Vanin levels, dendritic cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. They also found that a drug designed to inhibit Vanins prevented psoriasis from developing in mice.

Further investigation revealed why these enzymes might play such an important role.

Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient that cells need to produce energy. Pantethine is already sold as a nutritional supplement and is commonly used to help lower blood cholesterol because it can reduce cholesterol production.

This connection is particularly interesting because cholesterol does more than circulate in the bloodstream. It also influences how immune cells function. Previous research has shown that cholesterol can stimulate dendritic cell activity, while elevated blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for developing psoriasis.

The team discovered that excessive Vanin activity reduces the amount of pantethine available inside dendritic cells. As pantethine levels fall, cholesterol production increases, causing these immune cells to become unusually active.

Restoring pantethine levels interrupted this process. The supplement reduced cholesterol accumulation within dendritic cells and helped suppress the excessive immune activation associated with inflammation.

"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang says.

Common Supplement Shows Promise in Human Psoriasis Trial

Encouraged by the laboratory and animal findings, the researchers investigated whether pantethine might also benefit people living with psoriasis.

They conducted a small clinical trial involving 24 patients with the condition. All participants received a topical ointment containing calcipotriene/betamethasone, a combination treatment used to control psoriasis symptoms. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D derivative that helps regulate skin cell growth, while betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation.

Half of the participants also took pantethine tablets, allowing researchers to examine whether adding the supplement improved the results of standard treatment.

After 12 weeks, the patients who received pantethine alongside their prescribed ointment showed greater improvement in psoriasis symptoms. The benefits were especially noticeable among participants who had high blood cholesterol levels before treatment.

These findings suggest that pantethine could potentially serve as an additional treatment for psoriasis, particularly in patients whose cholesterol metabolism may be contributing to inflammation.

However, the trial included only 24 people, and the researchers emphasize that larger studies are necessary to confirm the supplement's effectiveness. The human results also do not establish that the same biological mechanism observed in laboratory experiments is responsible for the improvement in patients.

"Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang says. "Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell-mediated autoimmune diseases."

#5536. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5535. Spain’s Housing Crisis Sparks a Revolt Against Tourism. Could America Feel the Fallout?

Millions of workers walked off the job across Spain on Wednesday, demanding relief from soaring rents, evictions, and housing speculation. It was the the country's first general strike in 14 years.

In Barcelona, protesters rattled house keys and chanted, “O baixen els lloguers, o cremen els carrers," which translates to “Either rents fall, or the streets burn.”

Over the past decade, rents in the City of Counts have climbed more than 50%, with tourism adding pressure on an already strained housing market.

In the coastal city of Málaga, Mónica Reino, 56, has watched that transformation unfold in her own apartment building.

“Every year it gets worse,” she told AFP, estimating that half of its 20 apartments are now tourist accommodations.

Tourism is far from the only force driving Spain's housing crisis. In popular vacation destinations, property owners can earn more from short-term visitors than year-round tenants, creating a financial incentive to convert residential housing into tourist accommodations.

A day after the strike, lawmakers narrowly approved a package of housing measures, including a new 10% tax on qualifying vacation rentals.

The conflict mirrors one already playing out in vacation destinations across the United States, where booming tourism has helped sustain local economies while putting housing increasingly out of reach for residents.

But as restrictions on vacation rentals make accommodations scarcer and more expensive abroad, could more travelers turn to U.S. destinations, intensifying the housing pressures those communities are already struggling to contain?

Spain's efforts to restrict short-term rentals were already changing the market well before this week's protests and housing vote.

Available short-term rental listings fell 5.9% in October compared with a year earlier, while average nightly rates jumped 12.5%, according to a new analysis from AirDNA, which tracks vacation rentals across platforms such as Airbnb and Vrbo.

Part of the price increase reflects a shift toward more expensive properties as licensing restrictions remove rentals from the market. But even rates for comparable existing properties rose 8.2% over the past year.

Spain had an estimated 355,000 tourist dwellings in 2025, according to the Bank of Spain. Although they represented just 1.5% of the country's housing stock, they accounted for roughly 10% of its rental market, with much higher concentrations in tourist neighborhoods.

Research suggests those concentrations can have substantial consequences for local rents.

Airbnb's expansion pushed residential rents up 7% in Barcelona neighborhoods with the highest levels of activity between 2012 and 2016, according to a 2020 study published in the Journal of Urban Economics. Across the city, the estimated increase was 1.9%.

"Short-term rental activity can crowd locals out of homes that might otherwise serve as conventional rental homes, reducing the number of options available for those living in the area permanently and raising prices," Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com®, says.

But he cautions: "This effect is probably not the main factor affecting affordability."

Even so, Barcelona plans to let all 10,101 existing tourist-apartment licenses expire in 2028, while Málaga has suspended new licenses for three years.

The restrictions could return some tourist accommodations to residential use. Whether enough properties will become available to ease housing costs remains uncertain.

Spain welcomed more than 80.5 million international tourists during the first nine months of 2026—a 5.2% increase over the same period last year. Americans accounted for nearly 3.9 million of those visitors, with arrivals growing more than twice as fast as overall international tourism.

On its face, it's a counterintuitive trend: Higher accommodation costs have hardly deterred American travelers. But part of the explanation may lie in who can afford to keep traveling.

Higher-income households, supported by record household wealth, are driving a disproportionate share of U.S. travel spending, according to the U.S. Travel Association. While rising costs are forcing some households to adjust their plans, wealthier travelers are better positioned to absorb higher prices.

And generational wealth could add to the advantage, too. Visa estimates that $36 trillion will pass from baby boomers to younger generations over the next two decades, with housing and travel among the sectors expected to benefit.

If that pattern sounds familiar, it's because inherited wealth is also helping determine who can afford to own a home at all. In Spain, parents gifted their children more than 30,000 homes last year, while in the U.S., a record 10% of first-time homebuyers relied on an inheritance for their down payment, according to a November report from the National Association of Realtors®.

And if rising accommodation costs abroad encourage more travelers to vacation closer to home, those pressures could intensify.

There's no evidence yet that the restrictions sweeping across Europe are redirecting tourists to U.S. destinations, but domestic demand is already growing fastest in smaller, relatively affordable markets.

Nights booked in small-city and rural U.S. markets increased 8.4% in October from a year earlier, compared with just 1.1% growth in urban markets, according to AirDNA.

"The closest parallels are American tourism hubs where housing is limited and the conversion of homes into STRs force tourism industry workers to live far away," says Berner. "Think Hawaii, Mountain West ski towns, or New Orleans.

"In the more urban locations (like New Orleans), the upward pressure on rent is more concentrated in tourist-heavy neighborhoods than in the metro area at large. But in the more remote destinations without suburbia to absorb displaced locals, the effect is stronger," Berner says.

Nantucket, MA, offers a particularly telling example. The tiny island of just 48 square miles hosts nearly 2 million visitors annually.

More than half of the housing stock (55%) is reserved for seasonal or occasional use, according to a Realtor.com analysis. That scarcity set against high demand has helped push the median home listing price to $4,925,000 in June—more than 11 times the national median of $430,000.

And it's not just lower-income workers being priced out, either.

Roughly 1,080 renter households, including those earning well above the local median income, were effectively shut out of homeownership without significant financial assistance, according to a 2025 housing assessment.

The shortage is so severe that it’s threatening the island's ability to sustain its workforce. A 2026 workforce housing study found that 64% of surveyed employers had lost or declined to hire workers because of housing challenges.

Nantucket Cottage Hospital has identified housing as the leading reason candidates turn down jobs or employees leave.

"Workers get displaced, but communities get hollowed out, too," Berner says. "Schools get weaker, tax bases become more fragile as they are more exposed to tourism downturns, and entry into the community through homeownership becomes more difficult."

For communities that depend on tourism, restricting vacation rentals presents another dilemma: How much visitor spending can they afford to lose in the effort to preserve housing?

On Long Island's North Fork, officials are considering restrictions that would cap short-term rental permits in Southold Town at just 119 properties, compared with approximately 640 active listings in October.

Those rentals generate an estimated $27.5 million in annual revenue for property owners, according to town figures reported by Newsday.

But reducing that business doesn't guarantee more housing for residents. Nearly 37% of the town's housing units were seasonal residences in 2020, and many owners purchased their properties primarily as second homes.

As Realtor.com previously reported, those owners may simply stop offering short-term stays rather than sell their properties or convert them into annual rentals.

Diane Mollica, a local real estate agent with the Gambino Group, says many owners primarily use their properties for their own enjoyment, making a widespread shift to year-round housing unlikely.

Yet the housing shortage is already threatening the businesses that depend on tourism.

"We cannot build a sustainable tourism economy on the backs of a workforce that can no longer afford to live here," Amanda Giuliano, a Southold business owner and co-chair of the town's Economic Development Committee, told Newsday. "If we don't have people working, there will be no tourism."

Spain faces the same conflict on a much larger scale.

Tourism contributed €200.7 billion (about $221 billion) to the Spanish economy in 2024, accounting for 12.6% of GDP, according to the country's National Statistics Institute. The industry supported more than 2.7 million jobs, representing 12.3% of employment nationwide.

That economic dependence helps explain why then, even against a backdrop of a nationwide general strike, the 10% tax on vacation rentals passed only in a 35 to 34 vote.

The new levy is scheduled to take effect on Dec. 1. But even so, the measure could be short-lived. Spain faces a snap election on Nov. 29, triggered by parliament's earlier rejection of the government's housing decrees, and the opposition Popular Party has pledged to repeal the measures if it takes power.

And even if the restrictions survive, reducing tourist accommodations could still come at a cost to the businesses and property owners who depend on them, without producing enough homes for local workers.

Berner argues that increasing housing supply offers a way to accommodate both.

"Encouraging more homebuilding is the only long-term solution to a housing shortage and has the ability to expand tourism capacity as well," he says.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5534. October Existing-Home Sales Sink to 16-Year Low; Rates Only Partly to Blame

The National Association of Realtors®’ (NAR) Existing-Home Sales report for October came in on a somewhat dismal note: Existing-home sales decreased 5.5% month-over-month to a rate of 3.75 million.

That marks the lowest level since August 2010’s 3.68 million, according to Realtor.com®  Chief Economist Danielle Hale.

Year-over-year home sales were down 8.8% compared to October 2025, which recorded a sales pace of 4.11 million.

Month-over-month sales declined in the Midwest, South and West, but held steady in the relatively “inventory-constrained” and “competitive” Northeast market, Hale noted. Year-over-year sales, however, declined for all four regions.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun blamed mortgage rates. “Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010,” he said.

As the housing market enters its slowest season, rates that have held above 7%—a huge leap from before the Iran War, when they touched 6%—have depressed demand and discouraged many buyers, who already face longer-term issues with housing affordability.

Hale concurred with Yun’s diagnosis. According to her, climbing mortgage rates in September (the time when many October closed sales would have been in contract) “were the highest rates of 2026 at the time…and they likely derailed some homebuying plans.”

If mortgage rates “derailed” home-buying plans in October, could the recent ease in mortgage rates signal a gentler turn in the market in the coming months?

Hale thinks the story is not so simple. In her words, the October market “reflect(ed) a perfect storm of an abrupt shift in the financial environment and large uncertainties in the pre-election period for both policy and the economy just as the housing market usually slows for the season.”

She added that “several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go, including a strong economy and jobs market, persistent inflation, and an expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments.”

Overall, Hale said she “expect(s) to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”

Sean Fergus, VP of Economic Research at builder-focused data and analytics firms NewHomeSource and Zonda, largely came to the same conclusion as Hale.

“Rates have since eased,” he said, “but buyers need to trust that relief will last before they come back in force.”

Yun had a more positive outlook, predicated on whether mortgage rates continue to decline. In NAR’s press release, he said that “(b)ased on the current underwhelming home sales pace at a time of consistent job growth, there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline.”

Yun also commented on the relatively good financial position of homeowners currently, saying that they “are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation.”

As evidence for this claim, he pointed to the “historically low” number of distressed property sales, which “remains…at only 2% of all transactions.”

As a final sort of snapshot on the real estate ecosystem, total unsold inventory ticked up 1.3% to 1.59 million units, or the equivalent of 5.1 months’ supply. September 2026 recorded 4.7 months’ worth of unsold inventory, still higher than 4.4 months’ unsold inventory in October 2025, from which 1.59 million units represents a 4.6% yearly  increase.

Median existing-home sale prices increased more modestly, only crawling up 0.4% year-over-year to $416,700. The same median price was $414,900 last October. Even so, this is the 40th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases.

Audrey Jiang is an editorial intern for RISMedia.

“A price cut tells you the seller’s first number did not work. It does not tell you what the home is worth,” says one real estate professional. “Some reductions create a legitimate opportunity. Others simply bring an unrealistic price closer to where it should have started.” Read more.

#5533. Thanksgiving Is the Worst Day of the Year for Cooking Fires—Is Your Kitchen Prepared?

If you’re hosting loved ones this Thanksgiving, now is the time to get your kitchen ready. Otherwise, a nice holiday meal could turn into a costly and dangerous ordeal.

According to the latest data from the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), about 1,139 home cooking fires were reported to U.S. fire departments on Thanksgiving Day 2024.

That’s a 321% increase over the daily average, making Turkey Day the leading day of the year for home cooking fires.

“People don’t ever set out to leave the kitchen unattended, but a minute is all it takes for a grease and oil fire to take over, and there’s a greater risk of that happening on Thanksgiving when every burner is going,” says Payton Kashani, personal injury attorney, president, and managing partner of Sunset West Legal Group PC in Los Angeles.

By preparing your kitchen ahead of time, you can reduce the risk of fires and enjoy a delicious and safe celebration with family.

The NFPA says that unattended cooking is the leading cause of home cooking fires. And that’s quite common on Thanksgiving Day.

Many dishes are usually being cooked at once on the stove, oven, and various countertop appliances. Add in a house full of guests that bring constant interruptions and you’re left with a risky situation.

“Thanksgiving fires aren’t usually about cooking appliances going wrong. They tend to happen in those few minutes when someone steps away to greet a guest at the door. Distractions like this can wind up causing serious burns with long, painful recoveries that shake up a family’s normal life,” explains Amanda Demanda, founder of Amanda Demanda Injury Lawyers in Miami.

Grease and oil fires are particularly concerning because there are so many dishes cooking at the same time.

Additionally, despite the fact that the NFPA strongly discourages the use of oil-based turkey fryers due to fire and burn risk, many people put a frozen or wet turkey into hot oil and cause a fire.

“Fires can also stem from flammable items that get left near the stove, like kitchen towels or food packaging. Loose sleeves may get caught up in the mix, and when things catch on fire, many of the injuries that arise happen from people trying to fight the fire themselves,” adds Demanda.

Before Thanksgiving cooking gets underway, prepare your kitchen and anyone who’s going to be in it or near it.

When you’re frying, boiling, or broiling, stay in the kitchen and set timers so you’ll know when dishes are ready. Once they’re done, check that all burners and your oven are off before you leave the room.

Keep everything that can catch fire well away from the burners, oven, or any other appliance that generates heat. These include towels, paper and plastic bags, oven mitts, wooden utensils, and food wrappers.

“If you’re going to wear long sleeves, make sure they’re close-fitting rather than loose,” says Demanda.

Demanda recommends keeping a lid on standby.

Your fire extinguisher should be within reach as well. Just make sure it’s always near the stove and everyone in your home knows how to use it.

In addition, skip the task of oil-frying your turkey if possible. If you like the taste, buy it already fried or use an oil-less fryer instead.

“In the event you do use a traditional fryer, keep it away from your house, place it on a flat, even surface, and ensure [the turkey] is fully thawed,” says Stephanie Fox, national spokesperson at American Red Cross.

Lastly, direct kids and pets out of the cooking area.

“Kids and pets running around your kitchen are a burn injury waiting to happen, so make sure you have a spot for guests to gather away from your cooking zone,” adds Demanda.

Rich Repich, home services expert at Cinch Home Services in Boca Raton, FL, recommends setting up appetizers and drinks in a different room so guests don't crowd the cook and giving them a separate table to leave any used dishes.
