#5494. Built for Tech Execs: This $4.7M Midcentury Estate Near D.C. Features Radiant-Cooled Floors and a Secret Bar

Located about 25 miles outside Washington, DC, on 5.03 acres in Clifton Reserve, a private collection of just three bespoke new construction homes, the 10,154-square-foot midcentury modern home is being built with wellness designed into it.

Listed for $4.7 million, the six-bedroom home will have natural stone, wood details, high ceilings, and expansive windows that let in abundant natural light.

“The cool thing is it features hydronic water, which is a technology that was brought over from Europe to warm the floors during the winter and cool them during the summer,” said listing agent Katherine Massetti of Serhant. “It was also designed to reduce allergen risks with less airborne dust (than forced air).”

The homes in the gated enclave, built by ACG Custom Homes, will have clean angles, low-slope roofs, and cantilevered overhangs.

“This is true midcentury modern new construction,” Massetti said. “It’s a two-level home that is focused on entertainment and living space. It’s a one-of-a-kind masterpiece that will be completed in Q1 2027.”

Designed to flow with the outdoor space, the open floor plan will have retractable glass walls that open to a heated saltwater in-ground pool with waterfall features, a spa, a sun deck, and a covered pavilion with an outdoor kitchen and private shower.

The main-floor primary suite will be silently cooled through its floors and ceilings, which helps keep humidity steady. The suite will have a stone fireplace, plaster walls, custom wood paneling, dual dressing rooms with revolving shoe towers, and a spa-inspired bath with full-height Viola marble shower walls and marble flooring.

The home will also have a secluded en-suite bedroom that could be used for multigenerational living.

“The target audience is someone in the tech business world,” Massetti said. “It’s about 15 minutes from the Tech Corridor. I think the next buyer will be someone who is wellness focused and wants to entertain with retreat style living.”

The gourmet chef’s kitchen will have a 10-foot ribbed Pietra Grigio marble hood, full-height stone backsplash and counters, contrasting Statuary marble double-waterfall islands, integrated LED lighting, custom European white oak cabinetry, and high-end appliances. A separate catering kitchen will be designed for hosting larger gatherings.

Other amenities will include a full spa on the nearly 5,000-square-foot walkout lower level, which will also have a sauna, a fitness center, a hidden speakeasy with a full bar, a wine wall, and a 12-foot LED screen.

The private lot will also have EV infrastructure, solar power with battery backup, and a climate-controlled three-car garage.

“Clifton offers a lot of acreage with a small-town feel,” she noted. “It has lots of Victorian homes dating back to the 1800s, so it has this old vibe, but it also has highly rated restaurants. It also has a community vibe with local ice cream and coffee shops as well. It’s super cute and has a getaway feel to it tucked away from northern Virginia and DC life.”

#5493. View Homes Debuts New Brand Identity to Match Future Growth

View Homes has unveiled a new brand identity designed to create a more consistent presence across its operations in Colorado, New Mexico, and Texas.

Led by CEO Natasha Gandhi, the rebrand brings the company’s existing Aspen View, Desert View, and Horizon View divisions together under the unified View Homes name. The new identity will roll out across offices, model homes, communities, and the builder’s public-facing materials in the coming weeks.

“View Homes has spent decades earning a reputation for quality homes and a people-first culture,” said Gandhi, who became CEO in the spring of this year. “This evolution doesn’t change what the company stands for. The new brand is organized around four pillars: Exceptional Experience, People-First, Design-Forward, and Premium. The launch comes as the 35-plus-year-old builder grows its footprint. View Homes currently operates in Northern Colorado, Colorado Springs, Las Cruces, San Antonio, and El Paso, and is expanding into the Denver market at Sterling Ranch.

“We build homes with intention and care that are designed for the way people actually live,” Gandhi said. “Premium doesn’t mean out of reach. It means doing it right at every price point, in every market we build in.”

The new identity is anchored by the brand line, “View Homes. Uncompromising quality. Genuine heart. Built to last.”

#5492. Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings

In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new.

A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance?

Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate.

Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets

Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey, nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home.

Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap, a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns:

Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter.

And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time.

Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat

Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live.

In July, we partnered with The Weather Company, owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month.

Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for:

Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in.

Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options

For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie, the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-sale listings.

Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as:

Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise

While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data.

#5491. Google releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a lower-cost model said to outscore Argon

Google LLC today released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a lower-cost model in its Gemini 4 artificial intelligence family that it says outscores its frontier Gemini 4 Argon model on an independent intelligence ranking.

Measured on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level, Hydrogen scored 51 to Argon’s 50, according to Google. A fourth thinking level called xhigh, new with Hydrogen, takes the score to 54.

The rollout is different, too. Argon spent nearly two weeks with members of Google’s Fairwind Program, a group of vetted cybersecurity defenders, before paying developers could get at it on Oct. 13. Hydrogen skipped that stage. Anyone can use it from today, including people on the free version of the Gemini app.

Koray Kavukcuoglu, who became head of Google DeepMind in August when Demis Hassabis moved into a chairman role, wrote in the announcement that Hydrogen is “built for rapid execution.”

Orchestrator, which Google added to its Antigravity coding tool today, picks between Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon as a session goes along. Google’s runs of the Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding test found Orchestrator getting close to Carbon’s success rate on an average of 24% less quota.

Gemini 3.8 Flash, which came out in September, is the yardstick for most of the other numbers in the announcement. Against it, Hydrogen finished tasks 2.5 times faster at the default setting. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, which tests work done at a command line, Hydrogen more than tripled the older model’s 18.2% with a score of 57%.

Among the early testers Google quoted, Andrew Carr, a former OpenAI scientist who is now chief scientist at 3D animation startup Cartwheel Inc., said the model caught two problems with an approach his team had been stuck on for 10 days. Discovery Loop Inc., the startup former Google Chief Scientist Jeff Dean co-founded after leaving in August, was another.

#5489. Las Vegas Is Running Short on $100K-a-Month Rentals as A-Listers and Athletes Drive Demand

While Las Vegas drowns in unsold homes and priced-out buyers sit on the sidelines waiting for lower mortgage rates, the luxury rental sector is booming, fueled by visiting celebrities, professional athletes, and out-of-town millionaires eyeing a permanent move.

In October, Las Vegas’ overall housing inventory reached an all-time high of nearly 11,450 units, up roughly 10% compared to a year ago, as mortgage rates topping 7% left many buyers priced out.

Yet at the very top of the local rental market, the exact opposite is happening.

Local brokers say that demand for rental mansions in Las Vegas and neighboring Henderson, NV, priced between $50,000 to $100,000 per month is severely outstripping supply.

"In the ultraluxury rental space, there's a huge shortage," Natalia Harris, global real estate adviser with Las Vegas Sotheby's International Realty, tells Realtor.com®. There are currently fewer than 10 super-luxury rentals on the market.

"We personally, day to day, feel the frustrations of the shortage of the inventory of these rentals, because we get requests and we can't even keep up with them."

Harris and her husband, fellow Sotheby's adviser Ben Harris, have been actively encouraging developers and investors to create more extravagant rental inventory to keep up with demand.

Alongside celebrity renters, the Harrises often work with out-of-town executives and entrepreneurs who are considering a relocation to Las Vegas but are not sure where exactly to put down roots.

"They're renting for a year maybe, or six months, while they're browsing and shopping for a home and figuring out where they want to be," says Natalia. This class of clients gravitates toward rentals in the $50,000- to $60,000-per-month bracket.

While in the past the biggest feeder market for high-end rentals in Vegas was California, Natalia says over the past year, momentum has shifted to Seattle. Wealthy Washington residents are increasingly eyeing tax-friendly Nevada following the recent passage of the "millionaires tax"—a 9.9% state income tax on earnings exceeding $1 million a year.

Behind this premium rental surge is the valley's rapidly rising cultural cachet.

"Vegas used to be a place where you get a cheap dinner and you gamble, maybe catch a show. But now, Vegas has become the sports and entertainment capital," says Natalia.

In recent years, Las Vegas has cemented its reputation as a top destination for world-class sports, culminating with hosting Super Bowl LVIII in 2024.

The city's jam-packed calendar includes the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix, the NASCAR Cup Series, college football and basketball tournaments, and high-stakes championship boxing. In 2028, Vegas will host the NCAA Men’s Final Four, followed the next year by Super Bowl LXIII.

Beyond headline-making marquee spectacles, Las Vegas has built a thriving local sports scene anchored by championship franchises like the Stanley Cup-winning Vegas Golden Knights and the WNBA champion Las Vegas Aces.

"Vegas has completely evolved, and the attention that we're getting from high net worth individuals ... or celebrities and athletes that are coming here for some of those events, it's just created a whole new dynamic," says Natalia.

Sports is not the city's only draw. As part of the valley's cultural evolution, the Strip has been increasingly attracting A-list entertainers at the peak of their careers, marking a major shift from decades past.

"Vegas used to be a place where artists came when they were toward the end of their career," says Natalia. "Elvis, Frank Sinatra—they would come here as they're winding down for their residencies. Now, that's not the case at all."

The city's most prestigious new venue, the Sphere, has recently featured Backstreet Boys, Metallica, and U2. Pink and John Mayer are slated for upcoming residencies.

"For us in the rental space, that's really where we're seeing our demand, because these artists aren't people that can just walk through the hotel and grab some dinner and be unnoticed and left alone," notes Natalia. "They're going to be swarmed by fans wanting photos, and they need somewhere where they can escape while they're in Vegas."

Affluent clients working with Natalia and her husband often travel with family and aides, and they seek a refuge from the frenzy of the Strip, which they can find in guard-gated golf course communities nestled in the mountains just 15 minutes outside city center.

"A lot of them don't realize there's life off the Strip," says Ben. "Once they find out about that and they stay once, they want to keep coming back."

Demand for luxury rentals in the valley predictably spikes around major events. During the Super Bowl, the Harrises secured accommodations for the families of five top starters from both the San Francisco 49ers and the Kansas City Chiefs.

Summer is a particularly busy season, drawing NBA players to town for the Summer League or off-season workouts at the elite IMPACT Basketball training facility.

These high-profile clients typically rent mansions for one to three months in ultraexclusive enclaves like MacDonald Highlands—a 1,320-acre master-planned golf community nestled in the foothills of the Black and McCullough mountains in Henderson.

The undisputed poster child for this sector of the market is 750 Dragon Ridge Drive in Henderson, which the Harrises rented out for a record-setting $100,000 per month.

The 2.2-acre property features indoor and outdoor basketball courts, a gym, a tennis court, a bowling alley, a spa, and a tour bus hookup that Ben and Natalia had installed at the request of visiting performers. It also includes a separate structure with additional bedrooms and en suite bathrooms to house a celebrity's entourage.

Beyond the square footage and high-end finishes, the most coveted amenity among most big-name Vegas renters is a panoramic view of the glittering Strip.

"Just like if you're going on a beach vacation, you want to make sure your hotel has the oceanfront views, they want to make sure they have that unobstructed Strip view so they can pull out their phone and FaceTime somebody like, 'I told you I'm doing it big in Las Vegas, look at this view of the Strip at night shining.'"

For the Harrises, witnessing their A-list clients take in that view for the first time never gets old.

"It doesn't matter how big the celebrity is, they still get so excited," says Natalia. "And it's so fun to watch that 'awe' moment when they walk into the home and just have the panoramic view of the Las Vegas Strip in front of them. That's our favorite moment."

There are some exceptions, though. Ben shared an anecdote about how, on one occasion, the aides of an unnamed Grammy winner who was staying in town insisted that all the windows be completely blacked out so he could get a good night's rest before his show the following day.

"I'm in there trying to show them the amazing views, and they're like, 'No, we can't see anything but black.' I'm like, 'Oh, just peek out for a second, please!'" he recalls with a laugh.

Once the rental agreement is signed, keeping the world-famous renters happy is the main objective.

"One of the reasons people like to rent through us is because we don't really say no," says Natalia. "If they want something, we make it work. All these homes are definitely dialed in and ready to go, but sometimes people have things that are really special to them."

Typical requests include providing a specific brand of mattress or bed, installing a cold plunge, or reconfiguring the space to create more bedrooms for staff.

Other times, the customization requests are purely for fun, such as painting an NBA team's logo on the basketball court at 750 Dragon Ridge Drive.

"You've got to make it happen at these price points," says Ben. "'No' is not an acceptable answer."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5488. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. #5487. CNCF data shows cloud native is the on-ramp to AI, and maintainers are paying the price

The global population of cloud-native developers has topped 21 million, but the headcount tells only part of the story. Artificial intelligence is changing what those developers build and how open-source projects absorb their work.

Fresh research is putting numbers on that shift. The latest State of Cloud Native Development report from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData Ltd. counts more than 21 million practitioners, or 41% of developers worldwide. Yet that figure likely misses many people who rely on cloud-native infrastructure without knowing it, according to Bob Killen (pictured, right), director of technical program management at CNCF.

“The big thing is it actually might be undercounting a significant amount of them,” Killen said. “Because there’s a very large amount of people that are essentially consuming cloud-native applications without even realizing it.”

Killen and Liam Bollmann-Dodd (left), principal market research consultant at SlashData, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the latest State of Cloud Native Development findings, AI adoption, the strain on open-source maintainers and the shift toward cost discipline. (* Disclosure below.)

The report’s most striking finding concerns AI. About 75% of cloud-native developers use AI in some form, compared with only about 55% of other developers, Bollmann-Dodd noted. The gap mirrors a broader trend of agentic AI pushing Kubernetes into a second act.

“It’s a massive difference,” Bollmann-Dodd said. “So somehow being cloud native enables you and your organization and your personal stack to do AI in all its forms.”

The same AI wave is straining the people who keep the ecosystem running. Sustainability dominated the Maintainer Summit ahead of KubeCon, as maintainers face a flood of pull requests frequently generated by agents, Killen explained.

“How do we as maintainers keep up with the flooding of PRs and issues and things like that?” Killen said. “Especially when many of them are frankly just slop. And the real frustrating part is they’ll be just good enough.”

Cost discipline is the next shift. Just as financial operations practices followed rising cloud bills, cloud-native developers will soon manage model and token spending closely, according to Bollmann-Dodd.

“I think token maxing is dead and it’s going to stay dead forever,” Bollmann-Dodd said. “And I think it’s going to become much more focused on how you spend your money and how you spend your tokens.”

#5486. AI agent tooling provider LangChain secures $300M investment

LangChain Inc., a startup with a set of popular open-source tools for building artificial intelligence agents, has raised $300 million in funding.

The Wall Street Journal reported today that Alphabet Inc.’s CapitalG fund led the round. It was joined by IVP, Sapphire Ventures, GIC and DFJ Growth. LangChain is now worth $3 billion.

San Francisco-based LangChain is best known for the eponymous open-source framework it released in 2022. The software reduces the amount of work involved in building AI agents. LangChain makes it relatively simple to connect an AI agent to a large language model, integrate it with tools and add a system prompt. The framework also enables developers to customize details such as the format of prompt responses.

LangChain’s second open-source tool, LangGraph, is designed for situations where a task is too complicated to be automated by a single agent. LangGraph can link together multiple LangChain-powered agents into a single automation workflow. It can also add in other elements such as a mechanism that requires humans to approve sensitive actions.

The third component of LangChain’s open-source portfolio is Deep Agents. It extends LangChain and  LangGraph with features that make it easier for agents to perform complex work. There’s a virtual file system in which agents can keep data, a work planning tool and a subagent generation feature.

LangChain generates revenue with a suite of paid products called LangSmith. Developers can use it to not only build agents but also to maintain them once they’re in production.

An AI agent usually goes through multiple iterations before it’s released to users. LangSmith enables software teams to save those iterations in a centralized repository. If an update introduces a bug into an agent’s code base, developers can use LangSmith to quickly restore an earlier, bug-free version. Furthermore, they can compare the output quality of different agent versions to identify the one that should be deployed to production.

LangSmith also includes a set of observability features. It generates traces, logs that describe every single step of the workflow through an agent processed a prompt. LangSmith analyzes those traces to find technical issues. From there, it prioritizes them based on their severity and generates code fixes.

After its previous funding round last year, LangChain disclosed that its open-source tools were being downloaded about 90 million times per month. Its LangSmith suite, in turn, is used by Autodesk Inc., Cisco Systems Inc. and a long list of other tech firms.

LangChain reportedly plans to nearly double its headcount to 850 employees by the end of 2027. The company will hire infrastructure experts, AI engineers, salespeople and marketers.

#5485. How Daylight Saving Time Changes the Real Estate Showing Playbook

With Daylight Saving Time already ended, showings that previously took place in daylight may now happen entirely after sunset. For agents, this creates challenges, including scheduling, affecting buyer engagement and property presentation. Here are some key challenges:

Daylight Saving Time changes showing logistics for agents managing multiple buyers and listings. The clock change hurts most in the after-work window. For example, in Austin, the sun now sets around 5:30 p.m., so the 5:30 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. slot that used to cover two or three homes in daylight now covers maybe one. Agents with several active buyers have to stop routing by geography and start sorting by need. One buyer has to see a yard, a view or the street before they can decide, and another is fine walking a condo at 7 p.m. That means moving showings to weekends and lunch hours, and having that talk with buyers at the start of the week rather than in the car at 5:45 p.m.

Traditional open house strategies may or may not remain effective during shorter fall and winter days. The traditional open house was never great at selling homes. It’s great at finding buyers for the agent sitting it. Shorter days don’t change much on their own, since most open houses already run on weekend afternoons. What changes is the margin. Fewer buyers are out in November and December, so a three-hour Sunday open with no promotion behind it will be quiet. We’d rather see agents run shorter, promoted windows and invite the buyer agents who have already shown interest. The open house should be one tool in the showing plan, not the whole marketing strategy.

Agents can protect a property’s curb appeal and first impression when buyers arrive after sunset. Our honest answer is to avoid showings after dark when you can. On the buy side, we tell clients not to tour homes at night. You can’t judge the yard, the street, the drainage or the neighbors’ houses, so it’s a poor experience and usually means a second trip anyway.

On the sell side, we discourage evening showings, and that’s easier than people expect: it’s close to dinner, buyers are tired, and walking through a stranger’s house after dark just feels odd. If a buyer insists, we take the showing, because we want as many showings as we can get. When we do, every exterior light is on, including porch, landscape and garage lights, and every interior light is on too, so the house reads as warm and lived in from the curb. We also make sure the path to the lockbox is well lit, and we include daytime photos in the listing so the buyer already knows what the dark is hiding. Then we offer a daylight second look, because a buyer who liked it at night is almost always worth bringing back during the day.

Showing schedules should be designed around individual property characteristics rather than convenience alone. Scheduling for convenience treats every house the same, and they aren’t the same. A west Austin home with a Hill Country view or a big lot has to be shown in daylight, because that’s what the buyer is paying for. The rare exception is a property whose selling point is the night, like a downtown condo with a lit skyline. The listing agent should set the best showing windows at the pricing conversation and get the seller to agree to them upfront. A buyer who sees a property in the dark and walks away rarely comes back for a second look.

Brokerages can use showing data and buyer feedback to identify seasonal obstacles to buyer engagement. Most brokerages collect showing feedback and do nothing with it. Single comments don’t tell you much; the patterns do. Look at what time of day each showing happened, whether evening showings turn into second showings or offers at the same rate as daylight ones, and whether the same complaints keep coming back: couldn’t see the yard, dark street, hard to find the house.

If a listing gets plenty of evening traffic and no second looks, the problem is presentation, not price, and better lighting, better photos or a daylight window can fix it. Sellers will cut the price long before they ask why showings aren’t turning into offers, so the brokerage has to look first.

Eric Bramlett is the broker/owner of Bramlett Partners, an independent brokerage in Central Texas.

“A price cut tells you the seller’s first number did not work. It does not tell you what the home is worth,” says one real estate professional. “Some reductions create a legitimate opportunity. Others simply bring an unrealistic price closer to where it should have started.” Read more.

#5484. Inside Winter’s Buzziest Getaways—Where Celebrities and Influencers Flock for an Upstate Escape

With cold weather already settling in, A-listers and influencers who call New York City home are heading north to Beacon and the Catskills—turning these upstate towns into the ultimate winter hotspots.

Celebrities and influencers have have been heading over to for an upstate New York escape in winter's hotspots—and their appeal is easy to picture as the cold weather approaches.

Between Beacon’s waterfall-side boutique hotel and the Catskills’ mountain lodges with private soaking tubs, the destinations offer plenty of reasons to leave the city behind for a few days. For some visitors, a weekend away becomes the inspiration for something more permanent.

But what does it cost to buy a place in these coveted retreats, and how much attention are they attracting from New York home shoppers?

The Catskills have drawn Hollywood actors, reality stars, and influencers for vacations, weddings, and a quieter place to call home.

Olivia Wilde and Rami Malek have both stayed at a mountain lodge in Hunter. Jennifer Grey, Ali Wentworth, Olivia Rodrigo, and George Stephanopoulos also headed to the region in 2024 to celebrate the wedding of Schuyler Fox, the daughter of Michael J. Fox and Tracy Pollan.

That same summer, YouTube star Ethan Dolan and influencer Kristina Alice chose the Catskills for their own wedding. Alice later shared photographs from the celebration on Instagram, giving followers a glimpse of their romantic setting.

The fashion crowd has embraced the area, too. Vogue editor Naomi Elizée and Anthony Blue Jr. married in a meadow in Tannersville after welcoming guests for a weekend of festivities.

For Amanda Seyfried, the Catskills offered a place to put down roots. The actress purchased a 1930s farm in 2013 while looking for a retreat from Hollywood, and the property became her main residence.

Across the Hudson, Beacon draws visitors with contemporary art, vintage shops, and an easy trip from New York City. Model and creator Bri Scalesse documented a visit that included Dia Beacon and vintage shopping—an itinerary that works for a day trip or a longer weekend.

According to Realtor.com® data, the median asking price in Beacon was $700,000 in September 2026. In Woodstock, a town included in the Catskills analysis, the median asking price was $968,750 in October.

Those figures offer snapshots of two individual markets. The broader home-search analysis covers all of Dutchess County, where Beacon is located, and five Catskills counties.

According to Realtor.com data, the Catskills accounted for 1.17% of all listing views from the New York City metro in the third quarter of 2026, up from 1.03% a year earlier.

Dutchess County’s share rose from 0.53% to 0.58%, giving the Catskills roughly twice its share of NYC-area browsing.

Both destinations gained a bigger share of a shrinking pool of views. NYC-metro views of Catskills listings fell about 28% year over year, while views of Dutchess County listings declined about 31%. NYC-area views across all listings fell more sharply, by about 37%.

New York remained the largest source of listing views for both destinations, even as shoppers elsewhere accounted for more of their audience. NYC-metro shoppers generated 37.5% of Catskills listing views, down from 42.3% a year earlier. In Dutchess County, their share slipped from 43.3% to 39.8%.

“Winter getaway buzz hasn’t translated into a winter surge in home shopping,” says Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones.

“Interest in the Catskills and Beacon follows normal seasonal patterns, but both places hold on to the attention of New York–area shoppers better than most markets, and they’re taking up a growing share of what those shoppers look at. At the same time, New York–area shoppers make up a smaller share of the audience for each destination than they did a year ago.”

According to Realtor.com data, NYC-metro listing views fell 21% to 25% in the Catskills and 19% to 25% in Dutchess County between the third and fourth quarters over the three years analyzed. Those declines were broadly in line with the national seasonal slowdown.

NYC-area views across all listings fell more sharply, by 30% to 37%, allowing both destinations to capture a larger share of attention heading into the holidays. In 2025, for example, the Catskills’ share of NYC-metro browsing rose from 1.03% in the third quarter to 1.23% in the fourth.

From the fourth quarter to the first, NYC-metro views fell by 2%, 8%, and 15% in the Catskills and by 6%, 5%, and 16% in Dutchess County across the three winters studied. Over those same periods, NYC-metro views across all listings rose by 2% to 10%.

For buyers picturing a winter retreat, the figures show that home browsing in these destinations slows after the holidays, even as New Yorkers’ searches pick up elsewhere.

#5483. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

#5482. Surging AI chip revenue and Microsoft deal boost Cerebras Systems stock by 17%

Artificial intelligence chipmaker Cerebras Systems Inc. delivered third-quarter revenue that comfortably beat expectations in its latest financial report today while announcing a new deal with Microsoft Corp., sending its stock up almost 18% in late trading.

The company reported a loss before certain costs such as stock compensation of 67 cents per share, trailing Wall Street’s guidance of a 14-cent-per-share loss, though because of some accounting idiosyncrasies, its numbers are not directly comparable with that guidance. Meanwhile, core adjusted revenue for the period came to $230.9 million, up 70% from a year earlier and surpassing the Street’s target of $214.7 million.

The adjustments in Cerebras’ revenue are the result of some of the quirks in its accounting procedures. The company includes some pass-through revenue that’s subtracted from the total, and it also issues warrants to its major customers, which are then amortized as noncash reductions in revenue based on standard accounting rules, and so these are left out of the adjusted number.

Despite these complexities, investors were clearly impressed with the company’s growth over the quarter, and perhaps even more so by its progress toward profitability. Though Cerebras has not been able to show a profit yet, its adjusted operating margin of -14% was still significantly better than its earlier guidance of -24% from three months earlier.

Chief Executive Andrew Feldman (pictured) told analysts on a conference call that the company has an advantage over its competitors, which are struggling to keep up with customer demand and dealing with growing order backlogs. “I think there is opportunity created, particularly on the hardware side, the sale of hardware, where long lead times in GPUs and more expense creates opportunity for us,” he said, referring to Nvidia Corp.’s graphics processing units.

Cerebras does have a significant backlog for both hardware and cloud services itself, and that number rose from $25 billion in August to $26 billion at the end of the quarter. However, a significant portion of that backlog is related to the deal it struck with OpenAI Group PBC, Feldman said. This implies that other customers don’t have to wait so long for their orders to be processed.

Meanwhile, the chipmaker continues to expand its customer base. After recently signing deals with Amazon Web Services Inc. and Oracle Corp., the company today announced a new customer in Microsoft Corp., although it didn’t provide many particulars about that agreement. The small increase in its backlog doesn’t do much to settle concerns that all of those deals are on the small side, however.

“We believe revenue begins to show up in quarter one of fiscal 2027,” Feldman said after explaining that the agreement with Microsoft was signed and sealed a month earlier.

Holger Mueller of Constellation Research said investors will have been pleased to see the growth in Cerebras’ cloud services business, which gives it a more dependable revenue stream than straightforward hardware sales. However, he also questioned the cost of that impressive growth.

“Cloud and other services revenue was up 272% to $114.9 million, which is good, but the company’s R&D expense more than tripled during the quarter to $177 million. That’s why its earnings-per-share loss more than doubled,” the analyst said. “This is not sustainable over the long term, so Andrew Feldman is going to need to find a way to grow even faster, or else cut back on R&D spending in future. Investors will be watching closely to see what the longer-term plan for growth is.”

Investor’s concerns over spending are valid, because Cerebras is likely to find it much harder to secure capital going forward due to the growing concerns around the sustainability of the broader AI infrastructure buildout. Feldman told analysts that the company is now evaluating its financing options to find ways to meet customer demand and make inroads into its order backlog, but it’s not clear what that financing will look like.

Cerebras may perhaps be able to benefit from the uncertainty at its biggest rival Nvidia, which still dominates the AI chip industry, accounting for over 90% of all chip sales, according to some analysts.

Nvidia is in turmoil following the shocking resignation of its co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. It’s believed that Huang was likely forced to hand in his resignation after being outed for having an affair with an executive of a Singapore-based data center infrastructure firm, who is believed to have been acting as a spy for Chinese intelligence and a conduit for illegal shipments of GPUs into that country. Huang also had a second affair with one of Nvidia’s executives, according to reports that emerged yesterday, and reportedly a third one too.

It may take a while for Cerebras and other chipmakers to take advantage of the disruption to Nvidia, which is seeking to maintain stability through the appointment of longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO, but in the short term its prospects still look good. The company said it anticipates a core gross margin of 47% to 49% in the fourth quarter, with revenue rising to between $310 million and $330 million. Wall Street analysts are looking for a core gross margin of just 42.1% on sales of $271 million.

Moreover, Feldman told analysts on the call that the company believes its revenue will triple by the end of fiscal 2027. If that holds true, it would mean full-year revenue of around $2.85 billion, slightly below Wall Street’s long-term forecast of $2.92 billion in fiscal 2027.

#5478. Kubernetes now runs containers and VMs side by side

KubeVirt’s graduation from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) marks a turning point in a debate that once pitted containers against virtual machines. A decade on, Kubernetes is becoming one platform for legacy VMs, cloud-native apps and AI.

Enterprises still run much of their IT on VMs, even as AI pushes them toward new infrastructure. Red Hat Inc. is betting they won’t have to choose, with OpenShift 5 managing containers, VMs and AI workloads in one environment. Running two separate systems was never the goal, according to Fabian Deutsch (pictured), director of engineering for OpenShift Virtualization and Modernization and a KubeVirt maintainer at Red Hat.

“But you’ve also got VMs, right, where you’re running applications in the old way that we did for decades before. And do you really want to maintain these two systems?” Deutsch said. “So our vision was, how can we unite those worlds to eventually make it easier to have one paradigm to run both, all these compute workloads on one platform.”

Deutsch spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed KubeVirt’s graduation, running VMs and containers on one Kubernetes platform, AI’s influence on virtualization and what comes next for the project. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes has drawn open-source projects and commercial providers onto a common platform, and AI’s hunger for compute has deepened that pull. Much of KubeVirt’s recent innovation now comes from the AI side, Deutsch explained.

“You don’t want to repave your data center just because you’ve got a new workload that you need to address,” Deutsch said. “So you’re having that flexibility to run it in the way that you need it.”

The CNCF announced the graduation at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, seven years after accepting the project into its sandbox. Next on the list is passing GPUs, CPUs and memory into VMs, while AI is changing how the community values virtualization itself, Deutsch noted.

“There’s a lot of influx of features due to AI, by the way,” Deutsch said. “The isolation model, we didn’t get to it in the beginning, but the isolation of virtualization is helping, right, in the AI age as well.”

The project already runs on edge devices and in the cloud because it offers a consistent API across those footprints, according to Deutsch. Nvidia Corp. was an early adopter, and Microsoft Corp. is now stepping up, he noted.

“I think it’s about getting the right and next generation infrastructure into your house,” Deutsch said. “KubeVirt allows you to carry forward what you’ve got, what you invested in over the past decades, and not to leave it alone because you have to carry it forward.”

#5477. Inflation, Supply Policies to Have Most Impact on Housing Affordability Post-Elections: Economists

American voters made it clear that affordability was one of the main drivers that tipped them in favor of putting Democrats in control of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections.

Democratic candidates flipped both the House of Representatives and Senate blue, buoyed by voters who have seen their everyday living costs skyrocket under the second Trump administration—and made it clear they wanted change.

But now the real work of making those campaign promises a reality begins—with housing affordability a top concern. Any solutions Congress might come up with to combat rising housing costs will take time to put into motion and generally inspire bipartisan cooperation, three top economists tell RISMedia.

Before any policies come into play, economists say inflation is a critical risk to mortgage rate stability and, in turn, the health of the housing market.

Inflation, economic headwinds top issues to watch

Getting inflation under control and expanding housing supply without creating outpaced demand could help shape housing affordability, economists say.

October’s hotter-than-expected inflation reading, up 0.4% instead of the 0.3% forecasted month-over-month, makes it highly likely the Federal Reserve will hike rates when it meets in December. In fact, 90% of analysts polled by CME Group anticipate the Fed will hike its target rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4.00% to 4.25%.

“What matters most for buyers and sellers is whether inflation eases and mortgage rates become more affordable and the labor market stays healthy,” says Odeta Kushi, deputy chief economist with First American Financial.

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Another inflationary metric to watch is the U.S. national debt, Kushi notes, which now stands at more than $40 trillion. This will become even more urgent when the current debt limit of $41.1 trillion is reached by May or mid-2027. If there’s a congressional standoff over increasing the debt limit, that could drive inflation—and borrowing costs—higher while creating more financial market volatility, she explained.

But getting inflation under control depends on a lot of moving parts, according to Jake Krimmel, senior economist with Realtor.com®. Under the Trump administration, it’s impossible to pinpoint those moving parts amid a trade war (and tariffs), geopolitical tensions and mixed economic readings.

Krimmel stressed that inflation also erodes purchasing power. “Inflation eats away at paychecks and makes it harder for people to save.”

“The big wild card heading into 2027 is the same one that we’ve been talking about probably since February, which is the effect of the (Iran) War on the longer end of the curve, the Fed’s rate path and the economy more broadly, especially with respect to inflation, consumer confidence and consumer spending,” Krimmel says. “We don’t know what 2027 will bring, but uncertainty is a feature in this market.”

Mischa Fisher, Zillow’s chief economist, points to a simple formula that will bring mortgage rates down to more palatable levels for homebuyers to act.

“We know, generally speaking, that the best way out of this is higher incomes, lower mortgage rates and more supply,” Fisher says.

According to Zillow’s October housing report, the monthly mortgage payment on the typical U.S. home reached $2,004, up 12.8% from a year ago. That means a median-income household would need to spend 34.7% of its income on total housing costs—up from 32.7% a year ago and far beyond the typical 30% benchmark, Zillow reported.

Fisher noted that the Democrats’ sweep of the midterms hasn’t altered Zillow’s housing forecasts, which call for rates to stay in the 7% range, flat-to-lower sales volume compared to 2026 and home values that rise slightly on paper but decline slightly in real terms after adjusting for inflation.

Could Congress pull any meaningful levers for housing?

When the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, they’ll have their work cut out for them to deliver for voters who made affordability a central election motivation. However, with President Donald Trump already pledging to use the power of his pen to veto Democrat-led bills, will any meaningful housing legislation see the light of day?

“When we have this period where Congress is controlled by one party and the executive branch is controlled by the other party, typically, that doesn’t foretell close collaboration on policy,” Fisher says. “But I think we have seen that in the case of housing, there is a bipartisan agreement that there’s room to improve the environment. That’s what we’re watching to see play out.”

Fisher notes that the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed earlier this year, offers “a real bipartisan blueprint for how policymakers can work together to specifically improve housing.” The timing couldn’t be more crucial as the gap between Americans’ incomes and affordable housing widens.

Kushi adds that Congress should look at policies that make it “easier, cheaper and faster to build and bring more homes to the market.”

While it’s too early to know what lawmakers have in mind to help ease affordability pressures in the housing market, Krimmel cautions that any government stalemates—a shutdown or lapses in government funding—could be disastrous for the 10-year Treasury yield, which directly impacts mortgage rate movements. A government shutdown can also disrupt economic data collection, making it harder to gauge progress on inflation.

“We already have enough pressure on the 10-year,” Krimmel says. “We don’t need anything else.”

All three economists agree that improving housing affordability involves addressing the supply side, among other action items.

The U.S. has an estimated supply gap of 4.03 million homes, according to Realtor.com. Closing the gap, Krimmel says, means boosting new construction, which needs to be “easier to build.” Lawmakers should “encourage states and localities to adopt more permissive local zoning laws and also streamline that permitting process,” Krimmel says, cautioning that it will take time to see any gains.

For now, Realtors® should track local inventory and price trends to help guide their clients more effectively. Fisher notes that affordability-related softness and price pressures will persist in parts of the Mountain West and Sun Belt, while supply-constrained coastal markets where new building isn’t as robust face upward pressure.

Existing-home inventory is still being suppressed by the mortgage lock-in effect, as owners may be reluctant to sell and give up their pandemic-era low rates. More realistic pricing from sellers can help listings go under contract and give buyers more negotiating power. But a more buyer-friendly market doesn’t necessarily mean homes are affordable to more buyers, Krimmel says.

Only time will tell if income growth can keep up with housing costs—and if Congress can act quickly enough to start meaningfully improving affordability to help ease Americans’ financial strain.

Deborah Kearns is a freelance editor and writer with more than 15 years of experience covering real estate, mortgages and personal finance topics. Her work has appeared in The New York Times, Forbes Advisor, The Associated Press, MarketWatch, USA Today, MSN and HuffPost, among others. Deborah previously held editorial leadership and writing roles at NerdWallet, Bankrate, LendingTree and RE/MAX World Headquarters.

#5476. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. For more information about working with a Redfin real estate agent to buy or sell a home, visit our Why Redfin page.

Yingqi is a Senior Economist at Redfin. He studies housing market trends and explains what’s driving them for a broad audience. He previously led research on responsible AI at Freddie Mac, and also worked at Meta and the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Yingqi holds a Ph.D. in economics from Georgetown University, and his research is published in the American Economic Journal: Microeconomics and the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics.

Szu Yu Chen is a senior data visualization designer and developer who creates interactive graphics and data-driven experiences. Previously, she worked as a graphics reporter at The Washington Post and the Los Angeles Times.

#5475. Quantum sensor and software maker Q-CTRL raises $290M in funding

Q-CTRL Pty Ltd., a provider of quantum sensors and software for managing qubits, today announced that it has raised $290 million in funding.

Q-CTRL sells a series of quantum navigation systems called Ironstone Opal. The company positions the product family as a more reliable alternative to GPS. Q-CTRL says that the devices can withstand jamming attempts, adverse weather and other challenging conditions that interfere with GPS signals.

Ironstone Opal tracks the host vehicle’s position with the help of sensors known as quantum magnetometers and quantum gravimeters. The sensors use variations in the Earth’s magnetic field and gravity as navigation cues.

Gravity is weaker at the top of a mountain than at sea level because the peak is farther away from the Earth’s core. The Earth’s magnetic field, in turn, exhibits perturbations at regions that have mineral deposits. Such gravitational and magnetic anomalies act as a unique fingerprint of the location where they occur. When a quantum sensor detects the fingerprint, it can deduce its location with relative ease.

Q-CTRL’s quantum magnetometers collect navigation data using tiny glass structures filled with clouds of atoms. The atoms change in specific ways when they encounter an anomaly in the Earth’s magnetic field. According to the company, its sensors detect those changes with the help of laser beams. Quantum gravimeters operate on a similar principle.

Ironstone Opal includes not only sensors but also software that processes the data they generate. It filters erroneous measurements, combines the remaining data with logs from other sensors and compares the information against pre-loaded maps.

C-QTRL offers Ironstone Opal alongside a pair of software tools designed to make quantum computers easier to use. The first tool, Boulder Opal, helps researchers calibrate qubits in a manner that optimizes their performance. It’s complemented by Fire Opal, which makes quantum algorithms less prone to errors.

“The hard problem in quantum is not building the machine, it is getting useful output from it,” said Salesforce Ventures partner Robert Keith. “Q-CTRL solves that with AI-powered control software, and the proof is already public: a materials simulation on IBM hardware that any developer can now call directly from the IBM Quantum Platform, and the first quantum navigation system qualified for safety of flight.”

Q-CTRL will use the proceeds from the funding round to enhance its software and grow its international presence.
