#5437. Builder credit conditions tighten for 19th straight quarter

NAHB’s Q3 2026 AD&C Financing survey shows credit for land acquisition, development and construction tightened for the 19th consecutive quarter, mirroring Federal Reserve loan officer data. Contract rates moved only modestly and were offset by lower points, keeping effective borrowing costs elevated across most AD&C categories. Builders are increasingly using construction-to-permanent loans tied to end buyers, with 32% of respondents using them and, for those, 58% of homes financed this way. Persistent tight AD&C lending threatens to slow lot development and new-home supply, reinforcing structural housing shortages even as the mortgage market shows its own signs of stress.  AI Summary

Credit conditions for residential land acquisition, development and construction (AD&C) loans tightened again in the third quarter of 2026, extending a nearly five-year stretch of more restrictive lending for homebuilders, according to a National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) survey.

NAHB’s quarterly AD&C Financing survey showed a net easing index of -15.3 in Q3, meaning more builders and developers reported tighter credit than easier credit. It marks the 19th consecutive quarter of net tightening for AD&C borrowers, NAHB economist Paul Emrath wrote in an analysis published Nov. 13.

The findings closely track the Federal Reserve’s October survey of senior loan officers. NAHB reported that the Fed’s net easing index for residential AD&C loans came in at -15.5 in the third quarter. Aside from modest lender-reported easing in the second quarter of 2026, both lenders and builders have indicated that AD&C credit has been tightening steadily since early 2022. The Fed’s index has been in negative territory in 18 of the past 19 quarters.

For homebuilders and land developers, those readings underscore that bank appetite for risk in residential construction remains weak even as broader housing demand depends on new supply.

While credit availability continued to contract, AD&C financing costs showed only modest quarter-to-quarter movement in the third quarter, with no clear trend toward either higher or lower overall borrowing costs.

NAHB reported the following changes in average contract interest rates between the second and third quarters of 2026:

At the same time, initial points on AD&C loans declined across all four categories, NAHB found:

Those offsetting moves left effective borrowing costs — which combine contract rates and points — little changed for most types of AD&C credit:

For builders, the message is that even where nominal rates tick lower, the all-in cost of capital for lots and vertical construction remains high by historical standards. Combined with tighter underwriting, that environment can slow lot pipeline development, constrain spec building and push more risk and cost back onto builders’ balance sheets.

NAHB’s third-quarter survey also highlighted increased use of construction-to-permanent, or one-time-close, loans tied directly to the end buyer.

Among survey respondents who built single-family homes in the third quarter, 32% said they financed at least some production with construction-to-permanent loans to the ultimate homebuyer. On average, 58% of the homes those respondents built were financed this way, NAHB reported.

Those structures can help builders reduce their direct exposure to AD&C credit by shifting some financing to retail mortgage channels earlier in the process. They can also appeal to buyers looking to lock both construction and permanent financing terms in a single transaction, an important hedge in a volatile rate environment.

NAHB noted that market stress in residential mortgages – including a recent drop in applications and rising delinquencies – has drawn significant attention. But the group argued that constrained AD&C financing is an underappreciated bottleneck for adding new supply, especially in affordable and entry-level segments.

Because AD&C loans finance land pipelines, infrastructure and vertical construction, persistently tight lending standards can limit lot development, delay projects and reduce the number of homes that reach the for-sale market. That dynamic can amplify the impact of low existing-home inventory and keep upward pressure on home prices and rents.

For builders, developers and their lenders, the survey results suggest that planning assumptions for 2027 should continue to factor in restricted credit availability, elevated effective borrowing costs and a need for diversified capital sources, including joint ventures, private capital and greater use of buyer-based construction-to-perm structures.

More detail on credit conditions for residential builders and developers, including cross-tabs on lender behavior and loan terms, is available on NAHB’s AD&C Financing Survey web page.

#5436. Agent fleets drag the messaging layer from afterthought to AI’s coordination core

Data center telemetry, sandboxed AI workloads and fleets of agents are pushing more machine-to-machine traffic through infrastructure than ever before, exposing the limits of messaging systems built for steadier demand.

That shift is drawing attention to the Neural Autonomic Transport System, an open-source messaging system that lets applications and services exchange messages by topic. Created in 2010, NATS graduated from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation in November 2026. Its simple design suits AI workloads, according to Andrew Connolly (pictured, left), NATS project maintainer at Synadia Communications Inc., a provider of managed NATS services. When AI tools like Lovable can turn a plain-language prompt into a working web app, the messaging layer has to keep updates flowing as sandboxes come and go.

“What’s changed in the current context, or landscape, is everything is really ephemeral. If you take the Lovable example, connections coming and going really fast, tons of churn, tons of sandboxes, all these things spinning up, spinning down,” Connolly said. “Not every technology can handle that.”

Connolly and Waldemar Quevedo (right), project maintainer of NATS at Synadia, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how NATS handles traffic from short-lived sandboxes, carries data center telemetry and helps AI agents hand off work. (* Disclosure below.)

The demands go well beyond app sandboxes. The project itself has grown from single-cluster deployments into a system that spans data centers, regions and clouds, with one AI app builder recently rebuilding its real-time service on NATS to serve millions of subscriptions, Quevedo noted.

“NATS has evolved to be able to communicate multiple data centers with a super cluster topology with the gateways,” Quevedo said. “It is smart [at routing] the interest graph out to multiple regions, multiple availability zones, multi-cloud.”

Some data center operators use NATS to carry power and cooling telemetry, and Nvidia Corp. built its AI factory event bus on the system as part of its DSX reference architecture, Connolly said. NATS can also route messages across fleets of AI agents, with its JetStream persistence engine and key-value store preserving the state agents need to hand off work.

“In some sense, agentic systems are just microservices systems, but at a bigger scale,” Connolly said. “NATS was good for microservices. It’s going to be great for AI agents.”

#5435. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

Ze boden een oplossing die niet alleen aan onze huidige eisen voor de modernisering van het distributienet voldoet, maar ook schaalbaar is voor toekomstige integratie van hernieuwbare energie. #5433. Why Midwest buyer demand is holding up in the face of higher mortgage rates

Midwest metros, including Columbus and Cincinnati, are keeping pending sales near or above new listings as mortgage activity stays mixed. Lower list prices and smaller loan amounts appear to support demand, even with rates above 7% pressuring affordability.  AI Summary

Several Midwest housing markets are showing signs of resilient buyer demand compared to other parts of the country, with pending home sales keeping pace with new listings even as purchase mortgage activity remains largely flat or declines.

Columbus, Ohio, had 127 pending sales for every 100 new listings as of Nov. 6, according to HousingWire Data. Cincinnati followed at 125. These markets were well above the national average of 95 pending sales per 100 new listings, while Cleveland (91) and St. Louis (90) were running slightly below the U.S. average.

The same markets also had median list prices that were considerably lower than the national average of $429,000. Cleveland led the way at $174,000, followed by St. Louis ($225,000), Columbus ($255,000) and Cincinnati ($300,000).

In St. Louis, buyers remain active despite elevated mortgage rates, although they are being more deliberate about their decisions, said Greg Iverson, a divisional sales manager for Neighborhood Loans.

“I wouldn’t say it’s necessarily a buyer’s market, but it’s starting to become that way in certain areas,” Iverson said in an interview with HousingWire.

Like most buyers nationwide, affordability remains the biggest obstacle for his clients, Iverson said. Mortgage rates above 7% have added to the rising costs of property taxes, homeowners insurance, building materials and home repairs. Inventory has also increased in some price ranges, he said, but not across the board.

But Iverson said St. Louis continues to see activity from first-time and move-up buyers alike since the market’s lower home prices have helped keep these buyers from being priced out entirely.

A similar pattern is playing out in smaller Ohio markets. Scott Snapp, a Findlay, Ohio-based branch manager at loanDepot, said his business has remained steady, with loan applications coming in at about the same pace as last year.

When comparing his October 2026 production with the same point a year earlier, Snapp said he had closed 57 loans totaling $12 million last year, versus 51 loans totaling $11 million at the time of the interview. Snapp said his average loan size is about $215,000.

“I’m not seeing a drop, realistically,” he said. “Applications coming in are still at the same pace as they were last year around here.”

Mortgage data platform Modex shows that purchase lending has been relatively steady in several Midwest markets, but it has not uniformly increased.

Cleveland was the only one of four Midwest metros in HousingWire’s comparison to record year-over-year growth in purchase loans from January through July, with 11,809 loans, up 0.9%. Cincinnati recorded 14,048 loans, down 2.2%, while Columbus had 12,820, down 2.7%. St. Louis recorded 9,811 loans, a 6.8% decline. The St. Louis figure excludes St. Louis County since 2026 county records were still being updated.

Modex data indicated that median purchase loan amounts in these Midwest markets ranged from $217,075 in Cleveland to $294,566 in Columbus. Lower loan amounts and home prices could attest to some of the Midwest’s relative resilience. More than 20% of purchase loans in Cleveland and St. Louis were for less than $150,000.

But the resilience is still being tested. Jason Harris, a Columbus-based branch manager at Rate, described September as a slow month for contracts that would have closed in October. And he expected October to be one of the slower months the market had seen in years due to higher mortgage rates.

But he added that contract activity improved over the course of October as mortgage rates eased.

“I feel blessed to be in Columbus because it’s still an area where you can purchase an affordable home,” Harris said. “Affordability is something that is so desperately needed by buyers right now. … Even three-eighths of a percent is having a meaningful impact on demand.”

Harris said first-time buyers, as well as borrowers using down payment assistance and state bond programs, typically make up a larger share of his business late in the year. These buyers, coupled with lower-priced homes, typically bring down his average loan size in the fourth quarter, while also driving more Federal Housing Administration loans and government-backed adjustable-rate mortgages, he said.

Back in St. Louis, Iverson said the metro area has continued to attract interest from real estate investors, including those who are becoming more selective about where they purchase as costs rise in other markets.

Snapp also pointed to local employment as a source of housing demand in his part of Ohio, citing new distribution centers and business activity, including facilities opened by Amazon and planned by Sheetz.

“We’re seeing a lot of businesses coming into this area and opening up, and that’s helped us,” he said.

The market has also benefited from buyers relocating from other states, Snapp said. Some have moved for work, while others are returning to the area to be near family.

St. Louis and smaller Ohio markets contrast with areas where mortgage professionals have reported weaker activity. Iverson said he has heard of homes sitting longer in markets such as San Diego, while Snapp said colleagues in Las Vegas and Seattle had described slower conditions.

Harris said he expects demand in central Ohio to pick up again as the market moves into 2027, even if some buyers are postponing purchases until the spring. He said the region’s underlying need for housing remains strong.

“The number of people that need homes and want homes in central Ohio over the next five years is going to be good,” he said.

#5431. Will the Fifth Circuit keep FinCEN anti-money laundering rule off the books?

ALTA and TLTA urged the Fifth Circuit to uphold a March ruling that vacated FinCEN’s residential real estate AML reporting rule. The groups argue FinCEN underestimated compliance costs and exceeded its authority under the Bank Secrecy Act.  AI Summary

The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network’s (FinCEN) Residential Real Estate Rule is not currently in effect and the American Land Title Association (ALTA) and the Texas Land Title Association (TLTA) would like it to stay that way.

In late October, ALTA and TLTA filed amicus briefs asking the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit to uphold a ruling that vacated FinCEN’s nationwide anti-money laundering (AML) rule.

The AML rule mandated reporting for any non-financed residential real estate transfer where ownership was held by an entity or trust — with no geographic or price threshold.

The rule was overturned in late March by a federal judge in the Eastern District of Texas after the law had been in effect for less than three weeks. In early May, FinCEN appealed the ruling.

This ruling and subsequent appeal are part of a lawsuit filed by Flowers Title Companies, LLC, which argued that FinCEN lacked authority under the Bank Secrecy Act to impose such sweeping reporting requirements.

In their briefs ALTA and TLTA argued that the rule “imposes significant costs and operational burdens on title and settlement professionals without adequately demonstrating that its benefits justify those requirements.”

According to ALTA, FinCEN’s cost estimate of implementing the policy of $559.4 million was too low, as the association felt FinCEN did not fully account for the cost to title companies for employee training, technology changes, record keeping and the time it takes to get information from buyers and sellers. Additionally, ALTA argues that title professionals have no authority to force buyers or sellers to provide them with beneficial ownership information and that financial institutions already collect beneficial ownership information from their business customers when accounts are opened.

In its filing, TLTA adds that the transactions FinCEN’s rule targets are routine and legal, noting that FinCEN’s legal authority only applies to “suspicious” transactions, not an entire class of transaction.

It remains to be seen how the appeals court will rule on this issue. However, FinCEN has also said it will not require retroactive reporting for transactions that would have been reportable during these legal proceedings.

FinCEN had argued the rule was necessary to close loopholes that allowed money launderers, drug traffickers and other illicit actors to use shell companies and trusts to purchase property with anonymity.

Fidelity National Financial (FNF) has also challenged FinCEN’s AML rule in court, but this resulted in the rule being upheld. That decision has since been appealed by FNF in the Eleventh Circuit.

#5430. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

#5429. Mirendil raises $1B in funding to speed up AI model development

Mirendil Inc., a provider of software that speeds up artificial intelligence development, has raised $1 billion in early-stage funding.

The startup stated on Thursday that Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital jointly led the Series A investment. They were joined by more than a half-dozen others including Google LLC.

Mirendil was launched last year by two former Google DeepMind and Anthropic PBC researchers. Chief Executive Officer Behnam Neyshabur is a co-inventor of SAM, a popular algorithm that makes AI models better at tasks they were not specifically trained to perform. Chief Technology Officer Harsh Mehta, in turn, spent his time at Google DeepMind and Anthropic working on pretraining projects. Pretraining is a term for the initial phase of the AI development workflow.

Mirendil’s first product, Lor, is a platform that automates many of the tasks involved in model training runs. The company says that the software does so by splitting work among hundreds of AI agents.

Large language model development involves a significant amount of trial and error. Researchers create multiple versions of an algorithm that differ from one another in small ways and compare them to find the most performant variant. According to Mirendil, Lor can automate that workflow. If an error crops up during the evaluation, the platform fixes it automatically.

Earlier this year, Mirendil asked one of its researchers to build a coding model that can compete with leading open-source LLMs. Usually, such projects are carried out by teams of specialists. Mirendil says that its automation technology enabled the researcher to build the model without any help from colleagues. The project cost $10 million and took about 3.5 months to complete.

The company’s agents wrote more than 99% of the code that powers the model, which is called Mirendil-Base. They set up infrastructure, found a suitable training algorithm and collected training data from the web. The agents then refined both the training dataset and Mirendil-Base’s architecture to boost output quality.

The LLM is the foundation of a specialized coding model called Fern that the company unveiled last month. According to Mirendil, it’s designed to automate programming challenges commonly encountered by AI labs. Fern can process 10 million input tokens per prompt, or 10 times more than Claude Opus 5.5. That’s the equivalent of about a half-million lines of code.

Fern is based on a version of Mirendil-Base with 100 billion to 500 billion parameters. Late last month, the company previewed two upgraded versions of the latter model with between 500 billion and 10 trillion parameters. Mirendil plans to use those algorithms to develop more capable LLMs.

#5428. Zcash Price Fate: ZEC Crypto to Bounce or Fall Further From Critical $1,000 Support?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

The breakdown puts a major psychological level in view, with traders watching if bulls can reclaim $1,000 before another wave of selling hits. Zcash is also approaching its 0.5 Fibonacci retracement level, an area that could attract buyers looking for a potential relief rally.

Strangely enough, the decline comes despite Grayscale committing $1 million to support the Zcash ecosystem. Its investment campaign and development funding have failed to reverse the selling pressure. A technical bounce will depend heavily on Bitcoin stabilizing after its own recent weakness. If BTC continues falling, ZEC could struggle to find enough demand to establish a lasting bottom.

Zcash price latest decline has erased much of its September rally, when ZEC climbed toward $1,700 before momentum started fading. The coin fell 13% to 15% during the latest major sell-off, briefly touching $960. Its weekly losses have now exceeded 26%, putting it among the weaker performers in the large-cap market.

Not just that, Grayscale has also launched a nationwide Zcash marketing campaign, starting with a front-page advertising wrap and a full-page ad inside The Wall Street Journal promoting its Zcash ETF (ZCSH).

Some are calling it the greatest edition of @WSJ yet. Grab your copy.The Zcash $ZEC takeover. @ZcashInvest https://t.co/LMcEuSHTb0 pic.twitter.com/0ArtKaVY7b

The first $400,000 has already been distributed among four organizations, including the Zcash Foundation, Shielded Labs, Project Tachyon, and Pretty Good Policy for Zcash. Grayscale also intends to reinvest 100% of its Zcash ETF sponsor fees into network development, marketing, and education for up to one year.

Grayscale’s Zcash ETF, trading under the ticker ZCSH, recorded $46.25 million in outflows during October. November withdrawals have added further pressure, with nearly $30 million leaving the fund through November 11.

Derivatives traders have also faced significant losses. ZEC liquidations reached approximately $18 million over 24 hours, with leveraged long positions accounting for around 72% of the total.

Technically, Zcash is approaching an important decision point after losing the $1,000 psychological level. The 0.5 Fibonacci retracement is now attracting attention as a potential area for buyers to defend. This midpoint could decide whether a correction is becoming exhausted or another leg lower is playing out.

A successful defense could give ZEC room for a short-term recovery, particularly if Bitcoin manages to stabilize and restore confidence across the altcoin market. The first challenge is reclaiming $1,000. ZEC needs to turn that former support into resistance-turned-support again before bulls can build a convincing recovery case.

A sustained move above $1,000 could open the way toward $1,100, followed by the $1,200 region. The latter also aligns with an important technical recovery area after the recent breakdown.

But the bearish scenario remains firmly on the table. If ZEC loses its 0.5 Fibonacci support, traders could start looking toward $900 and potentially the $800 region. That would extend the correction and give September’s rally further room to unwind.

The Relative Strength Index is also approaching oversold territory, with recent readings near 34. This shows that selling momentum has become stretched, although it does not guarantee an immediate reversal.

$1,000 remains the level bulls need to reclaim, while the 0.5 Fibonacci retracement could determine whether the latest correction is nearing exhaustion or has another painful chapter ahead.

#5426. Stubborn input inflation pressures builders despite energy pullback

NAHB’s analysis of the October Producer Price Index shows total inputs to new residential construction up 0.3% on the month and 10.4% year over year, outpacing overall PPI inflation. Goods costs were flat in October, but building materials rose 0.5% and 5.8% annually, with diesel, plywood and board products elevated. Service inputs climbed 0.7% in October and 11.3% year over year, led by double-digit gains in trade services and transportation. The data underscores ongoing pressure on bids, budgets and pro formas, even as headline energy prices ease.  AI Summary

Residential construction input costs continued to outpace overall inflation in October, as gains in building material and service prices offset a monthly decline in energy, according to a National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) analysis of this morning’s Producer Price Index (PPI) release.

The price index for inputs to new residential construction — which combines goods and services — rose 0.3% in October and is 10.4% higher than a year ago, NAHB economist Jesse Wade said. By comparison, the PPI for final demand overall increased 0.3% in October and 6.5% year over year.

For builders, that gap underscores a persistent cost squeeze even as some headline inflation measures appear to cool.

Goods make up roughly 60% of the residential construction inputs index. Overall, the price of input goods used in new residential construction (including energy) was unchanged in October, following a 1.7% jump in September, and is up 9.8% over the past 12 months.

That stability at the top line masks diverging trends beneath the surface:

Key product categories continue to move higher:

For single-family and multifamily builders, the mix of slightly moderating year-over-year gains in some materials and still-elevated levels in others complicates bid setting, option pricing and value-engineering decisions heading into 2027 build cycles.

Service inputs to residential construction, which cover distribution margins, transportation and a range of other services, rose 0.7% in October and are 11.3% higher than October 2025, according to NAHB.

The services side of the index is split into three major components:

All three are running well above general inflation:

Because services often adjust more slowly than commodity prices, this side of the index tends to be “stickier.” For builders, that means even if some material categories ease, fully loaded installed costs can remain elevated due to freight, storage and distribution charges.

The October PPI data reinforces several themes for homebuilders, land developers and their capital partners:

Heading into 2027 selling and construction seasons, the NAHB analysis suggests that homebuilders should not assume relief in headline energy prices will translate directly into lower house costs. Instead, monitoring both material and service-side inflation — and baking higher contingencies into pro formas — will remain critical as the industry navigates persistently high input inflation alongside tighter capital markets and cautious buyers.k

JOHANNESBURG, 15 novembre 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A fronte della crescente complessitÃ  dei servizi delle reti di distribuzione, i dispositivi di distribuzione di Cemig facevano principalmente affidamento su reti pubbliche in leasing per il backhaul dei dati. Tuttavia, questo modello presenta notevoli rischi.

Dopo i test sul campo, il cliente ha potuto constatare di persona i vantaggi offerti dalla rete wireless privata, rafforzando la propria fiducia nella modernizzazione della rete di distribuzione e alimentando grandi aspettative per la futura transizione energetica: "Huawei ha presentato la migliore proposta durante la gara d'appalto, offrendo una soluzione che non solo soddisfa i nostri attuali requisiti di modernizzazione della rete di distribuzione, ma Ã¨ anche scalabile per la futura integrazione delle energie rinnovabili. Huawei vanta una vasta esperienza nel settore energetico. Grazie alla soluzione di rete privata di Huawei, Cemig potrÃ  garantire una rete di comunicazioni privata di alta qualitÃ . Per Cemig, questa partnership va ben oltre la tecnologia; Ã¨ fondamentale per la nostra crescita aziendale futura."

2. Rischi aziendali mitigatiLa rete wireless privata puÃ² ridurre sensibilmente le perdite di linea, SAIDI e SAIFI, aiutando cosÃ¬ Cemig a evitare sanzioni normative.

4. Espansione delle applicazioni di produzione principaliIn quanto infrastruttura di comunicazione fondamentale per le operazioni di produzione di energia, la rete wireless privata offre una connettivitÃ  affidabile dell'ultimo miglio per l'automazione della distribuzione odierna. Inoltre, supporta future applicazioni principali, come l'integrazione massiva di contatori intelligenti, la rapida adozione del fotovoltaico distribuito e la gestione complessa delle microreti, favorendo la transizione dalla tradizionale generazione di energia basata sul carico a un'interazione dinamica tra fonte, rete, carico e accumulo.

#5423. PRMG hires 100-person team from Gold Star in organic growth push

PRMG has recruited the Responsive Mortgage team from Gold Star Mortgage. The move fits PRMG’s strategy of organic, team-based growth instead of acquisitions and is the second large group to join in 90 days.   AI Summary

Paramount Residential Mortgage Group (PRMG) has hired a roughly 100-person team of loan officers, processors and underwriters from Gold Star Mortgage Financial Group, leaning on recruitment as its primary growth strategy.

Responsive Mortgage‘s move comes during what PRMG chief lending officer and partner Kevin Peranio described as a seasonal window for larger team transitions.

“I call this time of year the peak transition season,” Peranio said in an interview with HousingWire. “When the year slows down between August and February, larger teams typically make the moves.

“Everyone’s busy in the spring — it’s purchase season — so people don’t really make moves during that period. Then they have some time to reflect over the summer, and if they are going to make a transition, they typically do it when the leaves are changing.”

RETR data on loan officer migration patterns shows that LOs changed companies at a relatively steady pace throughout 2025, but “mega producers” that close more than 100 units per year have been more likely to move in October and May.

According to data from InGenius, 55 loan officers moved from Gold Star to PRMG. They’ve produced about $252 million since January, with most of that volume in Texas and Florida.

Peranio said the Responsive team, led by Mike Benton, had another proposal from a large retail lender that included a sizable signing bonus. But they chose PRMG based on what Peranio called a “cultural fit and a model match,” as well as alignment on technology.

“The Responsive team has proprietary technology in building relationships between Realtors and originators, and they wanted to continue to build that out and maximize the investment that they’ve made in their own technology,” Peranio said. “We plug into that technology to bring the loan into our fulfillment.”

PRMG has reached about $2.7 billion in total production year to date, per InGenius. Data from the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System shows the lender had 805 sponsored loan officers and 117 active branches as of Friday.

Gold Star, based in Ann Arbor, Michigan, has originated about $1.6 billion year to date, compared to $1.9 billion during the same period last year, per InGenius. NMLS shows Gold Star with 221 sponsored loan officers and 48 active branches. A spokesperson for Gold Star did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Peranio said PRMG is focused on organic growth and does not buy companies.

“We don’t acquire companies. We’re like a nice, slow, controlled grower. We’ve been around for 25 years,” he said. “Originators like to feel they control their destiny. And when a single owner — or whatever the ownership group is — just sells people to another group of people, it inherently doesn’t sit right. It’s like, what am I doing here if I can be sold to another company without my permission or being asked about it?”

Peranio added that when these transitions work, it is typically because there’s a leader within the group who’s transparent and communicates clearly with the team ahead of the move.

The Responsive team is the second large group — defined by PRMG as more than 20 people — to join the company in the past 90 days. Peranio said PRMG structures deals with upside on future revenue and offers some upfront funding to support transitions, rather than signing bonuses.

“If you write a check to trap someone for a certain amount of years, the reason that’s a trap is because the lenders that write those checks usually give them worse pricing,” Peranio said. “We think that doesn’t make any sense, especially when all pricing is getting more and more competitive in this new world of AI.”

#5422. Exclusive: Onyx Security brings AI agent governance to Glean’s enterprise AI platform

AI agent security startup Onyx Security Inc. today announced an integration with enterprise artificial intelligence platform company Glean Technologies Inc. to help enterprises govern the AI agents they build and run on Glean.

Onyx and Glean are pitching the integration at companies that are moving quickly to roll out autonomous, connected agents across their departments. Onyx claims, however, that most of them are not yet prepared to manage the risks that agents bring.

According to Onyx, security teams now need to keep continuous track of agent access, actions and policy compliance. Under the partnership, Glean provides the platform to build, deploy and operate the agents, while the Onyx secure AI control plane is used to extend governance and security across the AI environment.

At the core of the integration is discovery, with Onyx able to inventory every Glean agent and the access and capabilities it holds. Ownership, business purpose and a risk classification can then be assigned to each agent, according to the companies.

Enterprise AI governance and compliance policies can also be applied through the integration, after which Onyx continuously assesses changes to the permissions, tools and data access granted to each agent. Intent-aware runtime controls, which Onyx applies to prompts, responses and agent actions, provide protection while the agents are running.

Unsafe requests can be blocked outright under the controls. In other cases, the controls are said to steer unintended agent actions back in line with company policy. Centralized audit evidence is also maintained across AI environments. From deployment through ongoing operation and expansion, the companies say, agents fall under a single governance model.

“As agents gain greater access and autonomy, security teams need visibility and control over what they can do,” said Gil Elbaz, co-founder and chief AI officer at Onyx, who previously worked under Nvidia Corp.’s chief technology officer. “By combining Glean’s enterprise context with Onyx’s security control plane, customers can govern agent activity consistently and confidently across their AI environment.”

Glean regards context and governance as “foundational to making enterprise AI both useful and trustworthy,” according to Zubin Irani, the company’s vice president of partnerships. The Onyx integration is said to build on that foundation as organizations deploy agents across their business.

Coming into the partnership, Onyx has raised $153 million to date, including a $113 million Series B round led by Bessemer Venture Partners in July. The company launched in March with $40 million in seed and Series A funding.

Glean, for its part, last raised $150 million in a Series F round at a valuation of $7.2 billion in June 2025.

#5421. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”

#5420. Movement Mortgage seeks to recoup $1.2M from former LOs

Movement Mortgage is moving to enforce an arbitration ruling that says former loan officers Victor Shkolnikov and Igor Velyunskiy must repay $1.235 million in signing bonuses after leaving about a year into their three-year commitments.  AI Summary

Movement Mortgage wants two former loan officers to pay back a total of more than $1.2 million in signing bonuses after they left the company about a year into their three-year agreements.

According to court and arbitration documents, Movement paid a total of $1,235,000 in “start-up payments” to loan officers Victor Shkolnikov and Igor Velyunskiy when they joined the company in March 2022. Shkolnikov received $835,000 and Velyunskiy received $400,000.

The contracts said these payments were advances on future wages and had to be paid back in full if the loan officers left before working 36 consecutive months at the company. If they left early, the money was due within 30 days.

Both Shkolnikov and Velyunskiy left Movement around March 2023, roughly one year into their three-year commitment. Public records show Shkolnikov now works as a loan originator with United Lending Team in Illinois, while Velyunskiy is with Smart Rate Lending LLC.

Movement and the two former loan officers did not immediately respond to HousingWire’s requests for comment. National Mortgage News first reported the dispute.

Movement started arbitration in February 2024, and the cases were combined before arbitrator H. William Constangy. The LOs pushed back, filing counterclaims that accuse Movement of breach of contract, unjust enrichment, fraudulent inducement and violations of the Truth in Lending Act.

In July, the arbitrator ruled in favor of Movement. The decision said the employment agreements were valid contracts and that the two breached the contracts when they did not repay the start-up payments after leaving before the 36-month mark. All of their counterclaims were dismissed.

The award says the repayment amount will also accrue interest at North Carolina’s legal rate of 8% per year, starting in April 2023, which the arbitrator treated as the date of the breach. The arbitrator did not order either side to pay the other’s legal fees, so each party must cover its own attorneys’ costs.

In early November, Movement asked the U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina, Charlotte Division, to confirm the arbitration award and turn it into a court judgment. That would make it easier for the lender to collect the money if it isn’t paid voluntarily.

#5418. NAR’s latest data, must-have AI tools, Compass’ 15 new lawsuits

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this big news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

EXTRA: What Compass’ leadership ban signals for agents and associations

#5417. Apartment rents diverge: San Francisco rises, the Sun Belt falls

RealPage reported a 1.7% year-over-year rise in October rents nationally, with the Bay Area posting the strongest gains and many Sun Belt and Florida markets still declining. Deliveries and absorption are nearing balance, and occupancy was 95%.  AI Summary

America’s apartment landscape has become a tale of two opposing rent trends. Rents are climbing in the Bay Area and the Midwest, while much of the Sun Belt is still sliding.

National same-store asking rents edged up 1.7% from a year earlier in October, the biggest annual gain since May 2023, apartment industry data firm RealPage reported Nov. 11.

The national figure hides a wide gap. San Francisco rents jumped 14.7%, evidence of why city officials are pressing the supply button to drive housing construction. San Antonio rents dropped 2.6%.

The month-over-month picture illustrates less dramatic change. RealPage showed that rents fell 0.7% in October, the first monthly cut of 2026. The company said the annual gain came less from strong pricing than from weak months dropping out of the calculation, making for stronger year-over-year comparables.

Other trackers show the same upward drift, with different monthly readings. Yardi Matrix reported rents up 0.1% in October, with annual growth of 1.4%, the strongest in more than three years. Apartments.com put annual growth at 1.6%, even as rents slipped 0.15% for the month.

Supply and demand are edging toward balance. RealPage said renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year ending in Q3 2026. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units over the same period, almost half the late-2024 peak.

Occupancy eased to 95%, down 20 basis points from September. It is still up 40 basis points this year and 10 basis points above October 2025.

Improving rents haven’t translated into a property buying spree. Camden Property Trust, a large apartment landlord, walked away from two acquisitions and canceled two planned development projects. The Federal Reserve’s rate hike was a main reason, rental economist Jay Parsons wrote on LinkedIn.

Two deals under contract fell through after the hike, Camden CEO Alex Jessett said on the third-quarter earnings call. Camden asked for lower prices, and the sellers declined.

Buying also beat building on cost. Camden bought an asset at about $370,000 a door, while building it would have cost north of $600,000, Jessett said.

Camden’s earnings show an unevenly improving market. Funds from operations, a standard earnings measure for real estate investment trusts, were $1.70 per diluted share in the third quarter. Core funds from operations were $1.71, $0.02 above the company’s guidance midpoint.

“A higher-for-longer rate environment may equate to a lower-for-longer supply environment,” Parsons wrote.

Fewer projects penciling out means fewer new apartment options for renters.

Northern California took the top three spots for rent power among the 50 largest markets, RealPage said. San Francisco rose 14.7%, San Jose 9.5% and Oakland 8.5%. All three are running near 97% occupancy.

Midwest metros fill much of the rest of the top 10. Milwaukee led at 4.2%, followed by Chicago at 3.3%, and Kansas City and Cleveland at 3.1% each. Detroit and St. Louis each gained 2.7% and just missed the cut.

Most Sun Belt and Florida markets continued to decline. The South as a region returned to annual growth, but only by 0.5%.

San Antonio had the deepest decline in rents among big markets at 2.6%. Its occupancy of 92.5% was the lowest of the 50 largest markets. Houston fell 1.8%, followed by drops in Tampa of 1%, Charlotte of 0.9% and Denver of 0.8%.

Several Sun Belt markets have turned the corner, however. Jacksonville rose 2.6%, Raleigh 1.0%, Atlanta 0.8%, Austin and Miami 0.6% each, and Phoenix 0.4%.

#5416. Massive Microsoft outage disrupts businesses, government agencies worldwide

A glitch in Microsoft Corp.’s network has disrupted the work of businesses and government agencies in more than 70 countries.

The bug, which reared its head on Thursday about 12:35 p.m. EST, knocked the company’s popular Exchange Online platform offline. Organizations use the cloud service to store employees’ inboxes and calendars. Microsoft has still not fully restored its infrastructure.

Deployments of Exchange Server, a version of the platform that users run on-premises, are not affected. However, the outage did disrupt a number of Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Copilot 365 features that rely on data from users’ Exchange inboxes. Intune, a tool that administrators use to manage employee devices, is also experiencing technical issues.

The outage has hit numerous companies worldwide. Workhorse Group Inc., an electric vehicle maker, pushed back its earnings call from today to Monday. Shipping giant Maersk and stock exchange operator Euronext notified customers that they’re experiencing communications issues.

The public sector is also impacted. Several U.S. municipalities reported technical problems, while a number of court cases had to be delayed. In the U.K., the National Pharmacy Association warned that the Exchange Online outage may slow prescription processing. Hospitals, public transportation agencies and schools are affected as well.

The operator of Downdetector, an outage tracking service, received downtime reports from hundreds of thousands of users.

Parts of Microsoft’s infrastructure started recovering early this morning. In an update published at 2:30 a.m., the company stated that it was seeing “positive results” after patching an “upstream authentication/routing configuration” module. About three hours later, Microsoft’s systems in the Asia Pacific region began regaining service access. North America and Europe followed suit shortly there.

Microsoft shared its first explanation of what went wrong around noon today. “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company explained. “We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”

Microsoft added that the outage wasn’t caused by a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

The company’s status page indicates that infrastructure restoration work is still ongoing. As a result, some users may have trouble accessing Exchange Online and certain Microsoft products that interact with it. The company is monitoring the backlog of emails that piled up while the service was offline to ensure no data loss occurs.

Microsoft plans to release a detailed technical report about the outage once all its services are fully restored.

#5414. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”
