#5413. Legislative risk continues to cloud BTR’s capital outlook; here’s why

Despite a carve-out in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, BTR and SFR operators say Treasury implementation and legislative risk is still suppressing capital. NAA Q3 2026 data shows units under construction down 18.5% YoY, completions down 40.2%, and sales volume down 51.5%.  AI Summary

Despite securing carve-outs from the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act‘s institutional investor ban, build-to-rent (BTR) and single-family rental (SFR) operators continue to grapple with lingering legislative uncertainty that weighs on capital availability and new construction, both of which dramatically lag 2025 levels.

According to the National Apartment Association’s Q3 2026 Market Pulse, released Nov. 5, BTR units under construction fell 18.5% year over year, newly completed units declined 40.2% and sales volume of communities dropped 51.5%. Even against a broader nationwide slowdown in residential construction, the declining BTR pipeline continues to stand out.

The industry’s legislative uncertainty initially stemmed from an earlier version of ROAD, first introduced in March, that would have required investors and developers to sell newly built rental homes to individual buyers after seven years. The provision, among others, threatened the viability of the BTR business model, prompting investors to pull back from committing capital to new projects.

Although the final version of ROAD exempted and protected BTR, uncertainty remains around how Treasury will implement the institutional investor ban, along with the potential for new federal and state legislation that could impose further institutional ownership restrictions. That lingering uncertainty continues to weigh on capital flowing into the industry.

“I would say it hasn’t normalized. In other words, it wasn’t where it was a year ago, where capital was really flowing into the business,” Richard Ross, CEO at QuinnResidences, said when discussing the BTR market, in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

“I almost don’t care what the rules are, as long as you tell me what the rules are,” Ross added. “With uncertainty, people just aren’t going to invest.”

Ross cited the Strait of Hormuz as a timely and illustrative comparison. While oil is still moving through the Strait, traffic remains more restricted than it was a year ago. BTR, he suggested, finds itself in a comparable position.

“Capital’s coming in, but it’s not like it was pre-ROAD. The hope was that the regulatory process would give some clarity. And I think once it gets done, it will provide clarity, but you might remember this was only part one of the regulatory process,” he said, pointing to the prospects of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill. “Until capital knows what the rules are, it’s really hard for them to write checks.

According to Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group, a builder, buyer and manager of single-family rentals, the capital environment for BTR had been flashing signs of softening even before the federal government introduced the idea of an institutional investor ban. New projects often came with modest returns, and rent growth was moderating or even falling across many high-growth Sun Belt markets.

Add a steady drumbeat of policy risk from Washington, and many investors have simply taken their money elsewhere.

“When you add policy uncertainty to the asset, it just doesn’t have the return to pay for that,” Dobson said in an interview.

Invitation Homes CEO Dallas Tanner also acknowledged that the capital environment hasn’t bounced back from an uncertain 2026 during the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call on October 29.

“Capital’s just starting to poke its eyes up after the ROAD Act piece of it. The market’s still trying to find itself,” Tanner said.

In a Q3 2026 Form 10-Q document filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 5, 2026, AMH also called out ongoing legislative uncertainty as a concern.

“Further, the ROAD Act and the prospect of other such laws or regulations have adversely impacted and may in the future continue to adversely impact our access to capital markets and the attractiveness of our securities to certain investors,” the document warned.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury, which implements the institutional investor ban included in ROAD, released a notice of proposed rulemaking in October that would grant BTR communities a range of notable exemptions from the ban. However, concerns remain about some of Treasury’s proposed interpretations.

“If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, ‘all right, built-to-rent is carved out.’ But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Dobson said.

Quinn Residences, in an open letter to Treasury, outlined several concerns about Treasury’s proposed rulemaking. Chief among them is a proposal to exempt purpose-built BTR communities from the institutional investor ban provided they haven’t been owner-occupied and are purchased within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy.

Ross argued that this timeline isn’t sufficient, as the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy requirement could prevent institutional investors from acquiring purpose-built rental homes that have been operating as rentals for more than 18 months, even if they have never been owner-occupied. And building and stabilizing a community typically takes about 30 months, longer than the rule allows, Ross argued.

The rule, therefore, could prevent subsequent sales of newly built BTR homes among institutional investors, effectively limiting the pool of potential buyers and potentially discouraging investment into new projects.

Ross also signaled his opposition to another one of Treasury’s proposed rulemakings that would fail to exempt single-plat BTR communities zoned for multifamily use, despite congressional record statements indicating lawmakers intended those properties to be excluded from the ban.

For The Amherst Group, uncertainty continues to obscure how Treasury will define the exception for homes requiring substantial repairs under the ROAD institutional investor ban. Many of Amherst’s acquisitions are older homes, typically 25 to 40 years old, that require substantial renovations. While the renovate-to-rent exception could allow Amherst to continue acquiring and renovating these properties for rent, the lack of finalized parameters has left investors uncertain.

“There’s no money to be raised right now,” Dobson said, of capital for financing renovate-to-rent acquisitions.

What’s more, the possibility of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill raises even more concerns among many BTR operators and developers. They fear they face continued uncertainty and risk over whether future federal or state legislation could restrict the BTR business model.

However, it’s not yet clear whether any such legislation will gain traction in the next Congress. While many successful candidates for the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House of Representatives ran on a platform of opposing institutional ownership of single-family homes, campaign rhetoric and slogans don’t necessarily translate full-stop into policy.

“I worked campaigns for a number of years throughout the country, and the first thing they kind of teach you in campaigning out there is everyone needs a boogeyman. I think you campaign in slogans, and you govern in prose,” Owen Caine, Assistant Vice President of Federal Legislative Affairs at the National Apartment Association (NAA), said in an interview.

Despite the expectation that some members of Congress may push for more aggressive institutional ownership restrictions, Cain was encouraged by the widespread bipartisan pushback against previous provisions that would have undermined BTR. Caine hopes this bipartisan support will keep Congress from passing such far-reaching legislation in the future.

“The fact that we got to where we were with such bipartisan support, and with basically complete industry and nonprofit support, [means] messing around with that at this point, before it’s been fully implemented and before we’ve seen any benefits of the bill whatsoever, doesn’t make a lot of sense from a policy perspective,” he explained.

However, the new Congress comes with another challenge — the sheer size of the incoming freshman class. In the House of Representatives, for example, about 110 new representatives are expected, along with new staff members.

“Those are each offices we have to hit individually to educate about build-to-rent because the odds that the average person has any idea what a build-to-rent development is, is pretty low,” Caine explained.

Ross noted that lawmakers are usually receptive once they learn more about BTR and the legislative challenges facing the industry. A recent meeting with Senator-elect Roy Cooper (D-N.C.) was one example, with Cooper responding positively to those concerns.

“I spent 30 minutes with him personally, explaining what build-to-rent was. He said, ‘Oh, I understand. That makes sense.’ So that’s just something that everyone in this business will have to do again,” Ross explained.

While much of the attention has focused on federal legislation, state-level policy, particularly proposals to restrict institutional investors, may be just as critical an area to watch.

While it’s not clear what the newly elected state legislatures and governors may prioritize, several states have already considered bills limiting the influence of institutional ownership of housing.

In Virginia, for example, state lawmakers from both parties introduced legislation to restrict institutional home purchases. SB 693 and SB 1424 would have prohibited entities with more than $50 million in assets under management from buying single-family homes, but neither bill passed.

In Michigan, however, a similar measure, HB 6074, was signed into law on July 21, 2026. The bill prohibits corporations with a net worth of $375 million or more from owning more than 100 single-family homes in the state, while explicitly exempting build-to-rent (BTR) properties.

As more states consider restrictions on institutional ownership of single-family homes, will BTR secure the exemptions achieved in Michigan, or could operators face a tougher legislative environment in Congress and in other state legislatures?

That’s a key question to watch in 2027 and beyond.

The company appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while beginning its search for a permanent replacement. Harvey C. Jones, former Synopsys CEO, will become Nvidia’s first-ever board chairman.

The leadership shake-up has rattled investors across multiple markets. Nvidia sits at the center of the artificial intelligence boom, making its sudden leadership change a major shock for technology stocks and crypto traders.

Nvidia-linked contracts have also become a significant market on Hyperliquid. They ranked fourth in open interest, behind Bitcoin, Ethereum, and HYPE futures. Uncertainty grows around Nvidia’s AI ambitions. The company supplies critical computing hardware for major technology firms, cloud providers, and artificial intelligence developers. The disruption has, as expected, influenced sentiment across the entire AI investment trade.

#5411. The Pan-Mass Challenge Exceeds 2026 Fundraising Goal with Record-Breaking $80 Million Gift Fueling Lifesaving Research at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute

With its largest gift ever, the world's most successful athletic fundraiser continues to shatter fundraising records at a time when cancer research needs support most

BOSTON, Nov. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC), a bike-a-thon which has raised more money for charity than any other single athletic fundraising event in the world, today presented a record-breaking $80 million gift to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, one of the nation's top three cancer hospitals. Presented at a celebratory brunch at Rochambeau in Boston, this gift brings the PMC's total contribution to Dana-Farber's mission to more than $1.2 billion.

For the 20th consecutive year, 100 percent of every rider-raised dollar goes directly to Dana-Farber. Powered by thousands of riders and volunteers from across the world, every dollar raised helps fuel groundbreaking cancer research, lifesaving treatments, and patient care.

"$80 million isn't just a number. It represents the next clinical trial, the next breakthrough, the next life saved, and the next patient who gets to ring the bell at the end of treatment," said Billy Starr, PMC founder and chairman. "Now, more than ever, our riders, volunteers, donors, and corporate partners understood exactly what was at stake. They didn't just meet the moment, they rode right past it. I've never been prouder of this community, and I've never been more confident that the cures we ride for are within reach."

The record-breaking gift arrives at a pivotal moment in the nation. While federal research support and grant approval rates are shrinking, cancer rates continue to climb, with more than 20 million new cancer cases projected worldwide in 2026 alone. The PMC's sustained giving is one of the most essential forces keeping transformative research at Dana-Farber moving forward.

"We are immensely grateful for the PMC's longstanding support of Dana-Farber," said Benjamin L. Ebert, MD, PhD, president and CEO of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and PMC rider. "This unprecedented gift is an important milestone and will be used to shape the future of cancer care and research at Dana-Farber. I am honored to be one of thousands of committed PMC riders and volunteers who have played a role in making a big impact."

The PMC is Dana-Farber's single largest contributor, accounting for 67 percent of revenue for the Jimmy Fund, Dana-Farber's community fundraising arm. But the most significant measure of the PMC's funding is found in the discoveries that bring new hope to patients and families facing cancer. PMC support helped drive some of Dana-Farber's most significant recent breakthroughs, including the discovery of menin inhibitors, the improvement of multi-cancer early detection, and the development of new types of cell therapies such as CAR-T cell therapy and tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy.

The unprecedented gift reflects a full year of riding and fundraising. In addition to the flagship PMC weekend, crucial funding was supported by the PMC's further spokes in the wheel, including PMC Winter Cycle, an indoor spin event at Fenway Park; PMC Unpaved, a gravel bike ride; and PMC Kids Rides, mini bike-a-thons for children ages 2 to 15.

The PMC is co-presented by the Red Sox FoundationÂ® and M&T Bank. To learn more, get involved, or donate, visit www.pmc.org.

About the Pan-Mass ChallengeThe Pan-Mass Challenge (PMC) is a bike-a-thon that today raises more money for charity than any other single athletic fundraising event in the world. Founded in 1980 by Billy Starr â who remains the event's founder & chairman, an annual cyclist, and a fundraiser â the PMC has raised $1.2 billion for Dana-Farber Cancer Institute through the Jimmy Fund. As Dana-Farber's single largest contributor, the organization generates 67 percent of the Jimmy Fund's annual revenue. 100 percent of every rider-raised dollar goes directly to fueling cancer research and treatment at Dana-Farber. In addition to its two-day bike-a-thon across Massachusetts, the PMC is powered by further "spokes in the wheel," with initiatives including the PMC Winter Cycle, an indoor spin event, PMC Unpaved, a gravel bike ride, and PMC Kids Rides, mini bike-a-thons for children ages 2 to 15. #5410. NiCE’s next-generation Cognigy bets the hard part of AI agents is running them, not building them

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

The contact center has been the low-hanging fruit for the artificial intelligence industry. Ask any information technology or business leader what they want to use agentic AI for, and they will say it’s to improve the customer experience, which starts with the contact center.

However, to date, the industry has spent the past two years arguing over which AI agent is the smartest. That’s the wrong debate. Model capabilities are improving so quickly and are getting so much cheaper that raw intelligence and reasoning are becoming the least differentiated part of the stack.

The real challenge for enterprises is operating a fleet of AI agents reliably across complete customer journeys, with the visibility and control a large business requires. Without that, the human, or worse, the customer, is left connecting the dots among the outputs of the growing number of agents they are communicating with.

That’s the thesis behind the next generation of NiCE Cognigy, which NiCE Ltd. launched this week. The release includes a redesigned Agentic Experience Studio, an AI Assist companion spanning the building, testing and improvement of agents, reusable “skills” that package instructions and tools, turn-by-turn tracing and native voice-to-voice model support.

Default speech-to-text, text-to-speech and large language models are now included in the per-conversation price, with premium models from Deepgram, ElevenLabs and Anthropic available with a few clicks and billed by usage.

Ahead of the launch, I attended an analyst briefing with Nhu Ho, senior product marketing manager at NiCE Cognigy, and with Clement Boutier, director of product management, who leads the team that built the release and owns the platform roadmap.

Here are the important points from this release:

Ho opened with a chart showing how long AI can work on its own before a human has to step in. In 2020, it was seconds; in 2024, it was minutes; and this year it’s roughly 16 hours. The footnote was interesting, as it calculated that figure at a 50% success rate. “Capable and dependable do not always mean the same thing,” Ho said. “That is exactly where the platform matters.”

For CX leaders, that’s a solid benchmark to consider. A 50% success rate is a research milestone. In a contact center, it’s a churn event or a compliance violation. As models commoditize, value shifts to the system around them: testing, tracing, guardrails and deterministic fallbacks. NiCE doesn’t build frontier models, and frontier model builders don’t run contact centers. Positioning Cognigy as the layer that makes AI dependable is a smart place to plant a flag.

Cognigy earned its pre-acquisition leadership position by handling complex production deployments for large brands such as Lufthansa, Mercedes and DHL. But that flexibility and customizability added complexity. Boutier put it this way: “The large number of options when configuring an agent creates friction to get started, which slows things down.” The new studio lets a builder stand up an agent in a few clicks, with models already provisioned, while power-user tools, including full access to the agent’s system prompt, are available in advanced sections.

This is important because NiCE aims to create a “1+1=3” value proposition for its current customers. NiCE needs Cognigy to expand broadly across the CXone installed base, not just among expert teams at the largest enterprises. Boutier described three builder personas: smaller businesses building simple agents, contact center administrators and team leads, and engineers at technically sophisticated companies. AI Assist is aimed squarely at the first two.

In the demo, it built an agent, tested it, fixed the problems it found, and deployed it to WhatsApp. The flip side is that lowering the barrier means more agents built by less experienced people, which makes the governance features the real story of this release.

Despite all the agentic hype, most enterprises aren’t ready to hand over entire journeys to an autonomous agent. Boutier outlined three modes: traditional natural language understanding, hybrid and fully agentic. Hybrid “is actually where most of our customers are,” he said, while fully agentic deployments are at the “beginning of the adoption curve.” This approach lets customers ease into agentic, build confidence and move to fully autonomous at their own pace.

NiCE designed the product for that approach. An agent can serve as the orchestration layer, calling existing flows as tools. Flows can also be placed in front of agents, for example, to scrub credit card numbers or other personal data before any data reaches a model. Ho described the release as “an evolution, not a replacement,” with production deployments, application programming interfaces and integrations continuing to run unchanged.

That’s a meaningful advantage over AI-native challengers whose pitch effectively requires a rebuild. Contact centers are the fastest-moving environments, and deterministic workflows aren’t legacy baggage. They’re how a business enforces what a large language model shouldn’t be deciding.

“You can have the best builder experience, but if you don’t have any feedback loop on what you’re building, you’re never going to build a great agent,” Boutier said. The new tracing shows each turn: which skill loaded, which tool was called and with what arguments, and when the agent handed off to a flow.

The Simulator now supports multivariate testing of up to 10 variants, using an LLM-as-judge to run synthetic customers against an agent. Boutier ran the same agent on two models and found that one was faster and consumed fewer tokens. This shifts model selection from a preference to a data-backed economic decision.

Voice-to-voice support may be the first feature customers deploy. Boutier noted that buyers are open to using a speech-to-text and text-to-speech cascade, “but what they realize is that voice-to-voice models sound just better.” In the demo, the agent delegated tool calls to a separate model while continuing to talk, making the conversation sound far more natural.

Cognigy now serves as both a Model Context Protocol client and server and supports agent-to-agent connections, including one customer linking Cognigy to agents built with Microsoft’s tooling. NiCE is also co-developing the Personal Agent Protocol with Meta and Sierra, which isn’t live yet. Boutier described Cognigy as “the front door” of the contact center, where a consumer’s personal agent must authenticate before it can proceed. It’s great to see NiCE collaborating with Sierra, a direct competitor, on this, as it makes things easier for a customer.

The industry views agent identity as a shared responsibility. But as Sierra outlines, companies can also let personal agents work through their websites and APIs, so the front-door position depends on enterprises routing that traffic through Cognigy. This lets brands interact with personal agents safely.

There has been a wave of companies banning personal agents, which I think is a mistake. If something is good for a consumer, it will happen, so it’s better to be on the leading edge of enabling it rather than fighting it.

This release is less about new capabilities and more about NiCE betting on where value will accrue as AI agents mature. Intelligence is getting cheaper. Dependability, governance and the ability to blend autonomous reasoning with deterministic control are not.

NiCE is the market leader in contact center as a service, as Cognigy was in conversational AI. Now the challenge is to get an easier-to-work-with Cognigy into the hands of thousands of CXone customers without creating a sprawl of individually governed agents. This will allow NiCE to maintain its industry leadership as personal agents arrive. As it does that, the Cognigy acquisition will move from an add-on to a core component of the NiCE platform.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5409. The seasonal decline in housing inventory is in full force

Inventory declined to 895,988 as mortgage rates reversed higher to 7.50%. New listings remained fell slightly year over year to 53,162, while weekly pending sales showed 4 weeks of stabilization.  AI Summary

Even with volatility in mortgage rates last week, the seasonal decline in inventory is in full force. Weekly housing demand has continued to stabilize over the last four weeks and the new listing data is not showing any stress in the housing market. We had a lot of crazy things happen last week — in fact I’m writing this article still stuck in Dallas because of the FAA’s nationwide ground stop — but housing data never sleeps, so let’s take a look.

Housing inventory has picked up recently, after mortgage rates went above 6.64% and then shot up toward 7.60%. Inventory growth had been very tame this year, with some weeks negative year over year. As housing inventory returns to normal levels, it takes weaker demand to get stronger growth and rates moving toward 7.60% did that. Still, it’s more about sales taking longer to happen and demand being hit, because new listings data didn’t budge much recently. Now, we are in the full-blown seasonal decline as we get ready to prep for spring 2027.

Inventory growth is running at 7.11% over last year even with easier comps, as last year demand was running toward a 9-month high in December of 2025.

New listings have been in their seasonal decline since June and nothing abnormal with this data line has happened in 2026; in fact, it’s been the best year of new listings since 2022. One concern I had about higher rates is that more people might simply not list their homes — as they did in the second half of 2022 due to higher rates. However, that hasn’t happened; we did see a more noticeable year-over-year decline this last week, but for the most part it’s been a healthy year.

In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years.Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years:

Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%. At that point demand fell and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%.In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year and my -0.62% forecast may be hard to achieve, since most home-price indices show growth between 1% and 2%.However, with higher rates and a rising price-cut percentage, we will be closer to the forecast. Clearly, if rates hadn’t risen above 6.75%, pricing data wouldn’t have shown the recent slowdown.

In the 2026 HousingWire forecast, I anticipated the following ranges:

Last week wasn’t good for mortgage rates or the bond market: we had hawkish Fed statements and hot inflation data. We were getting closer to mortgage rates below 7% for the holidays, but they made a big reversal from 7.17% to 7.50%. In addition, President Trump talked about raising tariffs against Mexico and we still have no deal with Iran. Pretty much everything you needed for rates to go lower went the other way — something I talked about in this episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief  Sarah Wheeler.

Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they did improve last week. Traditionally, when mortgage rates escalate with the 10-year yield and then make a big reversal — like we just had from a 5.35% 10-year yield top that dropped down toward 4.82% — spreads do get worse to try to compress mortgage rate volatility. However, we had a big reversal higher, and spreads improved some as the 10-year yield rose toward 5.14%.

Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads fell to 2.13% from 2.27% a week earlier.

Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle.

Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data.

The key for the last four weeks: housing demand has stabilized, as our weekly pending sales have shown. Now, higher rates most likely will impact this week’s data more than last week, but the last four weeks have shown if we can get rates back below 7% and just have them stick, we can work with this.

Housing demand typically grows when rates get below 6.64% and fades when rates are above 7%, especially if the move in rates is fast, like we saw recently. Still, it was encouraging to see stabilization in the data when rates were trying to get below 7% again. Of course, we are seeing big year-over-year declines in this data line as rates were heading toward 6% last year.

Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years:

Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. We did have 8% week-to-week growth last week as rates tried to get below 7% the week before. I expect the next purchase application data to get hit as rates picked up. This data was very positive year over year when rates were under 6.64%, but not so much when it headed toward 7% and got to 7.60%.

Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026:

It’s going to be an interesting week because we have a ton of Fed members speaking and they really left their mark last week! We’ll get some housing data: the builder survey won’t be great, nor will housing starts. Pending home sales might lag our stabilization by one month, but if we do see some stabilization, remember it’s working from record-low levels. We have retail sales as well, and some of the economy has been beating to the upside. Also, we have to be mindful of Trump headlines with the Iran conflict and the trade war.

#5408. Bloomberg Indices and HKEX Launch Co-branded Offshore RMB Bond Index Family to Support Growing Investor Demand in the Dim Sum Bond Market

New index suite helps meet growing demand for index-based investment products in offshore RMB bonds

HONG KONG, Nov. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Bloomberg Index Services Limited ("BISL") today announced the launch of a new family of offshore RMB bond indices in collaboration with HKEX FICC Indices Services Limited, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX), providing investors and asset managers with transparent measures of the offshore RMB bond market, commonly referred to as the Dim Sum bond market.

HKEX earlier today introduced the HKEX Offshore RMB Bond Index, a benchmark administered and calculated by BISL. Serving as the parent benchmark for the broader index suite, it forms the basis of a family of co-branded Bloomberg HKEX indices designed for use across investment products including passive investment strategies such as exchange-traded funds (ETFs), as well as active portfolio management benchmarking and market analysis.

The initial list of indices to launch in the family includes:

In addition to the standard index family, BISL may develop customized indices based on the framework to support specific investment objectives and product needs of asset managers and other market participants.

The new indices screen bonds from the flagship Bloomberg Offshore Renminbi (CNH) Index, which includes eligible RMB-denominated Treasury, government-related and corporate debt securities issued in offshore China markets. An additional eligibility criterion requires securities to be listed on The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (SEHK) and/or lodged with the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU).

Using data as of the end of October, 2026, the Bloomberg HKEX Offshore RMB Bond Index universe would include 305 bonds representing approximately CNH 864 billion in market value. Government-related bonds accounted for 49.59% of the index, followed by corporate bonds (29.19%) and Treasury securities (21.22%). Issuers from China and Hong Kong represented the largest regional exposures in the index at 88.49%, followed by the United States (5.17%) and Singapore (1.98%).

"Bloomberg has a long history of providing transparent, rules-based fixed income indices to global investors, acting as a pioneer in supporting the development of local bond markets, exemplified by the inclusion of China onshore government and policy bank bonds into our flagship Global Aggregate Index," said Ji Zhuang, Head of Asia Pacific for Bloomberg Index Services Limited. "Together with HKEX, we're supporting the continued development of the Dim Sum bond market and our shared vision for RMB internationalization. We're encouraged by the strong interest from ETF issuers exploring products linked to the index family and look forward to supporting the growth of index-based investment solutions in the market."

Bonnie Y Chan, HKEX Chief Executive Officer, said: "Hong Kong is the world's leading offshore RMB financial hub, and the launch of the HKEX Offshore RMB Bond Index is a significant step forward in advancing its fixed-income market from an issuance centre towards an ecosystem with greater depth, liquidity and investability. By establishing a transparent and widely recognised benchmark anchored in Hong Kong's market infrastructure, we are supporting greater visibility and investability of offshore RMB assets, encouraging broader market participation and further advancing the internationalisation of the RMB. We are delighted to collaborate with Bloomberg, whose global index expertise and market reach will help broaden access to and deepen participation in the offshore RMB bond market."

Xinrong Wu, General Manager of E Fund and Chairman of E Fund HK, said: "As the offshore RMB bond market continues to expand rapidly, investor interest in allocating to and trading these bonds keeps growing. This index delivers the first transparent, trackable and product-ready benchmark for the offshore RMB bond market, precisely addressing a critical market need and laying a solid foundation for product innovation. As one of the first authorised managers, E Fund will utilize the Group's fixed-income investment and research capabilities, together with E Fund HK's local product development and distribution experience, to accelerate the launch of innovative index-linked products and help investors allocate to offshore RMB assets more efficiently. We look forward to working with HKEX, Bloomberg and all market participants to drive the offshore RMB bond market towards greater depth and breadth."

Bloomberg clients can access the new indices through {IN }, Bloomberg's index search and discovery function on the Bloomberg Terminal. Research and index methodology documents are available on the Bloomberg Indices Documentation page.

About Bloomberg Index Services LimitedBloomberg's index team has a proven track record in creating industry-leading and bespoke indices across asset classes, including their flagship fixed income, commodity and equity indices. BISL takes an innovative approach to delivering strategic benchmarks that help market participants address their evolving investment needs. The indices, which are seamlessly integrated with other Bloomberg solutions, draw on a comprehensive range of trusted data and reliable technology for calculations, analytics and workflow automation, along with distribution capabilities that can help amplify the visibility of our customers' products.

About BloombergBloomberg is a global leader in business and financial information, delivering trusted data, news, and insights that bring transparency, efficiency, and fairness to markets. The company helps connect influential communities across the global financial ecosystem via reliable technology solutions that enable our customers to make more informed decisions and foster better collaboration. For more information, visit Bloomberg.com/company or request a demo.

1 The Bloomberg HKEX Offshore RMB Bond Index mirrors the HKEX Offshore RMB Bond Index and is designed for use in a broad range of applications including passive investment products.

#5407. FAA grounds all domestic flights after reported network outage

The Federal Aviation Administration today grounded all domestic flights in the U.S.

The rare order was issued by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC. It’s an FAA facility in Northern Virginia that is responsible for monitoring air traffic and mitigating potential risks. When ATCSCC identifies issues such as airport congestion, it provides local officials with guidance on how to address them.

The ATCSCC sent today’s ground stop order to all 22 regional air traffic control centers in the U.S. The memo explained that the move was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy elaborated in a post on X that the FAA “issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

The post didn’t provide any details about the communication issue. According to CBS News, the problem affects a “private communications network” that connects components of the U.S. air traffic control system. The outlet cited sources as saying that an update caused the network to reboot, which in turn led it to crash.

On Tuesday, the FAA announced that it was expanding its use of an artificial intelligence system called SMART. The software analyzes weather patterns, flight paths and related data points to generate air traffic scheduling recommendations. The FAA says that the software is designed to reduce delays and fuel consumption.

The agency last issued a national ground stop in January 2023. It was a response to an issue in the FAA’s NOTAM system, which it uses to notify pilots about hazards such as closed runways. The shutdown lasted about two hours and grounded 9,500 flights.

The current shutdown is already much longer, having started at 3:54 p.m. EST. More than 13,000 flights have reportedly been delayed or canceled. Eurocontrol, an organization that helps European Union member states coordinate air traffic, suspended flights to the U.S. at the request of the FAA.

FAA officials said that inbound international flights will be “handled on a case by case basis.” American Airlines, meanwhile, stated that flights already airborne will proceed to their destinations. The airline reportedly expects the disruption to last all day.

#5406. Thunes Expands Real-Time Payouts to Bhutan, Unlocking the Nation's Remittance Market

Thunes' Direct Global Network enables instant, 24/7 payments to all bank accounts in Bhutan, empowering Members to support the nation's rapidly expanding remittance corridor.

SINGAPORE and THIMPHU, Bhutan, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Thunes, the Smart Superhighway to move money around the world, today announced the expansion of its Direct Global Network into the Kingdom of Bhutan, enabling its Network Members, including digital banks, money transfer operators (MTOs), and remittance service providers, to send real-time Consumer-to-Consumer (C2C) payouts to all licensed bank accounts in the country.

The direct integration allows Non-Resident Bhutanese and expatriates across Australia, the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and North America to send funds home in Bhutanese Ngultrum (BTN) in seconds, avoiding multi-day clearing cycles and unpredictable intermediary markups.

For Thunes' Members, the new connection unlocks three key benefits:

With over 70,000 Bhutanese nationals - nearly 10% of the population - living abroad, personal remittances account for 3% to 4% of national GDP and grew 69% from 2024 to 2025. Historically, these flows have relied on complex correspondent banking networks, incurring costs and delays.

With banks as the primary channel to send money home, Thunes clears these payments in seconds, supporting recurring salary transfers, personal savings, and family support for living expenses, healthcare, and education. Every transaction is backed by Thunes' Fortress Compliance engine for strict AML and regulatory adherence, alongside its SmartX Treasury System for advanced liquidity management.

Alex Young, Chief Network Officer at Thunes, said: "Bhutan represents a vital corridor where cross-border remittances serve as an indispensable financial lifeline for families. By connecting Bhutan's entire banking sector directly into our Direct Global Network, we have established an effective, transparent way to ensure hard-earned funds arrive safely, securely, and in real time."

Eugene Chua, Head of Network, APAC, at Thunes, added: "At Thunes, we are dismantling the friction that creates barriers to the global digital economy. Bhutan's diaspora has grown significantly, especially across markets like Australia and Southeast Asia. Enabling instant consumer account deposits ensures expatriates have access to a reliable, transparent, and direct payment rail to send money back home."

For more information, visit: https://www.thunes.com/

#5405. Amazon’s Ring tries again with a $250 flying home security drone and a $1,000 patrol robot

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 5:30 amNovember 10, 2026 at 5:49 am

Amazon’s Ring unveiled a $249.99 flying indoor security drone and a $999.99 mobile patrol robot for businesses, bringing back two ideas that stalled in earlier incarnations.

The Ring Drone Cam and Ring Rover Cam, announced Tuesday, are the first products under the Ring Robotics name, which the company calls “a new category of autonomous, mobile security.” Both devices use a system Ring calls AI Pilot to map a home or business, suggest spots worth checking, and find their own way around obstacles such as furniture and shelving.

The drone stays docked with its camera off until it’s sent out on a schedule, on demand, or automatically when another Ring device is triggered. The Rover patrols stores and offices, using a periscope camera to see over counters and shelving.

The Rover is available for preorder in the U.S. and is scheduled to ship Dec. 16. The Drone Cam is slated for Jan. 27, 2027, but Ring is only taking email sign-ups for now. The fine print notes that the drone hasn’t yet received the required authorization from the Federal Communications Commission.

Scheduled flights and patrols, and reviewing the Rover’s recorded video, require a Ring Protect subscription plan. Ring didn’t say which plans qualify.

Ring says customers wanted to see spots a fixed camera can’t reach, and rooms where they wouldn’t want one mounted.

“The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be,” said Jamie Siminoff, Ring’s founder and chief inventor, in a statement. “That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time.”

Ring unveiled a flying indoor camera called the Always Home Cam in 2020, also priced at $249.99. The company later opened an invitation list, but the device never went on general sale.

The original drone flew only along paths that owners mapped out with it in advance. Ring says the new one builds a floor plan as the owner carries it through the house, suggests spots to check, and plans its own routes.

The Rover Cam traces back to Astro for Business, a rolling security robot that Amazon launched in November 2023 at a starting price of $2,350. Amazon discontinued it less than a year later, refunding customers and shutting the robots off.

Astro for Business was a spinoff of Amazon’s Astro home robot, an Alexa-powered device on wheels that debuted in 2021 and can patrol the house on its own.

Ring says the new robot was inspired by Astro customers who said roving security was their favorite feature. The Ring team “leveraged the best of Astro” to build it, the company says. Ring is pitching the Rover as “not a home robot that also does security, but a purpose-built security robot.”

The original Astro for the home remains an invite-only product. Amazon has redeployed much of the Astro team to work on a new home robot, CNBC reported Sunday. In March, Amazon acquired Fauna Robotics, a New York humanoid robot startup, saying it would become part of a new Personal Robotics Group. Ring’s announcement doesn’t mention either effort.

The Rover also extends Ring’s push into commercial security, following a $5,000 surveillance trailer for parking lots that it unveiled in January. In security robots, it competes with companies such as Knightscope, which rents its robots through a subscription, and Cobalt AI. At $999.99, the Rover costs less than half what Astro for Business did.

On the security drone front, Indoor Robotics makes a ceiling-docking drone that patrols offices and warehouses, but flying security cameras for the home remain rare.

Siminoff, who launched Ring’s predecessor, Doorbot, in 2012 and sold Ring to Amazon in 2018, left the company in 2023 and returned last year to lead Ring and Amazon’s related home security businesses. Last month, Ring unveiled its first smart lock, a $249 deadbolt with no keyhole and a dial that recharges a dead battery by hand.

#5403. PitchBook to give early-stage startups free access, using their data to feed a new tool for VCs

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:23 amNovember 10, 2026 at 7:25 am

PitchBook announced a new program to give early-stage startups free use of its private-market data, if they share their financials and other company details.

The Seattle-based company says the new program, dubbed PitchBook for Startups, will feed PitchBook Origin, a new deal-sourcing product that helps venture capitalists and other investors find startups before they raise their first institutional round.

PitchBook announced both offerings Tuesday morning at Web Summit in Lisbon. Owned by Morningstar since 2016, the company has more than 3,000 employees and sells subscriptions to venture firms, private equity investors and dealmakers.

The launches come as first-time startup financings hit a record. There were an estimated 8,625 such deals in the U.S. through the third quarter, already more than the 8,507 in all of 2021, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. PitchBook attributes part of the surge to AI, which it says is making it easier to start companies.

The startup program is open to pre-seed and bootstrapped companies that haven’t taken money from a venture firm or other institutional investor, or raised a priced round, the type of funding round that sets a valuation.

Founders can use PitchBook to find investors who are active in their sector and stage, and to compare their valuation and growth against similar companies.

To keep their free access, startups must update their company information every quarter. PitchBook says that information can include financials, team growth and product milestones. Only “select portions” of that data will go into Origin, the company said, without saying which.

Origin covers about 25 million companies, including stealth, pre-funding and bootstrapped companies. About 15 million of them are new to PitchBook. It scores companies on how well they match an investor’s criteria and sends alerts when they show new activity.

“What’s been missing is visibility into the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see,” said Paul Santarelli, PitchBook’s chief solutions officer, in a statement announcing the products.

PitchBook didn’t disclose pricing for Origin, and the product’s web page currently asks investors to join a waitlist.

#5402. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5401. AT&T uses agentic AI to reinvent business processes from the ground up

CASE STUDY by Paul Gillin

AT&T Corp. is moving beyond using artificial intelligence to improve employee productivity, increasingly applying autonomous agents to redesign how its business operates. Nearly 500 agentic workflows are already in production, and the telecom giant plans to triple that number next year.

AT&T now processes about 45 billion AI tokens daily across the company, according to Luke Corbin (pictured, below), assistant vice president of digital transformation and AI at AT&T Business. Its agentic AI platform handles more than 1 million transactions monthly. Many of those workflows now operate autonomously, handling tasks ranging from customer provisioning to sales prospecting.

Speaking at an Amazon Web Services Inc. event in Boston earlier this month, Corbin said the company’s approach emphasizes rethinking entire processes rather than simply automating individual tasks. AT&T has moved quickly from experimenting with generative AI to systematically identifying business processes that can be redesigned around agentic capabilities.

At the heart of the transformation is Business Agent Foundry, a group established in early 2025 to work with individual business units. Rather than soliciting isolated automation ideas from employees, the foundry maps business processes using industry frameworks and identifies opportunities to eliminate unnecessary steps, organizational handoffs and legacy application dependencies, Corbin said.

One early initiative involved automating interactions with AT&T’s mainframe computers. Changes to customer fiber installation orders previously required employees to retrieve tickets from queues, manually update records and return them to the workflow.

Agentic automation eliminated portions of that manual process, reducing delays and accelerating service delivery.

“It was kind of cool having some of the most advanced technology talking to some of the oldest that we have,” Corbin said.

In another example, AT&T halved the time required to provision dedicated internet connections in buildings where fiber infrastructure was already installed.

AT&T’s architecture breaks from conventional approaches that build large numbers of independent, specialized agents. Instead, the company maintains a relatively small set of agents that execute business workflows using centrally managed business logic.

“We store the business logic in context or in memory,” Corbin said.

Retrieval agents identify applicable knowledge, while planning agents determine the actions, tools and data needed to complete a task.

“We’ve democratized agents to the point where people can use them for personal productivity, but not to where you would drive business workflows that could touch your customers or materially have an impact on your business,” Corbin said.

Every production workflow initially includes human oversight. Only after accuracy reaches the mid- to high 90% range within a permissible risk profile can agents operate autonomously. Continuous monitoring evaluates performance and detects drift.

Success metrics include labor savings, revenue generation, operating costs and customer satisfaction. Corbin said production AI investments are achieving fivefold returns within a year.

A 151-year-old company that has been using computers since they were invented “is built on a lot of legacy processes and applications,” Corbin said. “The cost of maintaining those applications, training employees to use them and ongoing maintenance is very high. When you can offset some of that with simpler generative workflows, you’ve got a business case that’s built for itself.”

Sales prospecting is one beneficiary. Agents identify promising customers by validating their locations and checking fiber availability before representatives invest time pursuing sales opportunities.

Scaling up those capabilities requires more than AI models. AT&T has had to consolidate fragmented data and provide reliable connectivity across data centers, cloud infrastructure and mobile workers.

“We’ve been through a lot of mergers and acquisitions,” Corbin said. “You can imagine what our data infrastructure looks like.”

Encouraging employees to come forward with ideas for using agents has helped limit resistance from those who worry AI could replace them. So has the opportunity to replace inefficient processes.

“There are a tremendous number of people in the organization who have knowledge and passion about the business process that they used to use but that they didn’t like,” he said.

Corbin said AT&T is now shifting its focus from improving existing processes toward using agents to launch services, enter markets and support new sales channels.

Ultimately, Corbin said responsibility for AI-driven business transformation should be distributed throughout the organization, rather than concentrated in a specialized team like Business Agent Foundry.

“I feel privileged to have the team that I do, but in the long run, my team shouldn’t exist,” he said. “What we do should be completely distributed.”

#5399. Allen Family Philanthropies gives $10M to hundreds of small arts groups across Washington state

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 9, 2026 at 2:56 pm

Allen Family Philanthropies and Seattle nonprofit ArtsFund awarded $10 million to 745 small arts and culture organizations across Washington state, and renewed the grant program for another $10 million next year.

The latest Community Accelerator Grant awards range from $2,500 to $25,000 and reach organizations in 37 of the state’s 39 counties. The 2027 renewal brings the program’s total to $50 million over five years.

For 2026, the program focused on groups with annual budgets under $1 million, which raised the average award by about 25%, from $10,753 last year to $13,423.

The change followed a sector analysis by Allen Family Philanthropies and SMU DataArts. It found that smaller arts groups lost an average of one staff position between 2023 and 2024, while organizations with budgets over $1 million added an average of five.

“The incredible reach of this program across our state, along with the significant findings from our report, show just how much this type of flexible support is needed to bolster Washington’s rich and diverse arts and culture sector,” said Lara Littlefield, executive director of Allen Family Philanthropies.

Of this year’s grantees, 496 are in Northwest Washington, 132 in Southwest, 67 in Eastern and 50 in Central Washington. Recipients include 12 of the state’s 29 federally recognized tribes, and more than 22% are in rural counties.

A handful of the organizations blend art and technology, including Tacoma’s Fablab Nonprofit ($25,000), Seattle-based Simulated Immersive Experimental Realities ($15,000) and Bellingham Makerspace ($2,500).

The Old Hotel Art Gallery in Othello, in Adams County, has received a $25,000 grant each year since 2024. The gallery used the money to pay staff a living wage, to keep operating until its annual fundraiser, and to renovate its historic building, which now brings in rental income.

Gallery director Samantha Copas said the 2025 award “truly kept our doors open.”

Allen Family Philanthropies, formerly known as the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation, was founded in 1988 by the late Microsoft co-founder and his sister, Jody Allen. Arts and culture is one of its core program areas, along with youth and the environment. Last year the foundation committed nearly $7 million to eight Seattle Center nonprofits, including KEXP and the Museum of Pop Culture, to expand youth access to the arts.

ArtsFund will hold a virtual webinar in the spring for organizations interested in applying for 2027 grants. Details will be posted here.

("Pony.ai") (NASDAQ: PONY; HKEX: 2026), a global leader in the large-scale commercialization of autonomous driving technology, and Toyota today announced the launch of fully driverless commercial services with their âcollaboratively developed bZ4X Robotaxi.

#5396. Data center developers brace for new reality as election backlash sinks in

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:25 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Data center developers already knew they had a public relations problem. This month’s midterm elections showed how much of a political problem it has become.

Voters approved data center restrictions in 44 of 45 local measures across a dozen states. Candidates who support stronger regulation of the facilities won 32 of the 34 gubernatorial races called so far. And political campaigns reportedly spent more than $380 million on TV ads referencing data centers, according to the Associated Press.

The results capped a year of accelerating resistance as tech giants plan to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on new facilities.

So what comes next? More outreach, more transparency and the expectation that states and local governments will pass data center rules, said leaders in the Pacific Northwest.

“We’ve been working and adapting our approach to meet the moment,” said John Wilson, chief financial officer of Sabey Data Centers, in an interview. “There used to be a time where we would say that our track record could speak for itself, and that’s clearly no longer the case.”

Communities nationwide have raised concerns about the facilities’ effect on rising electric bills, their water use for cooling electronics and the noise they generate.

Broader fears about artificial intelligence are also stoking the pushback, including worries that it will replace workers and appropriate human-created content, and that it can provide erroneous information, foster unhealthy relationships with users, or facilitate scams or terrorist attacks.

A renewed effort to regulate data centers is expected in January in Washington state — home to the headquarters of Sabey, Microsoft and Amazon.

Earlier this year, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, pushed legislation that included ratepayer protections, transparency on environmental impacts and clean energy requirements. Microsoft and the national Data Center Coalition opposed the bill, which failed.

“It’s going to be a very tech-heavy session,” Doglio said.

Before voters weighed in this month, tech companies launched efforts to assuage public fears.

In January, Microsoft released its “Community First AI Infrastructure” initiative, which includes promises to pay the company’s full power costs, reject local property tax breaks, replenish more water than it uses, train local workers and fund AI education and community programs.

Last month, Amazon announced its “Built Together” program, pledging to invest $1 billion over five years in the U.S. communities where it operates data centers, including support for education and civic projects. The initiative offers similar commitments to Microsoft’s on transparency and covering its energy costs.

Wilson said Sabey also works with communities to understand and meet their needs. When a proposed campus in Indianapolis triggered significant pushback, the company brought community members to Quincy, a central Washington data center hub, to tour a Sabey facility and hear from locals about their experience.

“It requires a lot of patience. It requires a lot of transparency in our communication,” Wilson said. Sabey’s Decatur Technology Park in Indianapolis is moving ahead, and the company aims to bring it online in 2030.

But the even bigger challenge now is statewide moratoriums and data center bans — a scale of resistance that is difficult to address even when there is local support.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. Umatilla, where Sabey is developing its first Oregon campus, declared a local state of emergency over the potential loss of investment and revenue, the Oregon Capital Chronicle reported.

Even with the surge in resistance, “we’ve been able to find our way through on every project that we’ve had,” Wilson said. “I’m knocking on wood as I say that.”

Corporate commitments alone may no longer be enough to win public confidence, said Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, in a GeekWire interview. Communities increasingly want laws requiring all data center developers to build responsibly — a shift he called a “watershed” moment, “but one we anticipated.”

“[P]eople want to see everyone who builds a data center do it in a responsible way,” Smith added, “and they feel that the only way that one can obtain that result is to have some new laws that are put in place.”

Come next year, that could include Washington and impact local tech giants, Sabey and others. Baxtel, a data center industry research firm, lists 29 Microsoft facilities operating in Washington and four under construction, with Sabey operating eight facilities.

Amazon plans to build its first large-scale data centers in Washington, with proposed campuses in Walla Walla County and the Tri-Cities. Amazon did not respond to repeated requests for comment on this story.

Doglio said the next version of her bill will be more stringent. “We have to have a strong bill,” she said, adding that the public and members of her party are calling for it. Microsoft did not publicly specify which provisions triggered its opposition to the previous bill.

Wilson hopes any legislation, in Washington or elsewhere, allows flexibility and recognizes that data centers vary widely in size, impact and application. Sabey provides data center space and infrastructure for customers ranging from major cloud companies to corporations and community organizations.

“Describing all data centers as one thing is just not accurate,” Wilson said, “and it doesn’t understand the realities of the industry itself.”

Smith expressed optimism that U.S. lawmakers can find a middle ground that meets the needs of communities and tech companies.

“There’s plenty of room to draft laws that enable people to go forward and build responsible data centers without chilling the economic contributions these data centers make, especially to local communities,” he said.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5394. Fintech giant Plaid opening Seattle engineering office, with plans to double local headcount

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 10, 2026 at 11:58 am

Plaid is opening an engineering office in Seattle’s Westlake neighborhood in January and plans to double its local workforce to about 80 people by next summer.

The San Francisco-based fintech company says the new 11,466-square-foot space at 1000 Dexter Ave. N. will serve as a hub for its technical teams, with most open Seattle roles focused on machine learning, data science and engineering.

Plaid said in a blog post that it chose Seattle because much of the cloud and AI technology behind modern financial infrastructure was built in the region. The company is developing AI models trained on its network to understand patterns in how money moves.

Plaid already has about 40 employees in the Seattle area, who currently work remotely, The Seattle Times reported. “There’s just great talent in Seattle, so it’s a little bit of a no-brainer for us,” Meghan Welch, Plaid’s chief people officer, told the Times.

Plaid’s careers page lists more than 50 open roles that include Seattle as a possible location, though most are also open in San Francisco, New York or other cities. About half are in data, engineering or security, with the rest spread across sales, legal, finance and other teams.

Founded in 2013, Plaid was valued at $8 billion in an employee share sale earlier this year, down from a 2021 peak of $13.4 billion. The company says more than 150 million people have used its technology to connect their financial accounts.

Plaid is led by co-founder and CEO Zachary Perret.

The new office will have views of Lake Union, an outdoor deck and event space, along with three catered meals a day, according to the company.

#5393. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.
