#5376. This NFL Quarterback Used to Work With NASA. It Inspired Him to Change How Athletes Travel.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Lions quarterback and former NASA intern Josh Dobbs wants to redesign how pro athletes fly.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Sports were Detroit Lions backup quarterback Josh Dobbs’ first love. He started playing baseball at 4 years old, then football a year later. Those passions stuck with him as he got older, but another interest began to take shape.

“When we would travel as a family, I enjoyed going on trips that required us to fly somewhere because I liked going to the airport and seeing airplanes take off and land,” Dobbs shares. “I was fascinated by how these massive tubes of metal are flying across the country.”

Now a 10-year NFL veteran, Dobbs is exploring a future in the other field he’s passionate about: aviation and aerospace.

“I want to build an aviation infrastructure that significantly improves the way athletes travel,” Dobbs tells Entrepreneur. And based on what he’s done so far, the quarterback known as “The Passtronaut” is already well on his way.

Dobbs attended the University of Tennessee, where he threw for more than 7,000 yards, rushed for over 2,000, and accounted for 85 total touchdowns. But unlike some athletes who view college primarily as a stepping stone to the pros, Dobbs wanted to pursue a field he was genuinely passionate about while giving himself options beyond football in case his playing career didn’t work out.

That’s where aerospace engineering came in. “It was the perfect mix of aviation, but also problem-solving, math, and science, which are things I was good at in school,” Dobbs says.

He also ties it back to football, citing the work ethic and processing skills required to succeed in each field (no pun intended).

“In engineering class, they’re giving you a problem, they’re giving you equations, you’ve got to solve them, go through that thought process, apply it, and repeat the process,” Dobbs explains.

“In football, it’s the same thing. A defense will give you various coverages that you have to attack for the game. Throughout the week, you’re generating solutions to the issues that they’re giving you, and you have to go out and execute a game plan.”

He believes the methodical approach to problem-solving required of a quarterback helped prepare him for a career in engineering, and vice versa.

Dobbs’ collegiate performance earned him a spot in the NFL, where the Pittsburgh Steelers selected him in the fourth round. While he was laser-focused on establishing himself as a successful quarterback, making it to the pros didn’t mean putting his passion for aviation and aerospace on the back burner.

“You get to the NFL, and you realize outside of the season how much truly free time you have,” Dobbs shares. “My goal is always to maximize my time and opportunity.”

He didn’t have to look far for an opportunity. During Dobbs’ rookie year, he was introduced to the NFLPA Externship Program, a career-development initiative run by the NFL Players Association’s Player Affairs department. The program connects active and transitioning players with real-world work experience, networking, and mentorship outside of football. One opportunity involved Fanatics, where players traveled to different company sites across the country to get a behind-the-scenes look at the sports merchandising business.

Dobbs was impressed by the experience but wanted to apply the same concept to an industry closer to his own interests.

“I kind of wanted to take that same thought process and get a behind-the-scenes look at how one of the top engineering companies, per se, in the world works,” he says. “And so I had some contacts at NASA and was able to put together an opportunity to do a similar deal with NASA at the Kennedy Space Center.”

Dobbs spent a month at the center, shadowing engineers across different NASA departments to better understand the aerospace industry. At the time, the agency was preparing the Artemis I rocket, an uncrewed test flight designed to lay the groundwork for humanity’s return to the Moon. Dobbs joined the instrumentation group responsible for the rocket’s mobile launcher, getting a hands-on look at how engineers developed and installed the equipment used to monitor the rocket.

His second assignment brought him even closer to the action. Dobbs worked with a team developing a lunar rover designed to mine regolith, or moon dirt. Although the rover has yet to launch, he researched potential commercial rockets that could carry it to the Moon.

“That was pretty unique because I really got to see a mission, a goal, an objective, and how I could fit in and create a solution for them,” Dobbs says.

Beyond the engineering work, he also got an inside look at the business of space exploration, learning how commercial space contracts worked and about companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin. It was Dobbs’ first real exposure to the aerospace industry, and the experience only deepened his interest in the field.

“There’s a lot of emerging opportunities in commercial space,” Dobbs explains, citing tourism, scientific research, and resource storage as a few. “But I would say that experience really drew my interest back to aviation.”

In college, he had interned with Pratt & Whitney, a major aerospace manufacturer specializing in aircraft engines and other propulsion systems. Later, while playing for the San Francisco 49ers, he earned his pilot’s license, choosing the Bay Area as his classroom.

“When I was talking with other people who had gone along the path of getting their pilot license, they said the best place to fly is the Bay Area, San Francisco. It’s beautiful, a lot of air traffic, a lot of nuance. It’s very hectic, but it’s a beautiful place to fly and a great place to learn,” Dobbs says.

After his experience at NASA, Dobbs was more motivated than ever to make his mark on the aviation industry.

“My goal is to create a charter option that improves team travel,” Dobbs shares. “I think the way that sports teams travel is very unique because it’s a logistical challenge. You’re transporting anywhere from 45 to 150 large human beings across the country so they can compete at the highest level. And right now, a lot of those solutions are based on the same commercial solutions that aren’t always adequate for the customers traveling, to say the least.”

Dobbs is uniquely positioned to speak from experience, having played 10 seasons in the NFL, during which he’s flown more than the average person does in their lifetime. He believes there’s a disconnect between how much professional teams invest in player health and how little attention they pay to travel conditions.

“When you’re spending millions of dollars on your athletes, not only from a salary standpoint, but also through investments in food, nutrition, training facilities and technologies that help them rest and recover, and then you’re putting them on a plane with inadequate seating arrangements and seats that don’t fit them, asking them to travel across the country hours before a game, it’s very counterintuitive,” Dobbs explains. “They’re investing a lot in their athletes, but the solution, which really comes down to the aircraft and equipment available to teams, is what’s missing. That’s where I think there’s a great opportunity.”

Dobbs says he’s since gone on a “deep dive” into NFL and collegiate team travel schedules, drawing on his own experience with the 49ers.

“We travel a lot. There aren’t many West Coast games,” he shares of those seasons. “You’re spending a lot of time on planes, and you get off feeling tight before having to compete at the highest level. Then you get back on the plane, prepare for practice and do it all over again the next week.”

He believes investing in better travel technology and accommodations would help athletes arrive rested and ready to compete, ultimately improving the product fans see on the field and court.

“I think we all love the product of sport that we’re seeing, and we want to see it more. But the key is for the athletes to be rested, recovered, and ready to go wherever they are playing,” Dobbs says. “Creating an adequate solution for the collegiate and professional levels would ultimately improve the product that we’re seeing on every field and every court. The key is to make it sustainable.”

As Dobbs develops his own plans for the aviation industry, he’s also focused on getting more young athletes involved in STEM through the Extraordinary Dobbs Foundation. “I’ve been fortunate to have great connections and opportunities to get into the industry, and so my goal is to give back to the next generation of aerospace engineers and student-athletes who also want to pursue STEM careers,” he says.

Last year, the foundation brought seven aerospace engineering students from the University of Tennessee to Kennedy Space Center to witness the Artemis II launch. As the foundation grows, Dobbs hopes to organize more experiences like this with NASA, as well as Cirrus, an American aircraft manufacturer whose planes he used during flight training.

“I’ve crossed paths with a lot of people who have similar interests but don’t know where to start. It’s about giving them that introduction to the industry so they can build long and promising careers in STEM,” he says.

Dobbs hopes to play many more years in the NFL, but when the time comes to hang up his cleats, the veteran quarterback already has a game plan for what comes next.

“I think through the work I’ll do when I finish playing, I’ll create a successful solution that can become a catalyst for growing sports, especially football, around the world,” Dobbs says. “Because if you want to play games in Tokyo and Dubai, you’ve got to be able to get there.”

Sports were Detroit Lions backup quarterback Josh Dobbs’ first love. He started playing baseball at 4 years old, then football a year later. Those passions stuck with him as he got older, but another interest began to take shape.

“When we would travel as a family, I enjoyed going on trips that required us to fly somewhere because I liked going to the airport and seeing airplanes take off and land,” Dobbs shares. “I was fascinated by how these massive tubes of metal are flying across the country.”

Now a 10-year NFL veteran, Dobbs is exploring a future in the other field he’s passionate about: aviation and aerospace.

#5375. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5374. India’s film industry hopes a $420 million mythological epic can be a global hit

India’s film industry is betting that one of its most popular stories can become a global blockbuster. But a sky-high budget, mixed reviews, and concerns over its use of AI, have raised those stakes even higher.

With a reported budget of 40 billion Indian rupees ($420 million), the two-part Ramayana is the most expensive film ever made in India. The film retells the mythological story of Prince Rama’s quest to save his wife Sita from the demon king Ravana, and is inspired by the ancient Sanskrit epic widely regarded as sacred scripture in Hinduism.

The mythological epic held its global premiere in Los Angeles on Oct. 27, drawing praise for its visuals and performances, as well as criticism over its slow pacing and a score that divided critics. The film currently has a 77% critic score and 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.

The film has since generated over $100 million at the global box office, though $67 million of that comes from India. Still, Ramayana was the first Indian film to top the U.K. box office.

The two-part film is among the biggest gambles in Indian cinema—and it is a test of whether a story rooted in Indian religious tradition can draw audiences worldwide. As the filmmakers pursue international audiences with dubbed versions and an effects-heavy spectacle, Ramayana’s reception could offer a measure of how far Indian cinema’s global ambitions can go.

The film’s first installment, titled “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” debuted globally on Nov. 5, with a U.S. release on Nov. 6, one day later, according to Box Office Mojo, which tracks the North American box office. Variety reported that the film had grossed $55.7 million globally during its opening weekend.

Indian films used to have global appeal, particularly outside the West. “Raj Kapoor’s film Awara (1951) was a huge success in the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe, China, Turkey, and North Africa. Mehboob Khan’s films like Aan (1952) and Mother India (1957) were also popular in all sorts of markets where diasporic audiences did not exist,” Tejaswini Ganti, a New York University professor who specializes in Indian cinema, says.

During the 1980s, Indian films continued to play well outside of the country, with Disco Dancer (1982) and Mard (1985) being particularly popular in the Soviet Union and West Africa, respectively. In the following two decades, romantic-dramas, such as Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge (1995) and Kal Ho Naa Ho (2003) were hugely popular among the Indian diaspora.

More recently, Dangal, released in 2016, grossed more than $190 million in China, while Secret Superstar, released in 2017, earned $117.7 million there, according to Box Office Mojo.

Ramayana’s filmmakers hope the film will attract global audiences. “For generations, the Ramayana has inspired people through its timeless humanity and enduring values,” producer Namit Malhotra said in a July 28 statement. “Our ambition has always been to honor that legacy while creating a cinematic experience worthy of audiences everywhere.”

But even if Ramayana was made for a global audience, whether its traditional Indian story will resonate with audiences of different cultures.

“Indian producers have been hoping for an international ‘crossover’ hit for a long time,” Philip A. Lutgendorf, a University of Iowa professor who specializes in Indian language and culture, says. “The strategy behind Ramayana’s release at this time seems to be to capitalize on the success of epic sci-fi, fantasy, and superhero films and film franchises.”

In the U.S., the film is being released in two different versions: the original Hindi-language cut, which runs for three hours and 15 minutes, and an English-dubbed version that’s about 30 minutes shorter, with musical sequences removed and other scenes trimmed.

“It remains to be seen whether this strategy will succeed and whether the Hindu mythological archetypes of the story will resonate with a broad international audience,” Lutgendorf says.

He says the film’s extensive CGI use could help it connect with a worldwide audience. “Ramayana, with its relatively clear-cut and polarized moral universec, does seem like the obvious choice for projecting a traditional Indian narrative and worldview into the current global entertainment realm of CGI-driven fantasy films and videogames,” he adds.

Ramayana has also faced criticism over its reported use of AI.

A promotional video says the film used “Brahma AI” to bring different language versions to the screen. The film has reportedly been dubbed into nearly 40 languages. Brahma AI is an “AI-native operating system that understands, organizes, and creates new content from enterprise content,” according to its official website.

Director Nitesh Tiwari said at the premiere that the dialogue and character voices were recorded by human performers. He said AI was used to adjust lip-sync for the localized versions. “As far as AI is concerned, it’s only been used to get the lip-sync so that we can present the film to the world in their language,” he explained.

Despite that clarification, the film has faced pushback from some U.S.-based critics. “A majestic epic falls victim to clunky action, eye-sore CGI, and awkward AI lip-syncing in what is, unfortunately, just a Part 1,” read one review on IGN.

#5373. Ex-Seattle startup DeltaGen acquired by new AI company backed by Veeam co-founder

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 5:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 5:51 am

DeltaGen, an AI startup that got its start in Seattle before moving to San Francisco this year, has been acquired by Worker.ai, a new small-business software company backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev.

Worker, which launched Thursday, acquired all of DeltaGen for an undisclosed price that included a substantial cash component and equity in Worker, DeltaGen co-founder and CEO Rene Bystron told GeekWire.

Bystron joins Worker as co-founder and COO, and nine other DeltaGen employees are coming with him, including co-founders Michal Studnicka and Matus Ondreicka.

Worker, led by co-founder and CEO John Roberts, a former private equity operator based in Raleigh, N.C., is building software that lets small businesses hand off recurring work to AI agents. DeltaGen’s voice technology captures decisions made in conversations and turns them into assigned tasks.

Roberts had been a DeltaGen customer before Worker needed voice technology, Bystron said. “We could have raised another round and kept building independently, but this gave us the capital and experience to move faster with people we trusted,” he said.

Launched in 2024, DeltaGen raised a $1.2 million pre-seed round in early 2025 to build generative AI tools for financial professionals, with a focus on streamlining mergers and acquisitions. The company relocated from Seattle to San Francisco earlier this year.

“I still love Seattle and miss it like crazy,” said Bystron, who is keeping his apartment in Belltown. “But being closer to the AI founders, customers and investors in San Francisco makes a real difference at this stage. It also didn’t help that Washington has been chipping away at its tax advantage.”

Timashev, who co-founded data backup giant Veeam, is backing Worker to help small businesses such as manufacturers, service companies and family businesses grow.

“AI can now give small businesses more capacity without asking already stretched owners to work longer days,” he said in a statement. “Worker is my bet on that shift.” The size of his investment was not disclosed.

DeltaGen’s current product is an AI voice platform, which will continue as it’s integrated into Worker. DeltaGen’s AI voice platform will continue as it’s integrated into Worker, which is opening access gradually through a waitlist.

#5372. What I Learned Spending Thousands on Meta Ads to Launch a New Product

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

I used to measure ad spend of tens of millions a month with a large team. Now I do most of that work on my own with AI, and here is what it can’t do.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

About a year ago, I was working for a global fintech headquartered in London. We had a budget of tens of millions of dollars per month to spend on marketing, so we worked with a fairly large marketing team. As director for growth, I was responsible for all sorts of technical marketing duties, including measurement, signals engineering, analytics and the measurement of performance in general.

We employed a large team of dozens of developers to do this. Now things have completely changed. I can do a lot of the things that I used to do with a team just on my own with AI. I wrote SQL code for years, but I’ve not written any SQL for over a year now. Most of my analyses are not done in dashboards, but via chatbot.

Having spent most of my career advising other people how to grow their business, I put it to work on my own product, RunInk, an app that turns your running routes into posters, and spent about $1,700 on Meta ads in the first month. Sales so far add up to around $200. I understand that there is a testing budget involved in these things. It’s not going to go immediately well. And in fact, it got more profitable once the ads had more to learn from.

There was a team of dozens of designers making different creatives, and many of them got released and tested and measured. Whereas now I can get Claude to make a ton of different ideas, and Meta’s AI can just test them.

It’s also not just a question of speed. Yes, AI’s creatives are often visually unappealing. But I’m not a designer. I can’t make nice things. I don’t know how to make nice things. But with the prompting, I can get AI to do it. I can focus on the winners and on getting lots of different variants out that I think might be useful.

Signals engineering was generally the martech job, and it was not an easy job — both for large companies like the one I worked for, which had a relative dearth of signals compared to ecommerce, and for small brands starting out. There can be a significant increase in performance by just doing this well.

Ad platforms run on machine learning, which requires lots of signals to be able to learn what type of person is interested in your product. Meta says an ad set needs about 50 optimization events a week to get out of its learning phase. However, if you’re starting out from zero, you have no one interested in your product. This is also the case if you sell few, but high-ticket items. You have relatively few people coming by, but you need to figure out who they are and somehow advertise something to them.

So what you start doing is breaking down the funnel into smaller steps. Do they land on my website? Do they create an account? In my case, do they connect their Strava account? Do they create an image? Do they export an image? Do they export various images?

Then you try to add some monetary value to all of these steps and break it down from there. And then you can slowly tune and adjust these values so that you stop paying for page views and for signups and eventually start buying purchases.

AI is a powerful tool, but it still makes mistakes. You need to double check AI, ask questions and validate everything. Not necessarily by manually redoing the numbers yourself, but by asking probing questions the way you would ask an intern.

Back when I managed a team, the way I would ensure numbers were right (or at least vaguely right) was by probing them. I’d tell my team: “Hey, that number seems high; are you sure about it?” or “That number seems off; can you double-check?”

Also, don’t forget that your AI agent often lacks the context you do. If you know that five of the last 10 purchases made on your site were you testing a new feature, tell it!

It is hard to build a product if you have no users. Once I had the first 100 or so users on the website, I surveyed the people who made posters.

I saw that there was some sort of demand, some happiness with the product itself. But 11 of the 16 who answered said the free digital file was enough for them. And the only way I made money was via printed posters!

This told me that I should offer a digital product. And it instantly became my best seller! Business success is about finding the right price point and the right product, and to do that, you need to talk to your customers.

If you’re starting out with a brand new product, be aware that it’s going to cost you a lot more than $1,000. To get this to work, you’re most likely going to have to spend more than that.

That being said, it’s a great way to get people to your product. If you want to find out more, I write about measurement and AI on my site.

About a year ago, I was working for a global fintech headquartered in London. We had a budget of tens of millions of dollars per month to spend on marketing, so we worked with a fairly large marketing team. As director for growth, I was responsible for all sorts of technical marketing duties, including measurement, signals engineering, analytics and the measurement of performance in general.

We employed a large team of dozens of developers to do this. Now things have completely changed. I can do a lot of the things that I used to do with a team just on my own with AI. I wrote SQL code for years, but I’ve not written any SQL for over a year now. Most of my analyses are not done in dashboards, but via chatbot.

Having spent most of my career advising other people how to grow their business, I put it to work on my own product, RunInk, an app that turns your running routes into posters, and spent about $1,700 on Meta ads in the first month. And in fact, it got more profitable once the ads had more to learn from.

#5371. Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader. He’s even eyeing the White House

An Elon Musk acolyte, Tesla driver, and serial entrepreneur, Teague Egan was imagining ways of breaking into renewable energy in 2018 while he took a vacation to Bolivia. He learned about the country’s salt flats, their lithium reserves potential and, eventually, about the industry’s antiquated lithium mining techniques.

“As an entrepreneur, I knew there had to be a better way. That was my ‘aha’ moment,” said Egan, now 38. He really began to think about how the lithium-ion batteries in Tesla’s electric vehicles are made and their massive global growth potential.

He quickly founded EnergyX—short for Energy Exploration Technologies—and this year became the only company mining lithium commercially in the U.S. with modern direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology at its new Project Lonestar site in East Texas. This summer, EnergyX also opened a project in Chile extracting 170 metric tons of lithium a year.

But these are still just demonstration plants. The real growth is about to begin, he touted.

“EnergyX is just going to keep our head down and move towards commercialization,” Egan told Fortune.

The plan is to commence construction next year. EnergyX aims to bring its Black Giant lithium project in Chile online by the end of 2028 with a first phase producing 7,500 tons per year and expanding to 52,500 tons annually by 2030. Project Lonestar in Texas would quickly follow with a 15,000-ton facility in 2029 and growing to 50,000 tons by 2031.

These are admittedly aggressive timelines, but Egan is confident the progress will pick up quickly after achieving a watershed moment in October of inking its largest customer.

But first, let’s take a quick step back. Two years ago, The Wall Street Journal ran this headline about Egan: “He Wants to Be the Lithium King. Run for President. And Live to 150.” The wording is brash but not inaccurate—yes, he says he still wants to occupy the White House and live well past 100—and he comes across as an over-the-top tech bro. Many didn’t take him seriously.

Egan went to work proving the doubters wrong. Since then, EnergyX opened its new Austin, Texas headquarters, nearly quadrupled its acreage footprint in the lithium-heavy Smackover Formation in East Texas and southwestern Arkansas, completed its Texas and Chile demo projects, and received a $225 million influx from Italian energy giant Eni.

Most importantly, in October, major energy trading house Trafigura signed a $2 billion, 10-year contract with EnergyX for 100,000 metric tons of lithium from its Black Giant and Project Lonestar enterprises.

“To have that type of customer is not only really encouraging for us, but also really validating to the rest of the market,” Egan said. “This is actually the single-largest DLE offtake in history. That’s a cool little feather in the cap. The major thing that investors or project lenders need to see is that type of contract.”

His expectation is that more buyers will quickly follow suit, bringing EnergyX close to commencing construction. The Trafigura deal also boosts EnergyX’s pending $690 million loan with the U.S. Export-Import Bank.

While EnergyX’s success is far from assured, Egan has proven his company must be taken seriously.

Egan’s mentor and idol is his father, Michael Egan, who became the majority owner of Alamo Rent a Car, grew the company nationally, and sold it in 1996, continuing to chair the business until 2003. Now retired, Michael Egan sits on the EnergyX board.

“I’m a serial entrepreneur. My dad was a serial entrepreneur. I learned from him,” Teague Egan said. “I don’t have an engineering or a chemistry degree. I’m an entrepreneur. I’m a problem solver. I feel like I have a Ph. D. in engineering from working at EnergyX for eight years.”

After growing up near Fort Lauderdale, Florida, Egan moved to Los Angeles to attend the University of Southern California. While a college student, he started a record label and sport agency. He quickly found success in music after signing the Boston rapper Sammy Adams, who hit No. 1 on the iTunes hip-hop chart in 2010.

Egan said his biggest regret might be declining to sign a deal with his label and Interscope Records because Egan didn’t find much continued success in music. Then again, if he had, EnergyX probably wouldn’t exist, he said.

His music profits though led him to invest many of his gains. He was an early investor in Tesla in 2013 when the company still had a market cap of less than $10 billion. Today, Tesla sits above $1.5 trillion. Egan said he used some of those proceeds to help start EnergyX.

Ever since, Egan has become an admitted follower of all things Elon Musk and his approach to business. And they’re both Austin, Texas-based now. “He’s transformed into arguably the greatest entrepreneur and innovator in the history of humanity,” Egan said. “People can say what they want about his political views and stuff but, in terms of his contributions to humanity, he’s like unmatched. He’s essentially my idol other than my father. He has that same sense of curiosity and problem solving.”

Driven by EVs and now also by battery energy storage, global lithium demand has jumped more than 400% this decade, to over 1.5 million metric tons per year. By 2035, that demand could approach 4 million tons.

With the lithium business focused on traditional hard-rock mining or evaporation ponds, Egan sought another way. Evaporation ponds can take two years to extract the lithium, literally waiting for the sun to evaporate the water and help filter out the lithium. Egan isn’t that patient.

He jumped into direct lithium extraction technology. He didn’t invent it, but he wants to perfect and commercialize it. Using advanced filtration technology, DLE operates much like oil and gas by drilling wells, pumping out the brine water, processing and refining the lithium, and returning more than 90% of the brine underground. DLE can take two days instead of two years, although the upfront costs are extensive.

But the legacy lithium industry wasn’t ready to embrace DLE, and especially not the required financial investments.

“Our original business model was just to license our technology to the existing pond producers. We said, ‘Hey, we have a better mousetrap. This will be much better for you,’” Egan said. “They strung us along and, finally, we realized that, and we said we’re going to have to go acquire our own resources and vertically integrate to prove this and scale it and realize the technology.”

That’s when EnergyX began acquiring its own acreage in Chile and the Smackover. Chile and Argentina count among the top lithium producers globally—with Australia and China—but the U.S. only accounts a little more than 1% of global lithium supplies. Those U.S. projects are concentrated in Nevada, including Lithium Americas’ Thacker Pass project currently under construction. EnergyX also is exploring a project in Utah.

“A decade ago, the total volumes of lithium demand didn’t warrant new innovation and investment,” Egan acknowledged. Everything has changed very rapidly.

But the Smackover region is believed to have the greatest potential to boom in the U.S. The challenge is the lithium is found in high concentrations within an underground aquifer that requires DLE. Vancouver-based Standard Lithium is scheduled to start construction on the first major DLE project in the Smackover early next year, at least a few months ahead of EnergyX.

Because of the similarities to oil and gas, ExxonMobil and Chevron are fast followers, having acquired massive acreage footprints in recent years.

“The U.S. is definitely at a tipping point for lithium production,” said Standard Lithium CEO David Park. “The area that has the greatest potential is the Smackover basin. When you think of the Smackover, you should really think of it as lithium’s Permian Basin. Through the introduction of relatively novel technologies, we’re able to open a once non-economic resource in a manner that can bring on projects of scale with world-class economics.”

While there’s room for multiple winners, Egan said he’s convinced EnergyX’s in-house lithium filtration technology will make it the choice producer for customers going forward. The lithium reserves in Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia in South America have fewer impurities than in the U.S., Egan said, but the Smackover is still a fantastic resource, and the U.S. needs to build up its own domestic supplies.

Even though EV sales are slower in the U.S. than much of the rest of the world, Egan sees the path forward from his Austin hub in a city that serves as the unofficial lab for self-driving vehicles and robotaxis—nearly all of which use lithium-ion batteries.

Early this month, Tesla said it is discontinuing the costly Cybertruck to make way for the self-driving Cybercab, while Waymo, Avride, and Zoox are all betting on robotaxis. Egan sees them daily. “Living in Austin is seeing the future, and that is only going to spread.”

That future requires EnergyX growing exponentially, he said. “I’m a long-term goals kind of guy. A lot of people call me the ‘king of lithium.’ We’ve taken steps, especially this year, to continue to build upon that. Our goal is to be producing between 500,000 and a 1 million tons of lithium per year by 2040 and become the biggest lithium company in the world.”

And, yes, after that, he does still have his eyes set on the White House and running for president.

“That’s still a long-term goal. I don’t think it’s unreasonable. The mindset of America has changed a lot over the past 10 years into who can lead the country. With [President] Trump, for better or worse, anything is possible now.”

Jordan Blum is the Energy editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of a growing global energy sector for oil and gas, transition businesses, renewables, and critical minerals.

#5370. Seattle’s Allen Institute helps create a ‘Rosetta Stone’ for brain cells to unlock clues to disease

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 11, 2026 at 5:15 pm

A coalition of 56 institutions across nine countries is publishing groundbreaking research today on the basal ganglia — a group of brain structures that help control movement, emotions, motivation and habits. The region is linked to psychiatric and degenerative disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and Parkinson’s disease.

The scientist have produced a biological Rosetta Stone that creates a shared system for naming and describing cells in the basal ganglia across species. The goal is to help researchers compare findings, collaborate and accelerate their understanding of this essential brain region.

“This is groundwork that is necessary to really make progress,” said Michael Hawrylycz, principal investigator with the Seattle-based Allen Institute who helped organize the consortium.

The project, called the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, or BICAN, produced a basal ganglia atlas that is publicly available for basic researchers, clinicians and others to use.

The research is being presented in a package of 26 articles in a special issue of the journal Cell. The data comes from humans, macaques, marmoset and mice. One of the benefits of comparing the basal ganglia between species is understanding which components are uniquely human, providing potential insights into neurological diseases.

Despite the critical and wide-ranging roles, the basal ganglia is relatively small — it’s about 2% of the brain with a volume roughly the size of a large gumball.

For the project, the researchers pulled information from 25.5 million brain cells, including 21 million human cells. They used a variety of techniques to tease out insights, including RNA sequencing to identify gene activity from single cells in precise locations; epigenomic studies revealing where genes are switched on or off; and measurements of electrical activity combined with cell shape and genetic information.

It’s a lot of data to stitch together and make sense of, Hawrylycz said. “AI is a perfect tool” for the job, he said, because it excels at finding patterns.

The findings could help guide future treatments, but the work remains basic research rather than clinical research, Hawrylycz said.

The new research is the first major installment of the third phase of a brain-mapping effort that began in 2014. The first phase demonstrated that scientists could analyze individual cells on a large scale. The second produced an atlas of the mouse brain.

BICAN aims to create a standardized atlas describing cells throughout the brains of humans and other primates. Hawrylycz said the work is expected to take another two or three years.

#5369. Tech Executives Tell Me What They Tell No One Else, and I Think ‘The Audacity’ Got Silicon Valley Mostly Right.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

An executive coach who hears what tech leaders say behind closed doors weighs in on how “The Audacity” gets Silicon Valley right.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

“More than physical pain, I fear humiliation.” That’s the first line of The Audacity, spoken by tech CEO Duncan Park (Billy Magnussen) to his therapist. I’ve coached tech leaders for more than a decade, including people who reported directly to Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Steve Huffman, and I can’t recall a client ever saying the word “humiliation” to me. They say “insecure” and “imposter syndrome” instead. The show names a real fear in its opening seconds, using a word I rarely hear.

The series aired on AMC this spring and landed on Netflix in August, where it’s finding a second audience.

Most of the reviews came from TV critics, but I watched it as the person executives say these things to. They tell me things they keep from their boards, their teams and their partners.

With that in mind, I wanted to share what the show gets right about the people leading the tech industry and what was stretched to make good TV.

In episode seven, Duncan says the fear of humiliation is behind every little lie. His therapist, Dr. JoAnne Felder (Sarah Goldberg), puts it another way: Everyone spins, even to themselves. That’s the most accurate line in the series.

Executives spin to me, too. It usually sounds like catastrophizing what a boss might say or fixating on the worst-case scenario of an important meeting or presentation. When I hear it, I ask them to pause and take a breath. Then we get clear on what they value and what they want. Then they pick one small step forward. It’s simple, and that’s why it works.

The pause does most of the work. Once a leader slows down, the spin falls apart on its own.

In the first episode, Duncan screams at his housekeeper for failing to catch a tungsten cube he throws to her. One recap called his outbursts one of the funniest elements of the premiere. I call it reality. I’ve coached executives whose CEOs screamed at them and berated people in executive meetings — at companies that have been voted “best place to work.”

The show also gets right the fact that founders and boards tolerate this behavior. When it’s the CEO yelling, the people in the room have few options. A senior executive I coached reported directly to a CEO like this. Our work focused on how to manage themselves long enough to get out and find a healthier environment, which they did. Sometimes the only fix is a new employer.

Carl Bardolph (Zach Galifianakis) is the billionaire Duncan wants to become. A teenager in the show describes him as worth a bazillion dollars and the saddest man you’ve ever seen. Everyone in the series has money and wants more of something else, whether it’s legacy, power, impact or control.

I hear this constantly. A client of mine had led teams through back-to-back acquisitions and an exit, and he told me it still didn’t feel like enough. I didn’t tell him he had a problem or suggest he look for happiness outside work. He brought the questions to me, and my job was to help him unpack them. He wanted to know:

He chose his career goal, C-suite roles and added conditions that had never been on the list, such as remote or hybrid work, time with his school-aged children and partner, real work-life balance and room to travel. Eventually, he landed a role on those terms.

Duncan blackmails his therapist. I’ve never been blackmailed by a client, and I’m confident that’s the norm. The jargon also runs heavier than real life. Silicon Valley loves shorthand, but “quant ben” for quantifiable benefits was new to me.

The biggest stretch comes from Ethan Stern (Patrick Gilmore), Orson’s biological father, who is back in Baltimore while his son gets shipped off to Palo Alto. He tells Orson the world there is not the real world, but Silicon Valley is the world for a lot of people. Meta alone reports 3.6 billion people using its apps on an average day. Carl also claims that every billionaire eventually decides whether to save the world or control it, and that “most of us go Dr. Evil.” In my experience, most of the leaders I work with are focused on making a positive difference. The bad ones just get more publicity.

One line made me laugh out loud, and it turned out to be accurate. In the first episode, Anushka Bhattachera-Phister (Meaghan Rath) refers to Xander, the AI her husband Martin (Simon Helberg) is building, as “a digital child.” I’ve heard a tech executive use that exact phrase. The realtor telling Dr. Felder “$2.5 mil is a steal around here” got me too, as did their portrayal of office space costing $175 an hour. That’s why I coach from my home office over Zoom.

It’s lonely at the top, and the show gets that right in every storyline. Each major character is isolated, and none of them says so out loud. Some leaders I work with run from that conversation with themselves. The ones I’ve watched make progress bring it to someone else instead, whether that’s a coach, mentor or therapist, and speak honestly about their feelings.

The Audacity packs stock fraud, blackmail, ayahuasca, a tungsten cube and a wildfire into eight hour-long episodes, and AMC renewed it for a second season before the first one even aired. I’d give it a thumbs up as a composite portrait of working in tech, two thumbs up for entertainment and a thumbs down for anyone hoping to feel better about the industry afterward. Nobody was watching it for that anyway. Remember, you’ve got this!

I’ve coached tech leaders for more than a decade, including people who reported directly to Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Steve Huffman, and I can’t recall a client ever saying the word “humiliation” to me. #5367. Americans fear the worst after Pentagon doomsday prepping, ‘Black October’ cyberattacks, stock crash, spy scandal, Microsoft outage, and airport chaos

The past month has seemed like one battle after another, and it’s taking a toll on Americans who are starting to feel like everything is breaking at once.

October began ominously after the Pentagon launched an initiative on Sept. 30 called FORTRESS, which seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military base can run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains.

The plan envisions portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage, and microgrids that can disconnect bases from civilian power networks. It also calls for strategic reserves of munitions, fuel, critical minerals, electronics, spare parts, and medical supplies.

Then came a month of cyberattacks that hit hundreds of companies and institutions around the world. Targets included the Federal Election Commission, Sony, John Deere, Oracle Health, Burger King Japan, and the State Bank of India. The hacking spree was so widespread that it was dubbed “Black October.”

Cyberattacks even reached freezers across Europe and at U.S. military bases, with temperatures hiked high enough to spoil frozen food. France blamed the freezer hacks on Iran, which had previously vowed to retaliate against the U.S. and its allies for the war against the regime.

Adding to the unease was the U.K. government’s campaign urging Britons to keep canned food, bottled water, and cash on hand to get through three days of disruption.

Cybersecurity experts also rushed to fix vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language that’s used in nearly 70% of all websites. The National Security Agency warned the vulnerability could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers. Black October reached a crescendo with the largest crypto heist in history: North Korean hackers swiped $6.3 billion from Binance.

Days later, U.S. voters delivered a stunning rebuke to President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans, as Democrats swept races across GOP strongholds in midterm elections. Several candidates who campaigned on pushing back against data centers rode to victory in the so-called blue tsunami, threatening the AI boom that has powered the U.S. economy and stock market in recent years.

While stocks jumped in the immediate aftermath of Election Day, they suddenly tumbled with top indexes suffering the worst losses since Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariff shock in April 2025. Tech companies saw especially steep declines, and on Nov. 5 the Nasdaq 100 marked its worst single-day performance since March 2020—during the early panic over COVID-19.

Markets regained some ground as dip-buyers rushed in to snap up bargains. But then another bombshell came last weekend, when Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. After a separate affair with an Nvidia employee emerged days later, Huang stepped down as CEO from the AI chip giant he cofounded.

Nvidia stock plunged as markets anticipated tougher restrictions on its chip exports, while the sudden loss of Huang, who hadn’t designated a successor, put at risk all the “circular” financing deals he made with companies throughout the AI ecosystem.

In addition to the stock carnage, the spy scandal also highlighted China’s extensive industrial espionage efforts, which could tip the scales in the AI race that may determine economic and military supremacy.

Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Wednesday. Then on Thursday, Microsoft’s suite of software tools went offline, shutting down email and calendars as well as collaboration and AI functions. The company attributed the outage to a technical issue—and not to cyberattacks or AI.

“The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” it said.

Workers around the world felt paralyzed by the Microsoft outage, so many suspected it had a role in the FAA’s order to ground planes at all U.S. airports on Friday, forcing airlines to cancel or delay thousands of flights.

Microsoft said it had no indication that the ground stop was related to its global outage. The FAA later blamed its drastic move on an upgrade from copper wire to fiber-optic cables at a communications node in Arkansas.

The changeover caused routers across the air traffic control system to be flooded with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Because it disrupted some radar feeds, the FAA ordered the ground stop to ensure safety. It was lifted about four hours later.

Still, when the problem first emerged on Friday, it was so alarming the White House situation room and national security apparatus went into action.

The FBI, the director of national intelligence, the Defense Department, the NSA, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency all got on a call to compare notes. They didn’t see any chatter or “footprints” that are normally associated with a cyberattack, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. But on Sunday, he didn’t completely rule one out.

“We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor,” Duffy told Fox News Sunday. “But we’re open. If we see something else, we’re going to continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement.”

The cumulative effect of all the disruptions has put Americans on edge. A cruise ship that overturned in New Orleans after getting hit by a tanker on Friday didn’t help either.

Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, who was stuck at Newark Liberty International Airport, told the Associated Press “There’s a lot of weird stuff going on” and wondered if it was all part of some form of attack.

“We talk about how wars aren’t done with bombs anymore,” he added. “They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy.”

Maxine Gustafson, a 34-year-old physician assistant from Minneapolis, was at Chicago’s O’Hare airport when she admitted to the AP that the week’s mishaps made her feel afraid and helpless.

“It makes you think, like, is this a cyberattack?” she said. “We don’t have control over a lot of this stuff.”

Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune, where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

#5366. Agentic AI Governance Doesn’t Have to Be Complicated. Most of It Comes Down to These 4 Questions.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Agentic AI governance frameworks look complicated, but every one asks your business the same four questions.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Leaders face a growing stack of agentic AI governance frameworks. Underneath the jargon, every one of them asks the same four questions about your AI agents.

When I ask leadership teams which agentic AI governance framework they follow, the answers usually split along geography. Some point to Singapore, some to the European Union (EU) and some to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in the U.S. Most assume these frameworks compete, and many conclude governance can wait until the rules settle.

The frameworks do not compete, and governance cannot wait. Underneath the acronyms, every serious framework for AI agents asks the same four questions: what an agent may do, who answers for it, how it can be stopped and how the business proves it. A company that can answer them has done most of what any framework will ask.

The 2026 AI Index from Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered AI shows why. AI agents completed 66.3% of tasks on a leading computer-use benchmark in 2025, up from about 5% in 2024, while reported AI incidents reached a record 362, up from 233 the year before.

My work advising retail and consumer companies across the Americas, Europe, Australasia and Japan gives me a split-screen view of this debate. The vocabulary changes from market to market, but the questions boards and regulators ask about agents are remarkably similar.

The landscape is smaller than it seems. In January, at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) launched what it describes as the first governance framework built specifically for agentic AI. NIST’s voluntary AI Risk Management Framework organizes the work into four functions, and researchers at the University of California, Berkeley published an agentic AI profile built on that structure in February.

Two other pieces complete the picture. ISO/IEC 42001, from the International Organization for Standardization, is the first global standard for an AI management system, and the law sets a floor in some markets. California’s rules on automated decision-making apply to covered businesses starting January 1, 2027, and the EU’s AI Act requires human oversight of high-risk systems, with most of those obligations now applying from December 2027.

Singapore’s framework starts here. It asks organizations to choose suitable use cases first and then limit each agent’s autonomy and its access to tools and data. The World Economic Forum proposed in May that every agent carry an authorization profile recording what it may do, under what conditions and with what oversight.

In practice, that means a written mandate before an agent goes live. It should state what the agent may decide alone, what it may spend or promise and when it must hand a case to a person. A customer service agent might issue goodwill credits up to a fixed amount but hand off any conversation that involves a safety issue or a legal claim.

The mandate should also name what the agent is measured on. Economists Bengt Holmström and Paul Milgrom showed in 1991 that when some duties are easy to measure and others are not, strong rewards on the measurable ones pull effort away from the rest. An agent scored only on speed will optimize speed, and the customer relationship quietly becomes the unmeasured duty.

Every framework insists that accountability stays with people. Singapore calls for checkpoints where human approval is required, and NIST places accountability structures inside its “govern” function.

California’s rules offer the most precise standard. Human involvement there means a reviewer who knows how to interpret and use the technology’s output, analyzes it alongside other relevant information and has the authority to make or change the decision. Covered or not, any business can use that as the job description for an agent’s owner.

One consumer business I advised gave its service agent a generous credit budget and no single owner. Credits crept upward for weeks because each team assumed another was watching. The fix took one meeting: a named owner, a ceiling and a weekly report.

The EU’s Article 14 states this question most clearly. It requires that the people overseeing a high-risk system can monitor it, override its output and intervene or halt it safely, for example with a “stop” button.

Singapore’s framework calls for technical controls across the agent’s life cycle, including baseline testing and restricting access to approved services. NIST launched an initiative this year that focuses in part on identity and authorization for AI agents.

This matters because an agent using an employee’s login leaves no clear record of who acted. The practical version is simple: Give each agent its own credentials, log every action and test the off switch before launch rather than during an incident. A short weekly review of what each agent decided, escalated and reversed will show whether its limits are too tight, too loose or simply unclear.

The final question is the one customers, auditors and boards eventually ask. ISO/IEC 42001 answers it by treating AI governance as a management system, embedded in everyday processes alongside existing quality and information security systems. Singapore’s fourth dimension adds transparency and training for the people who use agents.

Boards are already asking. More than 62% of directors in the National Association of Corporate Directors’ 2025 survey said they now set aside agenda time for full-board AI discussions. A one-page register listing every agent, its owner, its limits and its last review gives those discussions something concrete to examine.

The first three steps are simple. Build the agent register this quarter, starting with the agents already handling customers or money. Choose one framework as the spine, NIST for its widely used vocabulary or ISO/IEC 42001 when customers expect certification, and borrow Singapore’s agent-specific controls.

Then check the legal floor in each market where the business operates. Agents will keep getting more capable, and the frameworks will keep multiplying. The four questions will not change, and the leaders who can answer them for every agent at work will find that compliance becomes a byproduct of good management rather than a project of its own.

Some point to Singapore, some to the European Union (EU) and some to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in the U.S. Most assume these frameworks compete, and many conclude governance can wait until the rules settle.

The frameworks do not compete, and governance cannot wait. Underneath the acronyms, every serious framework for AI agents asks the same four questions: what an agent may do, who answers for it, how it can be stopped and how the business proves it. A company that can answer them has done most of what any framework will ask.

#5365. ‘We’re still here’: Technology Access Foundation keeps opening doors for students of color, 30 years later

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:11 amNovember 12, 2026 at 11:17 am

Editor’s note: Microsoft, which underwrites GeekWire’s Impact Series, is a longtime TAF supporter. The company was not involved in this story.

Back in the fall of 2002, then-Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer wrapped up a luncheon speech at Seattle’s Rainier Club by asking a question that few people in the room expected — least of all the college freshman he directed it to.

“So you want an internship this summer?” he asked Miya McClain, as she remembers it.

She was Miya Sneed then, 18 and homesick at Mills College in Oakland, Calif. She had come home to speak for Technology Access Foundation, the Seattle nonprofit where she had gone from knowing nothing about computers to building software and leading a team of student interns. Earlier in the luncheon program, she had shown the crowd a scheduling system she built for TAF.

Microsoft had planned the offer in advance and already had her resume, but she had no idea what was coming. A Seattle Times photographer caught the look of shock on her face, and the photo ran the next day on the front of the newspaper’s business section.

That internship, the first of two, led to a full-time job at Microsoft after college. She spent eight years there before moving into product leadership roles at Nordstrom, Cisco and Smartsheet. Today McClain is senior vice president of product management at SumerSports, a sports analytics company.

“Most of my jobs came through connections with TAF,” she said, crediting the organization for repeatedly “opening doors I didn’t even know could be opened.”

That’s the path Trish Millines Dziko had in mind when she left Microsoft 30 years ago to start TAF with her partner, Jill Hull Dziko: teach kids of color to work with technology, and get them hired by tech companies.

But about eight years in, she saw a problem. TAF’s interns were thriving, she said, but many couldn’t get into college computer science or engineering courses because their high schools had already steered them into lower-level math and science.

To change that, TAF would need to reach students by sixth grade, inside the schools.

So TAF went into public education. The organization, which marked its 30th anniversary Oct. 1, now co-manages a public middle and high school in Federal Way, Wash., and coaches teachers in other public schools.

“No matter what our kids do, we teach them to use STEM skills. They have to critically think. They have to solve problems. … They have to communicate. They have to lead.”

Executive director, Technology Access Foundation

Working with entire schools, rather than kids who signed up for a tech program, changed the goal, too. The focus now is on skills students can use in any field, whether or not it’s tech.

Students learn science, technology, engineering and math through projects that combine subjects and put classroom lessons to use. In 2020, for example, two students at TAF’s Federal Way school turned a gardening robot into a model 3D printer using a cake-frosting syringe, a threaded rod and a motor, as GeekWire reported at the time.

“What we want to make sure is, no matter what our kids do, we teach them to use STEM skills,” Millines Dziko said. “They have to critically think. They have to solve problems. … They have to communicate. They have to lead.”

The shift has cost TAF money. The organization has missed out on larger funding opportunities, Millines Dziko said, because it isn’t focused solely on tech and isn’t growing as fast as some funders would like. In the early 2010s, as education philanthropy flowed to charter schools, TAF couldn’t raise enough to open the additional schools it had planned.

“But we stuck with what was true, and what works for our kids,” she said, “and we’re still here.”

Millines Dziko grew up in New Jersey, raised by a single mother who cleaned floors for a living. She told the Seattle P-I in 1995 that she believed she’d been placed in a lower-level math class because of her race. She took summer-school classes to work her way into honors.

She studied computer science at Monmouth College on a basketball scholarship and began working at Microsoft in 1988 as the first tester on SQL Server. “She was always a force to be reckoned with,” said Bob Muglia, the longtime Microsoft executive who hired her, speaking with GeekWire at the organization’s 30th anniversary party in October. His foundation now supports TAF.

She later moved into a diversity role and took over Microsoft’s high school internship program, making it technical and filling it almost entirely with Seattle kids of color. When she pushed the company to reach students earlier, she said, “the attitude was, it’s not broken, so let’s not fix it.”

Then her partner, Jill Hull Dziko, a social worker in Seattle Public Schools’ behavior-disorder classrooms, brought seven or eight middle schoolers to campus. They were rowdy on the shuttle ride over and went silent when they walked into a room of high school interns testing a new handheld computer.

On the way back, Millines Dziko recalled, they were saying, “I want to be an engineer. I want to do what they did.”

She left Microsoft in August 1996 and put $150,000 of her own money into TAF. If she didn’t help others, she told the P-I the next year, her late mother “would want me to have my butt kicked.”

TAF set up in a Columbia City storefront next to a Taco del Mar. When they first opened the door, she said, they could see the basement through the subfloor, and the staff wired the network themselves. The first students started after-school classes in 1997, training for paid summer internships.

McClain joined the second class as she entered ninth grade, along with her older sister. Millines Dziko taught them to take apart a computer and write their first programs. “She’s encouraging, but she’s also very strict,” McClain said. “We all got jobs that summer, so obviously she taught us something.”

In 2000, TAF started a program for younger students called TechStart. At the anniversary party in October, Sherry Williams, TAF’s executive director of operations, who joined in 1997 as its fourth employee, told the crowd about a young girl who was afraid of math. The girl’s mother brought her every afternoon, and the girl kept working at it.

One day she walked in wearing a T-shirt that said “I love math.”

“Although her school wasn’t serving her, in our after-school program, she was being served,” Williams said. “And she knew she could do anything after that.”

TAF opened a public school, TAF Academy, with Federal Way Public Schools in 2008. Mike Miles, one of its first ninth-graders, went reluctantly. The school looked way too small, he told the Federal Way Mirror the following year. “I didn’t want to have six kids in my class, but my parents made me go anyway.”

He was ahead in math, and the new school couldn’t offer the class he needed, so he spent his first year in the back of the room teaching himself from a textbook.

The next year, TAF arranged for him to take math at another public school down the street. Looking back as a parent, he said in a recent interview, he appreciates that the school was willing to “swallow your pride a little” and acknowledge that it couldn’t give him what he needed. He got the math education there, and where he is today, he said, is “better than what I ever could have expected.”

Miles, now 32, graduated in 2012 with TAF Academy’s first class, earned a business degree at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and leads data teams at a cybersecurity startup in the Washington, D.C., area.

He remembers sitting in a circle in social studies, discussing the 2012 killing of Trayvon Martin, an unarmed Black teenager in Florida, and learning to keep disagreements from turning into “a shouting match,” a skill he relies on in his work now.

Federal Way wasn’t the original plan. TAF spent two years designing a school for Seattle Public Schools, and in 2006 it proposed one for Rainier Beach High School, first as a replacement for the school and then as an academy inside the building.

Many students and teachers saw it as a takeover. Teachers worried the academy would drain resources from the existing school, and families objected that the district had discussed the proposal for a year without telling them. At a packed community meeting that November, there was shouting, and the PTSA president walked out with dozens of students, The Seattle Times reported.

“It was just the dumbest and the most frustrating thing I had ever been through,” Millines Dziko said in a recent interview. “I said we’re done, no more.”

Federal Way Superintendent Tom Murphy read about it, called her and came up to Seattle to meet. After a couple of hours, she said, he told her, “You belong in Federal Way.” TAF is now working with its fifth superintendent there, she said.

The lowest point, she said, came around 2012, when TAF had to lay off staff for the second time. Education philanthropy was pouring into charter schools, a planned expansion into Renton had stalled for lack of money, she said, and TAF had just moved into a new building.

She recalled seeing reports that only a small share of major philanthropic funding went to nonprofits led by people of color, and she started asking herself a question. “Is me being a leader of this organization gonna hold us back from getting funding? Would it be better if we had someone who was white to lead the organization?”

She talked it over with Williams and Zithri Saleem, two of her top leaders, and “we almost went down that road,” she said. But she reconsidered. “That’s not the answer either,” she said. Instead, TAF had to “get out there and show them,” and find other people interested in its work.

Seattle came back around after Denise Juneau became superintendent. In 2020, the school board approved a TAF partnership at Washington Middle School in the Central District. Three years later, facing a budget shortfall, the district cut it, as GeekWire reported at the time. “It’s solely about money,” Millines Dziko told The Seattle Times then.

Asked whether she could see herself working with Seattle Public Schools again, she said, “No.” The district has “way too many problems,” she said, and dealing with them “takes our energy away from places where we could be having impact.”

In 2024, TAF was among the nonprofits chosen in MacKenzie Scott’s open call, after a process that included peer review. TAF expected $1 million and got $2 million. “It wasn’t the money; it was the belief in our work,” Millines Dziko said.

TAF used $500,000 for operating needs it had been saving for and put the rest in a certificate of deposit, she said.

TAF reported about $4 million in revenue and $5 million in expenses in its Form 990 for the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2025, and ended the year with about $11.4 million in net assets. Millines Dziko said the organization’s annual budget is now close to $7 million, and its fundraising team raises about 93% of it, mostly through grants.

TAF Academy had been recognized for test-score gains. It was named a School of Distinction in 2012 for improvement in middle-school reading and math. In 2016, the district cited three consecutive years of recognition as one reason for merging it with Saghalie Middle School. The combined school, TAF@Saghalie, opened in 2017, and TAF co-manages it with the district.

TAF@Saghalie’s four-year graduation rate for the class of 2025 was above 88.5%, compared with 82.6% statewide, according to state data. On state tests in 2024-25, 17% of the school’s low-income students who took the tests in grades 6–8 and 10 met the English language arts standard and 11% met the math standard, compared with 30% and 15% for low-income students in the same grades across Federal Way Public Schools.

Millines Dziko argues that standardized tests don’t measure what matters. They assume every student had a teacher who covered everything on the exam, she said, and “they demean kids,” charting their academic course as early as third grade.

TAF trains teachers to track each student’s growth and is building its own way to document it. Teachers score students from 1 to 4 against standards, backed by photos of projects and samples of student work. The data lives in the modern version of SQL Server, the Microsoft database Millines Dziko was hired to test in 1988.

The system is in the third year of a pilot. Only selected teachers are participating, and TAF is still working out how much time teachers can spend documenting students’ work while teaching, she said. TAF is bringing in an evaluator from the University of Washington Bothell to review the pilot, she said.

Millines Dziko’s goal is for every district in the country to use it, and for standardized tests to “go out the window,” with the money states spend on them going to teacher training instead. “I believe it will,” she said.

Miles liked the project-based learning but said he found gaps in his preparation when he got to college. “I took physics at TAF Academy, took physics in college, and I was not prepared,” he said. What he got in return, he said, was “a different way of thinking.”

TAF looked like a program for teaching technical skills, he said, but “they taught kids how to be people.” He tries to pass that on to his son, he said, including putting others first and using his gifts to help others.

TransformED, TAF’s teacher-coaching program, places a full-time coach in a partner school for five years. It works with five schools now and plans to add 10 more over five years, at about $200,000 per school per year, Millines Dziko said. In September, TAF hired a former Atlanta principal, Donya Loyd Kemp, to lead it, as GeekWire reported.

Millines Dziko is wary of the rush to bring AI into classrooms. Students can use it to find sources, she said, but then they have to investigate those sources themselves. “It should be used as a tool to gather quickly, so I can now use most of my time doing the thinking.”

Millines Dziko said the region’s tech companies should invest in public schools as a way to attract and keep families here, not just with donated products and the occasional volunteer day. “That’s performative,” she said.

What she wants are lasting relationships, like the ones TAF has with smaller companies that come back to its schools every year to give students real problems to solve. As for the big tech companies, “I need them to be more about pouring into instead of extracting out of,” she said.

Millines Dziko turns 70 in July. For the past year and a half, she said, Williams and Joshua Halsey, TAF’s executive director of education, have taken on more of the leadership, freeing her to spend more time raising money and building relationships.

She doesn’t expect to stop working, she said, predicting that she’ll never retire.

At the 30th anniversary party, she hugged about three-quarters of the room, by her count. Looking around at her former students, many with kids of their own, it hit her.

“This is 30 years, man, and look at y’all,” she said, recalling the moment later. “Y’all are good.”
